name: Homer

claims.text: The Iliad and Odyssey emerged from a long oral tradition using formulaic composition.
The poems reached something close to their present form in the 8th–7th centuries BC.
Some objects described in the poems reflect genuine Bronze Age material culture.
A single poet named Homer composed both epics.
Homer was a blind bard from Chios.

summary: The name attached to the Iliad and the Odyssey — the foundational poems of Greek literature, and the closest thing the Greek world had to scripture.
significance: Homeric epic supplied Greeks with a shared heroic past, a common poetic language, and the moral vocabulary that tragedy and philosophy argued with for centuries.
body:
Homer is the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, the epics that took shape in the 8th and early 7th centuries BC, probably in Ionia on the coast of Asia Minor. Nothing certain is known about him. Seven cities claimed to be his birthplace, and tradition made him a blind singer from Chios or Smyrna. Whether one poet composed both epics, or either, is still debated.

What is clear is that the poems come from a long tradition of oral poetry. In the 1930s Milman Parry showed that their repeated phrases — "swift-footed Achilles", "the wine-dark sea" — are the working tools of singers who composed as they performed, and confirmed it by recording oral epic singers in Yugoslavia who worked the same way. The modern debate about how the poems were made, the "Homeric Question", began with Friedrich August Wolf's *Prolegomena ad Homerum* of 1795.

The poems' world is layered. Bronze Age objects, such as the boar's-tusk helmet and the tall body shield, appear beside later Iron Age customs, such as cremation, and a society closer to the poet's own time. They are best read not as a record of the Mycenaean age but as a memory of it, reshaped over centuries of retelling.

For the Greeks, Homer was simply "the poet": the foundation of education, the source of their shared heroic past, and the text that later poets and philosophers argued with. The Homeric Hymns were also credited to him in antiquity, but are the work of later poets.

name: Hesiod

claims.text: The Theogony and Works and Days are the work of a single identifiable poetic persona.
The Greek succession myth shows structural borrowing from Near Eastern models.
Hesiod was roughly contemporary with the composition of the Homeric poems.
Works and Days includes the earliest surviving version of the myth of the Five Ages of Man, from a lost Golden Age to the poet's own harsher Iron Age.

summary: A Boeotian farmer-poet whose Theogony organised the Greek gods into a genealogy, and whose Works and Days is the first personal voice in European literature.
significance: Gave Greek religion a systematic cosmogony and supplied the myth of the Five Ages, the Prometheus story and Pandora in their canonical forms.
body:
Hesiod (active c. 700 BC) was a Greek poet from Ascra in Boeotia, author of the *Theogony* and *Works and Days*.

Unlike Homer, Hesiod tells us about himself: his father emigrated from Aeolian Cyme to the "miserable village" of Ascra, and his brother Perses cheated him in an inheritance dispute settled by corrupt "bribe-swallowing kings". Works and Days is addressed to that brother — part farming almanac, part moral protest.

The Theogony traces the cosmos from Chaos through Gaia and Ouranos to the reign of Zeus, in a succession myth with clear parallels in the Hittite Song of Kumarbi and Babylonian Enuma Elish — evidence of Near Eastern influence on early Greek thought. Works and Days also gives the earliest surviving version of the myth of the Five Ages of Man, a declining sequence running from a lost, effortless Golden Age through Silver and Bronze to the poet's own harsher, toil-filled Iron Age, a pessimistic framework for human history that later Greek and Roman writers returned to repeatedly.

name: Sappho

claims.text: Sappho composed monodic lyric poetry on Lesbos in the late 7th and early 6th centuries BC.
Her surviving corpus is overwhelmingly fragmentary, largely recovered from papyri.
Her poetry expresses erotic desire directed at women.
Sappho led a formal circle or school of young women.
Sappho leapt to her death from the Leucadian cliff.
A significant new Sappho papyrus, containing the substantially complete "Brothers Poem", was published as recently as 2014.

summary: The most celebrated lyric poet of antiquity, whose songs of desire and loss survive almost entirely in fragments.
significance: Turned Greek poetry from public narrative to interior feeling. Plato reportedly called her the tenth Muse.
body:
Sappho (c. 630–570 BC) was a lyric poet from the island of Lesbos, off the coast of Asia Minor, probably from Eresos or Mytilene. Little is securely known of her life: she had brothers, including Charaxus, and probably a daughter, Cleis, and an ancient chronicle says she spent a period in exile in Sicily.

She composed songs for a single voice with the lyre, in her local Aeolic dialect, including the stanza form now called Sapphic. Many address women by name with intense erotic feeling — the origin of the words "sapphic" and "lesbian" — and others concern weddings, family, memory and the gods. Ancient scholars collected them in nine books. Plato is said to have called her the tenth Muse.

Most of her work is lost. Only the *Hymn to Aphrodite* survives almost complete; the rest comes in fragments quoted by later writers or recovered from papyrus scraps found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt. New texts are still emerging, such as the "Brothers Poem" published in 2014, though the papyrus's provenance has since been seriously questioned.

Later ancient biographies invented much of her life, including the story that she leapt from a cliff for love of a ferryman named Phaon. Her poems, which turned Greek poetry towards personal feeling, have been read and imitated from Catullus to the present.

name: Solon

claims.text: Solon abolished debt-slavery for Athenian citizens.
Solon replaced birth with property qualification for holding office.
Fragments of Solon's own political poetry survive.
Solon redistributed land.
Solon travelled abroad for ten years after his reforms specifically so Athenians could not pressure him into amending his own laws.
He divided Athenian citizens into four property-based census classes that determined eligibility for office.

summary: Athenian lawgiver of 594 BC who cancelled debts, abolished debt-slavery and opened political office by wealth rather than birth.
significance: His reforms broke the aristocratic monopoly on Athenian politics and laid the legal groundwork that Cleisthenes later turned into democracy.
body:
Solon (c. 638–558 BC) was an Athenian statesman and poet, appointed archon in 594 BC with special powers to resolve a crisis. Poor farmers were falling into debt to the rich, losing their land and being enslaved for debt or sold abroad, and Athens was close to civil war.

His *seisachtheia*, "shaking off of burdens", cancelled existing debts secured on land or persons, freed Athenians enslaved for debt and brought back those sold abroad, and banned debt slavery for the future. He divided the citizens into four classes by wealth, measured in farm produce, instead of birth: the highest offices were open only to the richest, but even the poorest, the *thetes*, could attend the Assembly and sit in the popular law court. Any citizen could now bring a prosecution on behalf of someone wronged. He also replaced most of Draco's harsh law code.

Having passed his laws, Solon left Athens for ten years, so that he could not be pressured into changing them. Fragments of his own poetry survive, in which he defends having refused to satisfy either the rich or the poor completely.

His reforms did not end the conflict — Peisistratus later seized power as tyrant — but they broke the aristocracy's monopoly of power and laid the foundations on which Cleisthenes later built Athenian democracy.

name: Peisistratus

claims.text: Peisistratus ruled Athens as tyrant, with interruptions, from 561 to 527 BC.
The City Dionysia acquired its dramatic competitions under the Peisistratids.
Peisistratus commissioned an official written text of Homer.
He pursued a moderate policy of leaving existing Athenian laws and offices largely intact rather than replacing them.

summary: Tyrant of Athens who seized power three times and, paradoxically, strengthened the institutions that later made democracy possible.
significance: His public building, festival patronage and rural courts weakened the regional aristocracies whose power Cleisthenes would finally dismantle.
body:
Peisistratus took power in 561 BC, was twice expelled, and finally ruled securely from 546 until his death. Herodotus tells the story of his second return: he entered Athens with a tall woman dressed as Athena in a chariot, and the Athenians accepted the divine endorsement.

He expanded the Panathenaic festival, gave the City Dionysia its competitive dramatic contests, sent circuit judges into the countryside, and struck the first substantial Athenian silver coinage. The tradition that he had the Homeric poems fixed in an official text is later and uncertain. His son Hippias ruled harshly after Hipparchus was assassinated, and was expelled in 510 BC.

Unlike many tyrants of the period, Peisistratus was notably careful to leave Solon's legal framework and the existing offices of Athenian government formally in place, ruling through influence and patronage rather than wholesale institutional replacement — a restraint that later allowed reformers like Cleisthenes to build democratic institutions on a legal foundation that had never actually been abolished.

name: Cleisthenes

claims.text: Cleisthenes reorganised Attica into ten tribes composed of dispersed trittyes in 508/7 BC.
The Council of 500 was created as part of these reforms.
Cleisthenes introduced ostracism.
Cleisthenes belonged to the powerful Alcmaeonid family and enlisted popular support against rival aristocrats to push his reforms through.
He is credited with securing Spartan and Delphic backing that helped expel the tyrant Hippias from Athens shortly before his reforms.

summary: Architect of the Athenian democratic constitution in 508/7 BC, who rebuilt the citizen body from scratch to break the power of regional clans.
significance: Created the institutional machinery — ten artificial tribes, the Council of 500, the deme registry — that made mass self-government workable.
body:
Cleisthenes (active c. 525–507 BC) was an Athenian aristocrat of the powerful Alcmaeonid family who created the democratic constitution of Athens in 508/7 BC. After the tyrant Hippias was expelled in 510 BC, with Spartan help that the Alcmaeonids had encouraged through the Delphic oracle, Cleisthenes lost a power struggle with his rival Isagoras. He then turned to the ordinary people for support, promising reform. When Isagoras called in Spartan troops, the Athenian people rose and drove them out, and Cleisthenes carried his reforms.

He reorganised the whole citizen body. Attica was divided into about 140 local units called demes, grouped into thirty *trittyes* in three zones — city, coast and inland. Ten new tribes were formed, each combining one trittys from each zone, so that every tribe mixed men from all over Attica and no aristocratic family could dominate a tribe through local influence. Citizenship was registered in the deme, and men were officially identified by their deme rather than their father's name.

A new Council of 500, with fifty men from each tribe chosen by lot, prepared business for the Assembly of all citizens. The ten tribes also provided the army's regiments and, from 501 BC, the ten generals. Ostracism, the vote to exile a citizen for ten years, is traditionally credited to him too.

Cleisthenes then disappears from the record, but his system remained the framework of Athenian democracy for nearly two centuries.

name: Draco

claims.text: Draco produced Athens' first written law code, traditionally dated 621/0 BC.
A 409/8 BC re-inscription of Draco's homicide law survives.
Draco's code prescribed death for almost all offences.
Draco's law was the first Athenian legal code applied in writing to all citizens alike, rather than left to unwritten aristocratic custom.

summary: Author of Athens' first written law code in 621 BC — famously severe, and the origin of the word "draconian".
significance: Writing the law down took its interpretation out of the exclusive hands of aristocratic judges, however harsh its content.
body:
Draco was the first lawgiver of Athens, who around 621 BC wrote down the city's laws for the first time.

Ancient tradition held that Draco prescribed death for almost every offence, and that his laws were written in blood rather than ink. Solon repealed nearly all of them.

The exception is the homicide law, which survived and was re-inscribed in 409/8 BC — a copy of that inscription still exists. It is notably sophisticated: it distinguishes intentional from unintentional killing, sets out procedures for exile and pardon by the victim's family, and takes blood vengeance out of private hands. Its public display also made a rule available for scrutiny beyond an aristocratic judge's memory. The written code, not its proverbial severity, was the lasting achievement.

Before Draco, Athenian law existed mainly as unwritten custom interpreted at the discretion of aristocratic magistrates, which gave the elite considerable latitude and left ordinary citizens dependent on memory and social standing to know what the law actually required of them. Draco's written code, whatever its severity, changed that basic relationship by fixing rules in a form anyone could, in principle, consult and hold officials to — a structural shift in Athenian governance that mattered more in the long run than the harshness for which his name became proverbial.

name: Lycurgus of Sparta

claims.text: Spartans attributed their constitution and social system to a lawgiver named Lycurgus.
The Spartan system developed gradually rather than being designed at once.
Lycurgus was a single historical individual.
Spartans traditionally dated Lycurgus's reforms to a period of severe civil unrest that the new system was designed to resolve.

summary: The legendary lawgiver to whom Spartans attributed their entire social and military system.
significance: Whether or not he existed, "Lycurgus" is how Spartans explained and legitimised the most distinctive society in Greece.
body:
Lycurgus was the lawgiver to whom the Spartans credited their whole way of life. Ancient writers placed him anywhere between the 11th and 8th centuries BC, and Plutarch begins his biography by admitting that nothing about him can be stated without dispute — not his dates, his family or his deeds. Many historians doubt that he existed at all.

Tradition said he had travelled to Crete, Ionia and Egypt, and that his reforms, approved by the oracle at Delphi, ended a period of lawlessness in Sparta. The "Great Rhetra", an oracle-based statement of the constitution quoted by Plutarch, set out the roles of the two kings, the council of elders and the assembly. He was also credited with the *agoge*, the state training of boys; the common messes in which citizens ate; the division of land into equal lots; the ban on gold and silver money; and simple living for all citizens.

In reality this system was almost certainly built up over generations, much of it in the 7th and 6th centuries BC after Sparta's conquest of Messenia. Crediting it all to one wise founder backed by Apollo gave it an authority that gradual change could not.

Lycurgus was worshipped as a hero in Sparta. For later Greek and Roman writers, from Xenophon to Plutarch, he became the model of the wise lawgiver who shapes a whole society.

name: Thales of Miletus

claims.text: Thales proposed water as the fundamental principle of things.
A solar eclipse visible in Anatolia occurred on 28 May 585 BC.
Thales successfully predicted that eclipse.
Thales is also credited with estimating the height of the Egyptian pyramids by measuring shadows.

summary: The first Greek to explain nature without invoking the gods — traditionally the first philosopher and first scientist.
significance: Begins the Ionian tradition of natural explanation from which Greek science, and eventually European science, descends.
body:
Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC) lived in the wealthy Ionian city of Miletus, on the coast of Asia Minor, and was counted by later Greeks among the Seven Sages and as the first philosopher. He wrote nothing that survives, and what is known of him comes from later writers, above all Aristotle and Herodotus.

He held that everything comes from water, and that the Earth floats on water. The answer is wrong, but the question was new: asking what the world is made of, and answering in terms of natural materials rather than stories about gods, is the founding step of Greek natural philosophy. His successors at Miletus, Anaximander and Anaximenes, carried the enquiry on.

Herodotus says Thales predicted a solar eclipse that halted a battle between the Lydians and the Medes; astronomers date such an eclipse to 28 May 585 BC. How he could have predicted it is unclear. Other stories credit him with measuring the height of the Egyptian pyramids from their shadows and with geometrical theorems, and Aristotle tells how he made a fortune by renting all the olive presses before a good harvest, to show that philosophers could be rich if they wished.

name: Pythagoras

claims.text: Pythagoras founded a philosophical-religious community at Croton.
Pythagoreans identified numerical ratios underlying musical consonance.
The relation a²+b²=c² was known in Babylonian mathematics long before Pythagoras.
Pythagoras personally proved the theorem named after him.
Pythagoreans reportedly kept the discovery of irrational numbers secret, since it threatened their belief that all reality could be expressed in whole-number ratios.

summary: Founder of a religious-philosophical brotherhood in southern Italy that held number to be the substance of reality.
significance: Fused mathematics, music and mysticism into a tradition that shaped Plato profoundly and, through him, the whole Western idea of a mathematically ordered cosmos.
body:
Pythagoras left Samos for Croton around 530 BC and founded a community with strict rules — silence for initiates, communal property, dietary restrictions, and belief in the transmigration of souls. It held political power in several Italian cities before being violently suppressed.

The discovery that consonant musical intervals correspond to simple whole-number ratios (2:1, 3:2, 4:3) is the core Pythagorean insight, and appears to be genuine. The theorem bearing his name was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; whether Pythagoras proved it is unknown. Because members attributed their own discoveries to the founder, separating the man from the school may be permanently impossible. Later tradition holds that the school discovered irrational numbers — quantities, like the square root of two, that cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers — and tried to suppress the finding, since it directly threatened their core belief that whole-number ratios could describe the entire structure of reality; one legend even claims the member responsible for revealing the secret was drowned at sea for it.

name: Themistocles

claims.text: Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend the Laurion silver on a fleet of triremes.
Athenian naval power was decisive at Salamis in 480 BC.
Themistocles later took service under the Persian king.
Ostraka bearing his name survive in quantity from the Athenian Agora.
A cache of 191 ostraka against Themistocles, apparently pre-written by a small group of hands, has fuelled debate over political manipulation of ostracism votes.

summary: The Athenian who read the Delphic oracle's "wooden wall" as ships, built the fleet, and engineered the victory at Salamis.
significance: His naval policy created Athenian sea power — the basis of both the empire and the democracy that the poorest citizens, who rowed the ships, came to dominate.
body:
Themistocles (c. 524–459 BC) was the Athenian statesman who made Athens a naval power and led the Greek victory at Salamis. He came from an established but not aristocratic family, and was archon in 493 BC, when he began fortifying the harbour of Piraeus.

In 483 BC a rich new vein of silver was found at the state mines of Laurion. Themistocles persuaded the Assembly not to share it out among citizens but to build some 200 triremes, officially for a war with the island of Aegina. Three years later that fleet was Athens' defence against Xerxes. When the Persians came in 480 BC, he interpreted the Delphic oracle's "wooden wall" as the ships, had Athens evacuated, and held the Greek fleet together at Salamis. Before the battle he sent a servant to Xerxes with a false message that the Greeks were about to flee, luring the Persian fleet into the narrow straits, where its numbers counted against it.

After the war he had Athens' walls rebuilt over Spartan objections, delaying Spartan envoys while the work was rushed through. His power made enemies, and around 471 BC he was ostracised; a cache of 190 ostraka with his name, written by only a few hands, survives from an earlier vote. Condemned for treason, he fled and ended his life in the service of the Persian king Artaxerxes I, as governor of Magnesia in Asia Minor.

His navy, rowed by the poorest citizens, became the basis of Athens' empire and of its democracy.

name: Leonidas I

claims.text: A Greek force under Leonidas held Thermopylae for three days in 480 BC before being outflanked.
Around 300 Spartans, with Thespians and Thebans, remained for the final stand.
Persian arrowheads and a Greek rampart have been identified near the ancient pass.
Herodotus' figures for the size of Xerxes' army are reliable.
Leonidas belonged to the Agiad royal line and reportedly consulted an oracle prophesying that either Sparta or one of its kings must fall.

summary: Spartan king who died with his rearguard holding the pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes' army in 480 BC.
significance: The defeat became the defining Greek story of disciplined resistance against overwhelming odds, and remains one of antiquity's most durable images.
body:
Leonidas commanded a Greek force of perhaps 7,000 at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. For two days they held. Then a local, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the position. Leonidas dismissed most of the army and remained with 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans.

All the Spartans and Thespians died. Simonides' epitaph, recorded by Herodotus, is the most famous couplet in Greek: it asks the passer-by to tell the Spartans that here they lie, obedient to their words. The delay bought the Greek fleet time, and the moral effect of the stand outlasted the tactical loss by two and a half millennia. Leonidas belonged to Sparta's senior Agiad royal line, and Herodotus reports that before the campaign an oracle had warned that either the city of Sparta itself or one of its two kings must be destroyed — a prophecy Leonidas's decision to stay and die at Thermopylae is often read, in the ancient sources themselves, as deliberately fulfilling in Sparta's favour.

name: Pericles

secondaryImage.caption: Aspasia of Miletus, Pericles' companion for the last decades of his life. Their relationship scandalised Athenian opinion and made her a stock target of comic poets -- and, by the letter of Pericles' own citizenship law, their son was not legally an Athenian at all.

claims.text: Pericles was elected strategos in most years between 461 and 429 BC.
He introduced state pay for jurors.
Delian League funds were used for the Acropolis building programme.
Pericles died of the plague in 429 BC.
The Funeral Oration records Pericles' actual words.
Pericles' citizenship law of 451 BC later denied citizenship to his own son by Aspasia, until the Assembly voted an exception.

summary: The dominant Athenian politician for three decades, who rebuilt the Acropolis, extended democratic participation and led Athens into the Peloponnesian War.
significance: His name marks the height of Athenian power, and the buildings he commissioned remain the visual signature of Greek civilisation.
body:
Pericles was born around 495 BC into the Athenian aristocracy. His father Xanthippus commanded the Greek fleet at Mycale in 479 BC, and his mother belonged to the Alcmaeonids, the family of Cleisthenes, founder of the democracy. He was taught by the philosopher Anaxagoras.

From the early 450s BC until his death he was the leading figure in Athens. His power rested on being elected *strategos* (general) almost every year and on persuading the Assembly; he held no permanent office above any other citizen. Thucydides judged that Athens was "in name a democracy, but in fact rule by the first man".

He deepened the democracy, introducing pay for jurors so that poor citizens could serve. In 451 BC he carried a law limiting citizenship to children of two Athenian parents — a law that later caught his own son by Aspasia of Miletus, his partner, until the Assembly made an exception. He moved the Delian League's treasury to Athens and used allied tribute to fund the rebuilding of the Acropolis, with the Parthenon, the Propylaea and Pheidias' statue of Athena, despite critics who said Athens was dressing itself up with its allies' money.

When war with Sparta broke out in 431 BC, Pericles' strategy was to bring the people of Attica inside the walls, avoid battle on land and rely on the navy. Thucydides gives him the Funeral Oration for the first year's dead, the most famous statement of Athenian democratic ideals. But the crowded city was struck by plague in 430 BC; Pericles lost his two elder sons and died himself in 429 BC.

The great buildings of his era made his name a byword for Athens' golden age, the "Age of Pericles".

name: Aspasia of Miletus

claims.text: Aspasia was a Milesian metic who lived with Pericles and bore him a son.
Contemporary comic poets attacked her repeatedly.
She taught rhetoric or influenced Athenian intellectual circles.
She ran a brothel.
Her son with Pericles, Pericles the Younger, was later granted Athenian citizenship by special decree and served as a general.

summary: A Milesian woman in Pericles' household, credited by Plato and others with unusual influence on Athenian intellectual life.
significance: The best-documented non-royal woman of Classical Athens, and a test case for how thoroughly hostile male sources can distort a life.
body:
Aspasia (c. 470–400 BC) came from Miletus in Ionia to Athens, where she became the partner of Pericles.

As a *metic* — a resident foreigner — Aspasia was outside the restrictions binding Athenian citizen women, which is probably why she could appear in public intellectual settings at all. Plato's *Menexenus* has Socrates claim she wrote Pericles' funeral speech, though the dialogue's tone makes it hard to read straight.

Comic poets attacked her savagely, calling her a brothel-keeper and blaming her for starting two wars. These are jokes aimed at Pericles through her, not testimony. Almost everything about her comes through such filters, and the result is a figure who is unusually visible and unusually hard to see clearly.

Her son by Pericles, also named Pericles, was technically not an Athenian citizen under the very citizenship law his father had championed, since it required both parents to be Athenian. After the elder Pericles lost his legitimate sons to plague, the Athenians granted the younger Pericles citizenship by special exception, and he went on to serve as a general, later executed after the trial of the generals following Arginusae.

name: Herodotus

claims.text: Herodotus composed the Histories in the mid-5th century BC.
He explicitly distinguishes between what he was told and what he believes.
Scythian burial practices he describes have been confirmed by excavation.
His army and casualty figures are systematically exaggerated.
Herodotus personally travelled to all the places he describes.
Herodotus was born in Halicarnassus in Asia Minor, a city under Persian rule for much of his lifetime.
He is thought to have given public readings of parts of his work, including reportedly at Athens and at the Olympic Games.

summary: Author of the Histories, the first sustained prose enquiry into the human past — an account of the Persian Wars that ranges across the known world.
significance: Invented history as a genre: a named investigator, weighing evidence and reporting conflicting versions rather than reciting tradition.
body:
Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC) was born at Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum), a Greek city on the coast of Caria in south-western Asia Minor, then under Persian rule. After involvement in local politics he left his home city, travelled widely, and spent time in Athens and at Thurii, a new Athenian-led colony in southern Italy, where he may have died.

His *Histories*, written around 440–425 BC, are the first great work of history in the Western tradition. His opening sentence sets out his aim: to record his *historie* — "enquiry" — so that the great deeds of Greeks and non-Greeks would not be forgotten, and to explain why they fought each other. The book follows the rise of the Persian Empire and its wars with the Greeks, ending with the defeat of Xerxes in 480–479 BC.

Herodotus travelled to Egypt, the Black Sea, Babylon and Libya, and his descriptions of other peoples have no earlier parallel in Greek writing. He gave public readings of parts of his work. His method is to report what his informants told him, giving rival versions and marking his own doubts. He was called "the father of history" by Cicero, and "the father of lies" by critics such as Plutarch.

Archaeology has since confirmed many of his details, such as Scythian burial customs, though his numbers, especially for the Persian armies, are greatly exaggerated.

name: Thucydides

claims.text: Thucydides was an Athenian general exiled after failing to save Amphipolis in 424 BC.
His history breaks off unfinished in 411 BC.
He excluded divine causation from historical explanation.
The speeches reproduce what was actually said.
Thucydides' family held mining interests and connections in Thrace, which gave him access and property there during his exile.
His account of political breakdown during civil war at Corcyra is still widely cited in modern political science and international relations.

summary: Athenian general turned historian of the Peloponnesian War, and the founder of critical, evidence-based historical method.
significance: Stripped the gods and the marvellous out of historical explanation, replacing them with power, interest and human nature — the model for political history ever since.
body:
Thucydides came from a wealthy Athenian family with mining rights and property connections in Thrace, an inheritance that mattered enormously once his career turned against him: commanding an Athenian fleet in 424 BC, he failed to reach the strategically important city of Amphipolis before the Spartan general Brasidas took it, and was exiled for twenty years as a result. He used the exile productively rather than bitterly, travelling on the Peloponnesian side of the war as his own Thracian connections allowed and interviewing participants from both Athens and Sparta — which is precisely why the finished work reads as something closer to an even-handed inquiry than a partisan Athenian account of its own war.

He states his method explicitly and pointedly against Herodotus's example: he rejects poetic embellishment and traditional storytelling in favour of cross-checking eyewitness reports against one another, and warns his readers plainly that the result will be less immediately entertaining because of it. He intends the finished history, in his own famous phrase, as "a possession for all time" rather than a prize composition for one-off recitation. His analysis of how prolonged war corrodes ordinary language and morality — most notably his account of the vicious civil war (stasis) that tore apart Corcyra, where he observes that words themselves changed their accepted meanings to justify atrocities — is still routinely cited by modern political scientists and historians of civil conflict, and his broader account of how a rising power's growth and the fear it provokes in an established one can make war difficult to avoid has lent its name to the modern phrase "Thucydides trap," used in discussions of great-power rivalry today.

The history breaks off abruptly mid-sentence in the events of 411 BC, seven years before the war actually ended, and it fell to the historian Xenophon, among others, to pick up the narrative where Thucydides had left it.

name: Socrates

claims.text: Socrates was tried and executed in Athens in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth.
Socrates wrote nothing himself.
He served as a hoplite at Potidaea, Delium and Amphipolis.
As a member of the presiding council in 406 BC, he alone refused to allow the illegal mass trial of the Arginusae generals to proceed.
Plato's dialogues accurately report Socrates' own philosophy.
The trial was politically motivated by his association with the Thirty.
Socrates claimed to be guided by a daimonion, an inner divine sign that warned him away from certain actions.
He served without payment, unlike the professional sophists of his day, and left no writings of his own.

secondaryImage.caption: Jacques-Louis David's 1787 painting of Socrates' death, a defining later image of the philosopher.

summary: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, questioned everyone, and was executed by the democracy in 399 BC.
significance: Turned philosophy from cosmology to ethics — how one ought to live — and made cross-examination the method of philosophical enquiry.
body:
Socrates was born in Athens around 470 BC, the son of a stonemason, Sophroniscus, and a midwife, Phaenarete. He lived through Athens' greatest years and its defeat in the Peloponnesian War, and spent his life in the city's streets and gymnasia, questioning anyone who would talk to him. He wrote nothing.

His method was cross-examination. He asked people who claimed to know what courage, justice or piety were to define them, then showed that their answers contradicted each other. He said that when the oracle at Delphi declared no one wiser than him, he set out to test it, and concluded that his only advantage was knowing that he did not know. Unlike the paid teachers called sophists, he took no fees and offered no doctrine. He turned philosophy away from questions about the physical world towards ethics: how one ought to live, and whether virtue can be known and taught.

He was also a citizen-soldier who served as a hoplite at Potidaea, Delium and Amphipolis. He twice defied authority at personal risk: in 406 BC he alone opposed the illegal mass trial of the generals after Arginusae, and under the Thirty he refused an order to arrest an innocent man.

In 399 BC he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young. The trial had a political background: several of his followers, including Alcibiades and Critias, leader of the Thirty, had harmed the city. He was convicted by a narrow margin. Asked to propose a penalty, he first suggested free meals at public expense, then a fine of thirty minas guaranteed by his friends (Plato, *Apology* 36d–38b); the jury chose death, and he drank hemlock in prison.

He is known only through others — above all Plato and Xenophon, and Aristophanes' mocking portrait in *Clouds* — whose accounts differ. Separating the real Socrates from their versions is the "Socratic problem".

name: Plato

claims.text: Plato founded the Academy in Athens c. 387 BC.
The complete Platonic corpus survives, along with some spurious works.
Plato travelled to Sicily and involved himself with the court of Dionysius.
The Seventh Letter is genuinely by Plato.
The Atlantis story reflects a memory of Minoan Crete or Thera.
Plato was reportedly sold into slavery during one of his visits to Syracuse before being ransomed and returned to Athens.
The original Academy developed over roughly three centuries; later Athenian Neoplatonism was not an uninterrupted continuation of the same institution.

summary: Student of Socrates, founder of the Academy, and author of the dialogues that set the agenda for Western philosophy.
significance: Whitehead's remark that European philosophy is footnotes to Plato overstates the case, but not by much: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics and political theory all take their initial shape here.
body:
Plato founded the Academy around 387 BC in a grove outside Athens sacred to the hero Academus — a philosophical community whose successive heads developed and disputed his ideas for roughly three centuries. Its institutional history was disrupted in the first century BC. The much later Neoplatonic school at Athens should not be treated as an uninterrupted continuation of the same institution down to AD 529. His journeys were not confined to Athens: he travelled at least twice to Syracuse in Sicily, drawn by the ambition of shaping the tyrant Dionysius I, or later his son Dionysius II, into something resembling his ideal of a philosopher-king, ventures that ended badly enough that, according to a persistent and plausible ancient tradition, Plato was actually sold into slavery on one visit before being recognised, ransomed and returned safely to Athens.

His central doctrine is the theory of Forms: the changing, imperfect things people perceive with their senses are merely partial instances of perfect, unchanging realities that can only be grasped by reason rather than observation. The *Republic* builds an imagined just city as a working model for the structure of a just individual soul, argues at length for rule by philosopher-kings uniquely qualified by education to see the truth, and contains the Allegory of the Cave, in which ordinary people are compared to prisoners mistaking shadows on a wall for reality itself. His concrete political proposals in that dialogue are genuinely authoritarian by most modern standards — strict censorship of poetry and music, a rigid hereditary-seeming class structure softened only by exceptional individual promotion, and state control over reproduction and child-rearing among the guardian class — and treating him as a straightforward proto-democrat requires ignoring a great deal of what the text actually says.

Unusually for any ancient author, his complete body of work survives intact, alongside a handful of additional dialogues and letters, including the disputed *Seventh Letter*, whose authenticity as Plato's own genuine autobiographical account remains debated among specialists.

name: Aristotle

claims.text: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens in 335 BC.
He tutored Alexander at Mieza in Macedon.
Several of his zoological observations were confirmed only in the modern era.
The surviving works are lecture notes rather than published treatises.
Aristotle's father Nicomachus served as court physician to the Macedonian king Amyntas III, Philip II's father.
His logical treatises were later grouped and transmitted as the Organon, foundational to both Islamic and medieval European philosophy.

summary: Plato's student, Alexander's tutor, founder of the Lyceum, and the most systematically encyclopaedic mind of antiquity.
significance: Effectively founded logic, biology, literary criticism and political science as distinct disciplines, and dominated European and Islamic thought for nearly two thousand years.
body:
Aristotle (384–322 BC) was born at Stagira in Chalcidice, northern Greece. His father Nicomachus was court physician to King Amyntas III of Macedon. At seventeen he went to Athens and studied at Plato's Academy for twenty years, until Plato's death in 347 BC.

He then lived at Assos in Asia Minor and on Lesbos, where he studied animals with remarkable care; some of his observations, such as on the reproduction of the octopus and of a dogfish, were only confirmed in the 19th century. In 343 BC Philip II hired him to tutor the young Alexander at Mieza. In 335 BC he returned to Athens and founded his own school at the Lyceum, where he and his students collected the constitutions of 158 Greek states; only the *Constitution of the Athenians* survives, recovered on papyrus in 1890.

Aristotle rejected Plato's theory of separate Forms: the form of a thing exists in the thing itself. That turned philosophy towards study of the actual world. He wrote on almost everything — logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetry — and effectively founded logic, biology and literary criticism as subjects. His surviving works are mostly lecture notes, later edited by Andronicus of Rhodes.

After Alexander's death in 323 BC, anti-Macedonian feeling made Athens dangerous for him; he left, saying he would not let Athens sin twice against philosophy, and died at Chalcis the next year. Through Arabic and Latin translations his work dominated Islamic and European thought for nearly two thousand years.

name: Aeschylus

claims.text: Aeschylus fought at the battle of Marathon in 490 BC.
The Persians (472 BC) is the earliest surviving Greek play.
The Oresteia is the only complete surviving tragic trilogy.
Aeschylus introduced the second actor to tragedy.
Aeschylus reportedly travelled to Sicily at the invitation of the tyrant Hieron I of Syracuse, where he may have died.

summary: The earliest tragedian whose plays survive, and a veteran of Marathon who put the Persian Wars on stage.
significance: Added the second actor, making genuine dramatic conflict possible, and turned tragedy into an instrument for examining justice and the divine order.
body:
Aeschylus fought at Marathon and, by most accounts, at Salamis as well; his own epitaph, which tradition says he composed himself, mentions only his military service at Marathon and says nothing whatsoever about his plays, a striking choice for a man now remembered almost entirely as a playwright. His *Persians* (472 BC) is the only surviving Greek tragedy built around a contemporary historical subject rather than myth, and remarkably it stages the Persian defeat entirely from the perspective of the grieving Persian court back in Susa, deliberately inviting the Athenian audience's sympathy for the very enemy they had just defeated rather than simple triumphalism.

The *Oresteia* (458 BC) is the only complete tragic trilogy to survive intact from antiquity: Agamemnon murdered in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra on his return from Troy, his son Orestes' subsequent act of vengeance against his own mother, and Orestes' eventual trial at Athens, where the goddess Athena establishes a human court, the Areopagus, specifically to end the self-perpetuating cycle of blood vengeance running through the whole family. It functions, in effect, as a myth about the very birth of law and courts as an alternative to endless private retribution. Late in life Aeschylus reportedly travelled to Sicily at the invitation of the Syracusan tyrant Hieron I, and ancient tradition holds that he died there, killed, according to one improbable but persistent legend, when an eagle dropped a tortoise onto his bald head, mistaking it for a rock.

name: Sophocles

claims.text: Seven complete tragedies by Sophocles survive out of roughly 120 written.
Aristotle treated Oedipus Rex as the paradigm of tragic plot construction.
Sophocles held the office of general at Athens.
He introduced the third actor.
Sophocles served on the board of generals alongside Pericles during the Samian War.
He was reportedly involved in introducing the cult of the healing hero Asclepius to Athens.

summary: Tragedian of Oedipus Rex and Antigone, who won more dramatic victories than any of his rivals and served Athens as general and priest.
significance: Perfected tragic structure — Aristotle used Oedipus Rex as his model of plot — and shifted focus from cosmic justice to individual character under pressure.
body:
Sophocles (c. 497–406 BC) was an Athenian tragic playwright, born at Colonus just outside the city. He wrote around 120 plays over more than sixty years and won first prize at the festival of Dionysus about twenty times, reportedly never coming lower than second. Only seven tragedies survive complete, including *Antigone*, *Oedipus Rex*, *Electra* and *Oedipus at Colonus*, with much of a satyr play, *The Trackers*, recovered on papyrus.

He is credited with adding a third actor to the stage and enlarging the chorus, allowing more complex scenes between characters. His plays focus on individuals under extreme pressure — Oedipus hunting the killer who turns out to be himself, Antigone choosing to bury her brother against the king's command. *Oedipus Rex* was Aristotle's model of the perfect tragic plot.

Sophocles was also a public figure. He served as a treasurer of the Delian League, was elected general alongside Pericles during the Samian War of 441–439 BC, and later served on the emergency board set up after the Sicilian disaster. He was a priest of a healing hero and helped bring the cult of Asclepius to Athens, housing the god's image in his own home until a sanctuary was built.

He died in 406 BC, shortly after Euripides, just before Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War.

name: Euripides

claims.text: Nineteen plays attributed to Euripides survive.
He won markedly fewer dramatic victories than Sophocles or Aeschylus.
The Trojan Women was produced in 415 BC, shortly after the Melian massacre.
The Trojan Women was intended as a protest against Athenian policy at Melos.
Euripides spent his final years at the court of the Macedonian king Archelaus, where he died around 406 BC.

summary: The most unsettling of the tragedians, who gave voice to women, slaves and the defeated, and questioned the gods openly.
significance: His psychological realism and moral scepticism made him the least successful tragedian in his lifetime and the most read afterwards.
body:
Euripides (c. 480–406 BC) was the youngest of the three great Athenian tragedians, by tradition born on the island of Salamis in the year of the battle. He wrote around ninety plays and won first prize only four or five times, but nineteen plays survive — more than those of Aeschylus and Sophocles combined — because later readers valued him so highly.

His plays are full of psychological realism, clever argument and doubts about the gods. He gave strong voices to women, slaves and the defeated. *Medea* (431 BC) has a betrayed wife kill her own children and escape unpunished. *Hippolytus*, *Electra* and *The Bacchae* show passion and religious frenzy destroying their victims. *The Trojan Women* (415 BC), staged the year after Athens massacred the people of Melos, shows the sack of Troy through the eyes of its enslaved women, and is often read as a protest against the war.

He was a constant target of the comic poet Aristophanes, who in *Frogs* (405 BC) staged a contest in the underworld between Euripides and Aeschylus over which was the better poet.

Late in life Euripides left Athens for the court of King Archelaus of Macedon at Pella, where he wrote *The Bacchae*, and he died there around 406 BC. His influence on later drama, from Menander to Seneca and beyond, was greater than that of any other Greek tragedian.

name: Aristophanes

claims.text: Eleven complete plays by Aristophanes survive.
The Clouds caricatures Socrates as a sophist and natural philosopher.
Old Comedy named and mocked living public figures at state-sponsored festivals.
The Clouds materially contributed to Socrates' conviction.
Aristophanes also satirised the demagogue Cleon directly in The Knights, despite the risk of political retaliation.

summary: Master of Old Comedy, who lampooned living Athenians — generals, philosophers, poets — by name and to their faces.
significance: The only surviving Old Comedy, and an irreplaceable window onto Athenian daily life, slang and political argument.
body:
Eleven of his plays survive. *The Clouds* (423 BC) portrays Socrates suspended in a basket studying the heavens and teaching students to argue the unjust case successfully — Plato's *Apology* has Socrates cite it as a source of the prejudice that killed him.

*Lysistrata* (411 BC) has the women of Greece withhold sex until the men make peace. *The Frogs* (405 BC) sends Dionysus to the underworld to bring back a poet who can save the city, and stages a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides that is the earliest surviving work of literary criticism.

The freedom of this comedy is itself evidence: a democracy at war permitted its most prominent citizens to be ridiculed on stage at a state religious festival. He took this furthest in *The Knights* (424 BC), a sustained, almost reckless attack on the powerful demagogue Cleon, staged while Cleon was at the height of his political influence and reportedly performed with Aristophanes himself playing the role since no mask-maker in Athens would risk making a caricature mask of so dangerous a man.

name: Pheidias

claims.text: Pheidias directed the sculptural programme of the Parthenon.
His workshop at Olympia has been identified by excavation.
A cup inscribed "I belong to Pheidias" was found in that workshop.
No original work by Pheidias survives.
Roman-era visitors described the seated Zeus at Olympia as capable of consoling those in grief simply by its expression.
Ancient sources disagree on whether Pheidias died in prison at Athens or in exile at Olympia.

summary: Overseer of the Parthenon sculptures and maker of the colossal Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders.
significance: Defined the visual language of the Classical style — and none of his major works survives except at second hand.
body:
Pheidias (active c. 465–430 BC) was an Athenian sculptor, the most famous artist of Classical Greece. Pericles put him in charge of the sculpture of the Acropolis building programme.

He made the Athena Parthenos, a statue about 12 m tall of gold and ivory over a wooden core, which stood inside the Parthenon from 438 BC. His workshop produced the Parthenon's frieze, metopes and pediment sculptures, designed under his direction though carved by many hands. Earlier, he made the great bronze Athena Promachos that stood on the Acropolis. At Olympia he made the seated Zeus in gold and ivory, about 12 m high, counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. His workshop there has been excavated, with tools, clay moulds for the statue's drapery and a cup inscribed "I belong to Pheidias".

The great statues are all lost, melted down or destroyed in later antiquity, and are known only from descriptions, Roman copies and coins. His style survives in the Parthenon sculptures, which defined the calm, idealised manner of High Classical art.

Late in his career he was prosecuted in Athens, apparently for stealing gold or ivory meant for the Athena; ancient writers thought the charge was really aimed at Pericles. Accounts disagree on whether he died in prison in Athens or in exile at Olympia.

name: Hippocrates

claims.text: The Hippocratic Corpus is a compilation by multiple authors.
On the Sacred Disease argues explicitly against supernatural causation of epilepsy.
Hippocratic physicians recorded detailed longitudinal case observations.
Hippocrates wrote the Oath.
Hippocratic writers emphasised environmental factors such as climate, water and geography in explaining regional differences in disease and temperament.

summary: The physician of Kos whose name attaches to a body of medical writing that separated disease from divine punishment.
significance: Established medicine as a discipline based on observation, prognosis and ethical obligation rather than religious healing.
body:
The Hippocratic Corpus is around sixty works by many hands over more than a century; how much Hippocrates himself wrote is unknown. What unifies it is a naturalistic stance. *On the Sacred Disease* attacks the idea that epilepsy is divine: it has a natural cause like every other illness, and those who call it sacred are concealing their ignorance.

The clinical case histories in the *Epidemics* are careful daily observations that often end with the patient dying — recorded anyway, because the point was to learn the course of disease. The Oath, with its commitments to confidentiality and to doing no harm, remains the ancestor of medical ethics, though it is unlikely to be by Hippocrates.

The underlying humoral theory was wrong, and it dominated European medicine for two thousand years.

Another strand of the Corpus, represented by the treatise *Airs, Waters, Places*, looked outward rather than inward, arguing that a population's climate, water supply and terrain shaped both the diseases common to a region and even the character and physical constitution of its people — an early and influential attempt at environmental medicine that also shaded into a broader Greek habit of explaining foreign peoples' customs and temperaments by their geography.

name: Alcibiades

claims.text: Alcibiades promoted the Sicilian Expedition and was recalled to face charges in 415 BC.
He defected to Sparta and advised the fortification of Decelea.
He was later recalled to Athenian command and won naval victories.
Alcibiades was responsible for the mutilation of the herms.
He was raised in the household of Pericles after his father's death, giving him an unusually privileged political education.

summary: Brilliant, treacherous Athenian aristocrat who commanded for Athens, defected to Sparta, advised Persia, and returned to Athens again.
significance: His career is the clearest single illustration of how personal ambition destabilised Athenian democracy during the Peloponnesian War.
body:
Alcibiades (c. 450–404 BC) lost his father young and was raised by his guardian Pericles himself. It gave him an unusually privileged, front-row education in Athenian politics and power. The ancient sources dwell repeatedly on his charisma and good looks as central to his career.

In 415 BC he pushed Athens into the ambitious Sicilian Expedition, against more cautious advice. On the eve of the fleet's departure, the city's herms, boundary markers topped with the head of Hermes, were mutilated overnight in an act of sacrilege that badly unsettled Athens. Alcibiades was implicated and recalled from the fleet to stand trial. Rather than return to face charges that could easily prove fatal, he defected to Sparta. There he advised the Spartans to fortify Decelea inside Attica, a base that harassed Athenian territory for the rest of the war and did the Athenian economy lasting harm.

He then fell out with his Spartan hosts, reportedly after an affair with a Spartan king's wife, and moved on to the Persian satrap Tissaphernes. Eventually he negotiated his own return to Athenian favour and command. He won a string of real naval victories in the Hellespont region that briefly restored Athenian fortunes late in the war. A subordinate's unauthorised defeat during his absence gave his enemies at home the pretext to remove him from command a second time. He was assassinated in Phrygia in 404 BC, reportedly at Spartan or Persian instigation. His house was set on fire and he was cut down as he tried to escape.

He was also a close associate of Socrates, who, by Alcibiades' own later account, saved his life in battle at Potidaea. In Plato's *Symposium* Alcibiades gives a famous, half-drunken speech of admiration and unrequited love for Socrates at a private dinner party. Many Athenians blamed Alcibiades for the city's wartime disasters, and the association counted materially against Socrates at his own trial years later.

name: Xenophon

claims.text: Xenophon marched with the Ten Thousand and wrote a first-person account of the retreat.
Cyrus the Younger was killed at Cunaxa in 401 BC.
The Hellenica continues Greek history from where Thucydides stops.
The Anabasis influenced later Macedonian strategy against Persia.
Xenophon was formally exiled from Athens for his service alongside Sparta, and Sparta granted him an estate at Scillus in the Peloponnese instead.

summary: Soldier, student of Socrates and author of the Anabasis — the first-person account of ten thousand Greek mercenaries fighting their way out of Persia.
significance: Wrote the earliest surviving military memoir, and provides the main continuation of Greek history after Thucydides breaks off.
body:
Xenophon joined a large mercenary army hired by the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger in a bid to overthrow his own brother, the reigning Persian king Artaxerxes II. Cyrus was killed at the battle of Cunaxa in 401 BC, and shortly afterward the senior Greek generals were treacherously seized under a supposed truce and executed by the Persian satrap Tissaphernes. Left leaderless and stranded roughly a thousand miles inside hostile Persian territory with no safe route home, the surviving Greek soldiers elected an entirely new set of commanders — Xenophon prominent among them despite having no prior senior command experience — and fought and marched their way north through a brutal Armenian winter toward the Black Sea coast. Their collective shout of "Thalatta! Thalatta!" — "the sea, the sea!" — on finally sighting open water from a mountain pass is among the most famous single moments in all of Greek literature, a spontaneous eruption of relief after months of danger.

He later fought openly for Sparta, including at one point against his own native Athens, a choice of loyalty that led directly to his formal exile from the city; Sparta compensated him with a country estate at Scillus in the Peloponnese, where he lived for years hunting, writing, and entertaining guests before political upheaval eventually forced him to leave that too. He wrote widely and in strikingly varied genres: the *Hellenica*, continuing Greek history from precisely where Thucydides's own account breaks off; several Socratic memoirs offering a more conventional, less philosophically demanding portrait of Socrates than Plato's; a practical treatise on horsemanship; and another on the management of a private estate. His vivid first-hand demonstration that a disciplined Greek force could fight its way clean across the heart of the Persian Empire and survive was not lost on later readers, including, by most accounts, Philip II and Alexander themselves.

name: Lysander

claims.text: Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC.
Persian subsidies funded the Spartan fleet.
He installed the Thirty Tyrants at Athens in 404 BC.
Lysander was reportedly the first living Greek to receive cult honours and altars as though he were a god.

summary: The Spartan admiral who destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami and ended the Peloponnesian War.
significance: Won the war by building, with Persian money, the one thing Sparta had always lacked: a fleet.
body:
Lysander (died 395 BC) was the Spartan admiral who won the Peloponnesian War.

Lysander secured funding from the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger — an alliance that traded the Greek cities of Asia Minor back to Persian control in exchange for the ships that beat Athens.

At Aegospotami in 405 BC he caught the Athenian fleet beached and unprepared and captured nearly all of it. Athens, dependent on imported grain through the Hellespont, was starved into surrender within months. The Long Walls were pulled down to flute music.

He installed narrow oligarchies backed by Spartan garrisons across the former empire, including the Thirty Tyrants at Athens. He was reportedly the first living Greek to receive divine honours from cities, with altars, hymns and festivals established in his name at several of the states he had helped or dominated — an unprecedented and, to many contemporaries, alarming departure from the usual Greek reluctance to worship living men.

name: Epaminondas

claims.text: Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC using a massed left wing.
He liberated Messenia and refounded Messene as an independent city.
Spartan power declined permanently after Leuctra.
Philip II learned Macedonian tactics while a hostage at Thebes.
Epaminondas was celebrated in antiquity for personal incorruptibility, reportedly living and dying in poverty despite his military success.

summary: Theban general who broke Spartan military supremacy at Leuctra in 371 BC and freed the Messenian helots.
significance: Ended Sparta as a great power permanently, and pioneered the tactical asymmetry that Philip II — a hostage in Thebes as a youth — would later develop.
body:
At Leuctra, Epaminondas massed his left wing fifty ranks deep against the elite Spartan right, deliberately held back the rest of his own line at an angle, and shattered the best Spartan troops before the weaker Theban centre and right had even fully engaged. It was the first clear, deliberate use of an unequal battle line anywhere in Greek warfare, and roughly 400 of the 700 Spartiates present were killed in the process — a demographic wound the already-shrinking Spartan citizen body simply could not absorb or replace.

He then invaded the Peloponnese and carried out what proved to be the single most consequential act of the whole campaign: he liberated Messenia outright, whose enslaved helot population had farmed the land feeding the entire Spartan military system for roughly three centuries, and refounded its chief city, Messene, as a heavily fortified, independent city built with remarkable speed by a coalition of former helots and allied labour. Sparta, stripped permanently of the economic base its whole warrior society had depended on, never recovered its former power. Epaminondas was also celebrated by ancient writers for a personal incorruptibility unusual even by the standards they applied to other generals, reportedly living, and eventually dying, in genuine poverty despite commanding the dominant military power in Greece for most of a decade.

He was killed at Mantinea in 362 BC, struck down at the moment of another tactical victory, and Theban hegemony over Greece effectively died with him almost immediately afterward.

name: Demosthenes

claims.text: Demosthenes delivered a series of speeches opposing Philip II of Macedon.
He negotiated the Athenian-Theban alliance that fought at Chaeronea.
He died by suicide in 322 BC after the failure of the Lamian War.
He accepted money from Persia to oppose Macedon.
Demosthenes was orphaned young and later sued his own guardians for mismanaging his inheritance, an early legal victory that helped launch his career.
He was convicted and briefly exiled around 324 BC over the Harpalus affair, involving allegedly misappropriated funds from a fugitive Macedonian treasurer.

summary: The greatest Athenian orator, who spent his career warning that Philip of Macedon meant to end Greek freedom — and was right.
significance: His speeches are the finest surviving Greek oratory and the fullest contemporary record of resistance to Macedon.
body:
Demosthenes (384–322 BC) was the greatest of the Athenian orators. Orphaned at seven, he found as a young man that his guardians had squandered his inheritance, and he trained in rhetoric to sue them, winning part of it back. Plutarch says he cured a speech impediment by practising with pebbles in his mouth and speaking over the sound of the waves. He worked as a professional speechwriter before entering politics.

From the 350s BC he saw Philip II of Macedon as a deadly threat to Greek freedom. In the *Olynthiacs* and *Philippics* he urged the Athenians to act: to pay for their wars and fight in them themselves rather than relying on mercenaries. In 339 BC he built an alliance between Athens and Thebes, but Philip crushed it at Chaeronea in 338 BC, where Demosthenes fought. In his speech *On the Crown* (330 BC) he defended his whole career against his rival Aeschines and won.

In 324 BC he was convicted of taking money from Harpalus, Alexander's runaway treasurer, and went into exile; whether he was guilty is uncertain. After Alexander's death in 323 BC he returned to support the Greek revolt known as the Lamian War. When it failed, he fled to the island of Calauria and took poison in the temple of Poseidon rather than be captured by Antipater's men.

His speeches were studied as models of eloquence for two thousand years.

name: Isocrates

claims.text: Isocrates advocated a Panhellenic campaign against Persia under a single leader.
He addressed a published appeal to Philip II in 346 BC.
He starved himself to death after learning of Chaeronea.
His school at Athens trained a generation of prominent orators, statesmen and historians, giving him wide influence beyond his own published speeches.

summary: Athenian teacher of rhetoric who urged the Greeks to unite under a strong leader and invade Persia — and looked to Philip II to do it.
significance: Formulated the Panhellenic ideology that Philip and Alexander used to justify the conquest of Persia.
body:
Isocrates had a weak voice and never spoke in the assembly; he taught and published instead, and his school shaped Greek education for centuries. His *Panegyricus* (380 BC) argued that Greek unity could only be achieved against a common enemy.

In the *Address to Philip* (346 BC) he named the man: Philip should reconcile the leading cities and lead a united campaign into Asia. Whether this made him a visionary or a collaborator has been argued ever since — Demosthenes was making exactly the opposite case at exactly the same time.

He reportedly died shortly after Chaeronea, aged 98.

His real influence ran less through his own speeches, which he never delivered aloud, than through the school he ran at Athens for roughly half a century, which trained students who went on to prominent careers across Greek public and intellectual life, giving Isocrates a reach as an educator that arguably outstripped his direct impact as a political advocate.

name: Philip II of Macedon

secondaryImage.caption: The royal tombs at Vergina, ancient Aigai, opened by Manolis Andronikos in November 1977. He believed Tomb II, unrobbed since antiquity, held Philip's own remains -- an identification still argued over today.

claims.text: Philip II reformed the Macedonian army around the sarissa phalanx and Companion cavalry.
He defeated the Greek coalition at Chaeronea in 338 BC and formed the League of Corinth.
He was assassinated by Pausanias at Aegae in 336 BC.
He lost his right eye to an arrow at the siege of Methone.
Tomb II at Vergina is his burial.
Olympias or Alexander instigated the assassination.
Philip spent roughly three years as a political hostage in Thebes in his teens, where he observed the tactics of the general Epaminondas at first hand.
Manolis Andronikos discovered the unlooted royal tombs at Vergina in November 1977, identifying Tomb II as Philip's on the basis of its grave goods and skeletal evidence.

summary: The king who reforged Macedon's army, subdued Greece at Chaeronea, and planned the invasion of Persia his son carried out.
significance: Built the instrument of conquest. Alexander's campaigns are inconceivable without Philip's army, treasury and diplomatic groundwork.
body:
Philip II was born around 382 BC, the youngest son of King Amyntas III of Macedon, a kingdom on the northern edge of the Greek world. As a teenager he spent about three years as a hostage in Thebes, then the leading power in Greece, where he could watch the army of Epaminondas, which had just broken Sparta at Leuctra.

He took power in 359 BC, after his brother Perdiccas III was killed fighting the Illyrians, in a kingdom beaten and surrounded by enemies. He rebuilt its army from the ground up. His infantry carried the *sarissa*, a pike about twice the length of a hoplite spear, and fought in a deep phalanx; the noble Companion Cavalry became a decisive striking force; the army was paid, drilled and kept in the field year-round; and engineers built torsion catapults that could take walled cities. He lost an eye to an arrow at the siege of Methone in 354 BC.

He expanded by war, bribery and marriage — at least seven marriages, each sealing an alliance; Olympias of Epirus, mother of Alexander, was one wife among several. He took the gold mines of Mount Pangaion, destroyed Olynthus in 348 BC and steadily extended his influence into central Greece, despite the warnings of Demosthenes in Athens. In 338 BC he defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea, and the next year organised the Greek states into the League of Corinth under his leadership, to invade the Persian Empire.

He never led that invasion. In 336 BC he was stabbed to death by his bodyguard Pausanias at his daughter's wedding at Aigai. Whether Pausanias acted alone, or for Olympias, Alexander or Persia, is unknown. The rich royal Tomb II found at Vergina in 1977 is most often identified as his. His army, treasury and plans made Alexander's conquests possible.

name: Alexander the Great

secondaryImage.caption: The Siwa Oasis, deep in the Libyan desert, where Alexander made a gruelling detour in 331 BC to consult the Oracle of Zeus-Ammon -- and came away, by his own later account, told that he was the god's son.

claims.text: Alexander defeated the Achaemenid Empire in campaigns between 334 and 330 BC.
He founded Alexandria in Egypt in 331 BC.
He reached the Hyphasis river in the Punjab, where his army refused to continue.
He died in Babylon in June 323 BC.
He was poisoned.
He believed himself divine, or the son of Zeus-Ammon.
His attempt to introduce the Persian court gesture of proskynesis provoked open resistance from his Macedonian companions and was abandoned.

summary: King of Macedon who destroyed the Achaemenid Empire in a decade of campaigning, reached the Indus, and died at 32 without an heir.
significance: Redrew the political map from the Adriatic to the Punjab and made Greek the language of government and learning across the Near East for a thousand years.
body:
Alexander III of Macedon was born at Pella in 356 BC, the son of Philip II and Olympias of Epirus. From about the age of thirteen he was taught by Aristotle, and he kept a copy of the *Iliad* with him on campaign, seeing himself as a new Achilles. At eighteen he commanded the cavalry at Chaeronea.

He became king at twenty when Philip was assassinated in 336 BC. He quickly secured the throne, killing rivals, and crushed a Greek revolt by destroying Thebes. In 334 BC he crossed into Asia with about 40,000 men to carry out Philip's planned war on Persia. He defeated the Persian governors at the Granicus, and King Darius III himself at Issus in 333 BC. He took Tyre after a seven-month siege, was accepted as pharaoh in Egypt, where he founded Alexandria and visited the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, and in 331 BC won the decisive battle of Gaugamela. Babylon, Susa and Persepolis fell, and Persepolis was burned.

He pushed on through Central Asia, marrying the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana, and into India, where he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC. At the Hyphasis his exhausted army refused to go further. The return march through the Gedrosian desert cost thousands of lives.

Alexander kept Persian officials, adopted Persian court dress and ceremony, and in 324 BC held mass weddings at Susa between his officers and Persian noblewomen. This provoked Macedonian resistance — to the Persian bow of *proskynesis*, and in a mutiny at Opis — and his temper turned violent: he killed his friend Cleitus in a drunken quarrel and had Parmenion executed.

He died at Babylon in June 323 BC, aged 32, after a fever lasting about eleven days; poison and disease have both been proposed. He left no adult heir, and his generals fought over the empire for forty years. Their kingdoms spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to Central Asia, the beginning of the Hellenistic age.

name: Olympias

claims.text: Olympias was a Molossian princess of Epirus who married Philip II.
She held military and political power in Macedon during the succession wars.
She was executed on Cassander's orders in 316 BC.
She was involved in Philip II's assassination.
Hostile ancient portrayals of her exaggerate her cruelty and fanaticism.
Olympias reportedly encouraged stories that Zeus, in the form of a serpent, had fathered Alexander rather than Philip.
She forced Philip III Arrhidaeus's wife Eurydice to take her own life after defeating and capturing them both.

summary: Molossian princess, wife of Philip II, mother of Alexander, and a ruthless political operator in the succession wars after his death.
significance: One of the few women in Greek history who exercised open political and military power, and was executed for it.
body:
Olympias (c. 375–316 BC) was a princess of the Molossians, the royal house of Epirus in north-western Greece, which claimed descent from Achilles. Around 357 BC she married Philip II of Macedon, and in 356 BC gave birth to Alexander the Great.

Ancient writers, mostly hostile to her, describe her devotion to ecstatic Dionysiac rites, including handling snakes, and she encouraged the story that Alexander's real father was Zeus — a claim that suited his later ideas about his own divinity. When Philip married a young Macedonian noblewoman, Cleopatra, in 337 BC, threatening Alexander's succession, Olympias withdrew to Epirus. After Philip's murder in 336 BC she was widely suspected of involvement, and she had Cleopatra and her infant child killed.

She stayed influential through Alexander's reign, in constant conflict with his regent in Macedon, Antipater. In the wars after Alexander's death she backed his young son Alexander IV, and in 317 BC invaded Macedon with an Epirote army. The Macedonian troops went over to her; she had Alexander's half-brother King Philip III Arrhidaeus killed and forced his wife Eurydice to take her own life.

Cassander, Antipater's son, then besieged her at Pydna. She surrendered in 316 BC on a promise that her life would be spared, but was condemned by an assembly and killed by relatives of those she had executed. She is one of the few women of the Greek world known to have wielded open political and military power.

name: Hephaestion

claims.text: Hephaestion held the office of chiliarch, second to Alexander.
He died at Ecbatana in 324 BC and received extraordinary funeral honours.
Ancient authors likened him and Alexander to Patroclus and Achilles.
The two were lovers.
Hephaestion was given command of major portions of the army and fleet independently during the later campaigns, reflecting Alexander's practical trust in him beyond their personal closeness.

summary: Alexander's closest companion and second-in-command, whose sudden death at Ecbatana provoked an extraordinary public crisis of grief.
significance: The relationship is the best-attested personal bond in Alexander's life and shaped his behaviour at key moments.
body:
Hephaestion grew up with Alexander and rose to *chiliarch*, the second office in the empire. At Susa in 324 BC he married Drypetis, sister of Alexander's own bride Stateira, so their children would be cousins.

He died at Ecbatana later that year. Alexander's response was extravagant even by his standards: he reportedly lay on the body for a day, cut his hair, executed the physician, banned music, and ordered a monumental pyre at Babylon at enormous cost. He asked the oracle at Siwa whether Hephaestion could be worshipped as a god and settled for hero cult.

Ancient sources compared the pair to Achilles and Patroclus, and Alexander did visit their supposed tombs at Troy together. Whether the relationship was sexual is not stated in the surviving sources and cannot be resolved.

Whatever the personal dimension, Alexander's trust in Hephaestion was not merely sentimental: in the campaign's later stages he was repeatedly entrusted with independent commands, leading substantial detachments of the army overland while Alexander took other forces by a different route, and at times commanding sections of the fleet, responsibilities that mark him as a genuinely capable senior officer rather than simply a favoured companion kept close for personal reasons.

name: Parmenion

claims.text: Parmenion commanded the left wing in Alexander's major battles.
He was killed on Alexander's orders in 330 BC after his son Philotas was executed.
Philotas was genuinely guilty of conspiracy.
Parmenion had already served as one of Philip II's most trusted generals before Alexander's reign began.

summary: Philip II's most senior general, who served Alexander as second-in-command until Alexander had him killed.
significance: Represents the older Macedonian establishment whose loyalty Alexander eventually found incompatible with his own transformation.
body:
Parmenion (c. 400–330 BC) was a Macedonian general, the most senior commander of Philip II and second-in-command to Alexander the Great. He won major victories for Philip, including over the Illyrians in 356 BC, and in 336 BC led the advance force into Asia that prepared the way for Alexander's invasion.

In Alexander's great battles — the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela — Parmenion commanded the left wing, holding the line while Alexander attacked from the right. Ancient writers such as Arrian repeatedly show him advising caution and Alexander overruling him; this pattern is probably exaggerated to make Alexander look bolder.

In 330 BC his son Philotas, commander of the Companion Cavalry, was accused of failing to report a plot against Alexander, and was tortured and executed. Alexander then sent agents to Ecbatana in Media, where Parmenion was stationed, to kill him before he heard the news. There was no evidence of his guilt. The killing removed the most powerful representative of Philip's old guard, men whose loyalty was to Macedonian tradition rather than to Alexander's new, partly Persian style of kingship, and it shocked the army.

name: Ptolemy I Soter

claims.text: Ptolemy took control of Egypt after Alexander's death and founded a dynasty.
He diverted Alexander's funeral procession to Egypt.
He founded the Museum and Library of Alexandria.
His lost history of Alexander was Arrian's main source.
Ptolemy earned the epithet Soter, "Saviour," from the Rhodians after helping the city withstand a prolonged siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes.
He voluntarily abdicated in favour of his son Ptolemy II before his death, a rare peaceful succession among the successor kingdoms.

summary: Alexander's general and bodyguard who seized Egypt, hijacked his corpse, founded a dynasty that lasted three centuries, and created the Library of Alexandria.
significance: Built the most stable and intellectually productive of the successor kingdoms, ruled by his descendants until Cleopatra VII.
body:
Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367–282 BC) was a Macedonian general and boyhood friend of Alexander the Great, one of his seven personal bodyguards, who founded the Ptolemaic dynasty that ruled Egypt until Cleopatra VII.

After Alexander's death in 323 BC he took Egypt as his province. In 321 BC he seized Alexander's body on its way to Macedon and brought it to Egypt, a great source of prestige, and that year defeated the regent Perdiccas, whose invasion collapsed in a disastrous crossing of the Nile. Over the following decades he fought the other Successors for Cyprus, Palestine and the Aegean.
