His hold on power required removing Alexander's surviving family. Olympias, Alexander's formidable mother, had massacred Cassander's own relatives during the fighting; he besieged her at Pydna, had her condemned by an assembly of Macedonians too frightened to acquit her, and allowed her to be killed by the relatives of her victims rather than execute her himself. Around 309 BC he moved against the last real threat to his rule: he had Alexander's posthumous son, Alexander IV, and the boy's mother Roxana quietly murdered, ending the Argead royal line that had ruled Macedon for centuries.

He founded two cities that outlasted him by a very wide margin — Cassandreia and Thessalonica, the latter named for his wife and surviving today as Greece's second city. He took the royal title in 305/4 BC along with the other leading successors, and died of illness in 297 BC; his own sons did not hold Macedon for long after him.

name: Lysimachus

claims.text: Lysimachus was one of Alexander's bodyguards and became satrap of Thrace after Alexander's death.
He took the royal title around 306/5 BC along with the other leading successors.
He fought alongside Seleucus against Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BC and gained territory in Asia Minor.
He was killed fighting Seleucus at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC, the last of the original successors to die.

summary: One of Alexander's bodyguards who built a kingdom out of Thrace and western Asia Minor, and was the last of the original successors to die in battle.
significance: His death at Corupedium in 281 BC removed the last of Alexander's original companions from the board, closing the first, most violent phase of the wars over the empire he had left behind.
body:
Lysimachus received Thrace in the division of satrapies after Alexander's death — a difficult, thinly Hellenised assignment on the empire's edge that he spent years subduing rather than a ready-made kingdom. He built up strength steadily rather than dominating events early, and joined the coalition of Ptolemy, Seleucus and Cassander against Antigonus, fighting at Ipsus in 301 BC, where Antigonus was killed and Lysimachus took a large share of Asia Minor as his reward.

His later reign was troubled by his own family: he had his son by an earlier marriage, Agathocles, executed on the accusation of his second wife Arsinoe, a decision that alienated many of his own supporters and pushed some toward his rival Seleucus, the last of the old guard still standing against him.

The two men who had fought together at Ipsus met as enemies at Corupedium in 281 BC. Lysimachus was killed in the battle, and Seleucus, briefly master of nearly all of Alexander's former territory, was assassinated within months — leaving the settled three-kingdom map of Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids that defined the Hellenistic world for the next two centuries.

name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus

claims.text: Flamininus, as Roman consul, defeated Philip V of Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
He proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities at the Isthmian Games in 196 BC.
He later helped drive Antiochus III's forces out of Greece.
Diplomatic pressure from Flamininus is linked to the suicide of the exiled Hannibal around 183 BC.

summary: Roman general who defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and then declared the Greek cities free at the Isthmian Games.
significance: His declaration of Greek freedom, however qualified by Roman oversight in practice, marked Rome's first major intervention in the Greek world as arbiter rather than conqueror — a role it would abandon within a generation.
body:
Flamininus was unusually young for a Roman consul and unusually philhellene for a Roman general, reportedly fluent in Greek and genuinely engaged with Greek culture rather than merely conquering it. Sent to fight Philip V of Macedon, he won the decisive battle at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC, breaking Macedonian power in Greece for a generation.

The following year, at the Isthmian Games — one of the great pan-Hellenic festivals — a herald announced that Rome restored freedom, autonomy and immunity from tribute to the Greek cities that had been under Macedonian control. Ancient accounts describe an eruption of gratitude so loud it was said to have startled birds out of the sky. Rome's freedom proved to mean freedom to align with Roman interests rather than full independence, but the gesture, and Flamininus personally, were honoured across Greece for years afterward, including cults in his name.

He remained active in Greek affairs, helping curb Antiochus III's ambitions there, and was later sent to press the Bithynian king harboring the exiled Carthaginian general Hannibal to give him up; Hannibal took poison rather than be captured, an end later writers laid at Flamininus's door.

name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus

claims.text: Aemilius Paullus, as Roman consul, destroyed the Macedonian army of King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC.
The victory ended the Antigonid monarchy of Macedon.
He brought back an enormous quantity of plunder, including Perseus's royal library.
He lost two young sons to illness around the time of his triumph.

summary: Roman consul who destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC, ending the kingdom Alexander's dynasty had built.
significance: Pydna finished what Cynoscephalae had begun a generation earlier: it abolished the Macedonian monarchy outright, the last of Alexander's line of successor states in Europe to fall to Rome.
body:
Lucius Aemilius Paullus (c. 229–160 BC) was a Roman general and statesman, twice consul.

Sent against Perseus, the last king of Macedon, Aemilius Paullus won the battle at Pydna in under an hour once his legions found gaps opening in the Macedonian phalanx's line on uneven ground — a tactical lesson Rome had learned once already at Cynoscephalae and now applied decisively. Perseus was captured and paraded through Rome in Paullus's triumph; the kingdom was broken into four nominally independent republics and, within a generation, annexed outright as a province.

The plunder from Macedon was vast, and Paullus kept remarkably little of it for himself beyond Perseus's royal library, which he gave to his sons' education — one of whom, adopted into another family, became Scipio Aemilianus, later the destroyer of Carthage. Roman writers made much of the fact that in the days around his triumph Paullus lost two young sons to illness, framing the personal tragedy as a kind of cosmic balance against his public glory, whether or not that reading reflects how he experienced it himself.

name: Lucius Mummius Achaicus

claims.text: Mummius, as Roman consul, destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after defeating the Achaean League.
The population was killed or enslaved and the city's art looted and shipped to Rome.
He earned the honorific Achaicus for the victory.
Ancient sources present him as indifferent to the artistic value of what he was plundering.

summary: Roman consul who destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after crushing the Achaean League, earning the title Achaicus.
significance: The destruction of Corinth, in the same year Rome also destroyed Carthage, announced a harder Roman policy toward the Greek world than Flamininus's "freedom" a half-century earlier — resistance would now be punished with annihilation, not negotiation.
body:
Lucius Mummius Achaicus (2nd century BC) was a Roman politician and general, consul in 146 BC. That year he defeated the Achaean League, the last significant independent power in Greece, which had gone to war with Rome rather than accept Roman demands to break it up.

After defeating the League near the Isthmus, Mummius captured Corinth, one of the richest cities in Greece. On the orders of the Senate, as a warning to the Greeks, the city was destroyed: its men were killed, its women and children sold into slavery, its art treasures shipped to Rome and its buildings burned. Carthage was destroyed by Rome in the same year. Greece came under the authority of the Roman governor of Macedonia, ending Greek independence. Mummius took the surname Achaicus, "conqueror of Achaea", and celebrated a triumph in Rome.

Ancient writers portray him as an honest but uncultured soldier. The historian Velleius Paterculus tells how he warned the men shipping Corinth's masterpieces to Rome that if they lost any, they would have to replace them with new ones. True or not, the story became a byword for Roman philistinism. The historian Polybius, who saw the aftermath, helped organise the settlement of Greece that followed.

Corinth lay largely empty for a century, until Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC.

name: Lucius Cornelius Sulla

claims.text: Sulla besieged and stormed Athens in 86 BC after it sided with Mithridates VI of Pontus.
He felled the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum for siege material.
Aristotle's library was taken to Rome as part of the plunder from the campaign.
He also defeated Mithridates' generals in battle in Greece at Chaeronea and Orchomenus in 86 BC.
He later became dictator of Rome, 82–79 BC.

summary: Roman general who stormed Athens in 86 BC during the war against Mithridates of Pontus, and later became dictator of Rome.
significance: His siege and sack of Athens caused physical and institutional damage the city never fully recovered from, ending its centuries as a genuine political power even as it remained a revered centre of philosophy.
body:
Athens allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus against Rome, calculating that a rising eastern power offered a better chance of freedom than Roman rule had. Sulla besieged the city through a brutal winter — sources describe the population reduced to boiling shoe leather for food — before storming it on 1 March 86 BC. He is said to have stopped his own troops from continuing a massacre in the Kerameikos, remarking that he spared the many for the sake of the few, a reference to the city's past rather than any present merit.

He needed timber for siege works and took it from the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum, the philosophical schools founded by Plato and Aristotle, and shipped Aristotle's own library back to Rome among the plunder — a loss later scholars have mourned as much as the human cost. In the same year he defeated Mithridates' field armies in Greece at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, securing the province.

Sulla's later career took him back to Rome, where he marched on the city itself — the first Roman general to do so — and ruled as dictator from 82 to 79 BC, using the office to purge his political enemies before retiring and dying in 78 BC. His Greek campaign remains the episode most directly relevant to the Greek world he had, by his own account, saved from Mithridates while wrecking Athens to do it.

name: Cimon

claims.text: Cimon was the son of Miltiades, the victor of Marathon.
He led the Delian League to a double naval and land victory over Persia at the Eurymedon around 466 BC.
He championed cooperation with Sparta and was ostracised in 461 BC after Sparta rejected Athenian help during a helot revolt.
He paid off his father Miltiades' enormous fine to the Athenian state.
Cimon named one of his own sons Lacedaemonius, publicly signalling his pro-Spartan sympathies.

summary: Athenian general, son of Miltiades, who led the Delian League's greatest victory over Persia and championed cooperation with Sparta.
significance: His victory at the Eurymedon effectively neutralised Persia as a naval threat for a generation, and his pro-Spartan policy defined one pole of Athenian politics before losing out to the more assertive democratic and anti-Spartan course Pericles came to represent.
body:
Cimon inherited a family name under a cloud: his father Miltiades had died disgraced and indebted after the failed Paros expedition, and Cimon reportedly paid off the fine himself to recover the body for burial. He built his own reputation instead on aggressive, successful command of the Delian League's continuing war against Persia, culminating in the extraordinary double victory at the Eurymedon around 466 BC.

Politically he stood for close cooperation between Athens and Sparta, a position that came apart in 461 BC: called on to help Sparta suppress a helot uprising, Cimon led an Athenian force to assist, only for the Spartans, mistrustful of Athenian democratic sympathies, to send the force home unused. The humiliation discredited his policy at Athens, and he was ostracised the same year, while Pericles and the more radically democratic faction rose in his place.

He was recalled from ostracism early, in the 450s, and negotiated a truce with Sparta before dying during a final campaign against Persian-held Cyprus around 450 BC — active in Athenian affairs, on both fronts of his career, until the end. His pro-Spartan sympathies were public and deliberate rather than merely a matter of policy: he named one of his own sons Lacedaemonius, the formal Greek term for a Spartan, a naming choice contemporaries would have read immediately as a declaration of where his political loyalties lay.

name: Demetrius I Poliorcetes

claims.text: Demetrius, son of Antigonus I, destroyed Ptolemy's fleet at Cyprian Salamis in 306 BC, prompting his father to claim the royal title.
His year-long siege of Rhodes in 305–304 BC failed to take the city, earning him the epithet "the Besieger" regardless.
The bronze from siege engines he abandoned at Rhodes reportedly helped fund the Colossus of Rhodes.
He held the Macedonian throne from 294 to 288 BC before losing it and dying in captivity around 283 BC.
Demetrius married Antipater's daughter Phila and, later, several other royal wives as part of shifting political alliances typical of the successor kings.

summary: Son of Antigonus I, celebrated as history's greatest besieger of cities despite failing to take the one siege he is best remembered for.
significance: His naval victory at Cyprian Salamis triggered the wave of royal title-taking among the successors that made the Hellenistic kingdoms formally, as well as practically, independent monarchies; his failed siege of Rhodes indirectly produced one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
body:
Demetrius I Poliorcetes (c. 337–283 BC) was the son of Antigonus I, one of Alexander's leading successors, and a dashing commander on land and sea.

In 307 BC he "liberated" Athens from Cassander's governor and was hailed there almost as a god. In 306 BC he destroyed Ptolemy's fleet off Salamis in Cyprus, and his father took the title of king for them both — the first of Alexander's successors to do so. In 305–304 BC he besieged Rhodes with huge machines, including the nine-storey siege tower called the Helepolis, "Taker of Cities". The city held out and he withdrew; the Rhodians sold his abandoned equipment to help pay for the Colossus of Rhodes. The siege earned him the name Poliorcetes, "the Besieger".

At Ipsus in 301 BC his cavalry charge carried him too far from the battle, and his father was killed. Demetrius kept a fleet and some cities, and in 294 BC seized the throne of Macedon. He ruled it for six years before Pyrrhus and Lysimachus drove him out in 288 BC. After a last campaign in Asia Minor he surrendered to Seleucus in 285 BC and died in comfortable captivity two years later.

His marriages, including to Phila, daughter of the regent Antipater, served his alliances. His son Antigonus II Gonatas won Macedon back, and the Antigonid dynasty ruled it until the Roman conquest.

name: Anaxagoras

claims.text: Anaxagoras was the first philosopher known to have lived and taught at Athens.
He proposed Nous (Mind) as the force that set an initially undifferentiated cosmic mixture into ordering rotation.
He argued the sun was a red-hot mass of stone larger than the Peloponnese, and that the moon shines by reflected sunlight and has earth-like terrain.
He was prosecuted for impiety at Athens, probably as a political attack on his associate Pericles, and went into exile.

summary: Ionian philosopher, teacher of Pericles, who proposed Mind as the ordering force of the cosmos and was prosecuted at Athens for saying the sun was a stone.
significance: He brought Ionian natural philosophy to Athens itself and gave it a direct line into Athenian politics through his association with Pericles, while his trial demonstrated how dangerous purely physical explanations of the heavens could still be treated as impious.
body:
Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a philosopher from Clazomenae in Ionia who moved to Athens around 460 BC and taught there for about thirty years, the first philosopher known to have done so. He was a close associate of Pericles, and Euripides may have heard him.

He taught that originally everything was mixed together, with a portion of everything in everything. Then *Nous* — Mind, a separate, unmixed substance — set the mixture spinning, and the rotation separated out the world as we know it. Mind as the ordering force of the cosmos influenced later philosophers, though Socrates complained in Plato's *Phaedo* that Anaxagoras then explained everything by mechanical causes instead.

He gave physical explanations of the heavens. He said, correctly, that the Moon shines by light reflected from the Sun and that eclipses are caused by shadows, and claimed that the Sun is a red-hot stone larger than the Peloponnese. A meteorite that fell at Aegospotami around 467 BC was linked in ancient sources to his ideas.

To say the Sun was a stone rather than a god could be treated as impiety. Probably as part of political attacks on Pericles, Anaxagoras was prosecuted and left Athens for Lampsacus on the Hellespont, where he died; the people of Lampsacus honoured him with a yearly holiday.

name: Praxiteles

claims.text: Praxiteles was an Athenian sculptor active in the mid-4th century BC, working mainly in marble rather than bronze.
His Aphrodite of Knidos was, by ancient consensus, the first monumental Greek cult statue to show a goddess fully nude.
Pliny the Elder ranked the Aphrodite of Knidos as the finest statue in the world, not only among Praxiteles' own works.
No original work by Praxiteles survives; all are known through later Roman copies and, in one contested case, a marble found at Olympia.

summary: Athenian sculptor of the mid-4th century BC whose nude Aphrodite of Knidos was, by ancient reputation, the single most admired statue in the Greek world.
significance: He broke the convention that female divine images had to be draped, and later antiquity treated the resulting statue as a watershed rather than a scandal contained -- a measure of how far his influence outran the one Roman-era Greek city that first bought it.
body:
Praxiteles (active c. 375–330 BC) was an Athenian sculptor, the most celebrated of the 4th century BC.

Praxiteles worked in an Athens no longer the imperial power of Pericles' day, but still the artistic centre of the Greek world, and he worked mostly in marble, whose softer surface let him render flesh with a warmth bronze could not match. Ancient writers single him out for a particular quality: a sense of languid, almost melting grace that later critics called his hallmark.

His fame rests overwhelmingly on one commission. Offered a choice between a draped and an undraped Aphrodite, the people of Kos took the modest option and the people of Knidos took the nude -- and it was Knidos's statue that became, in Pliny's words, superior not just to Praxiteles' other work but to every statue anywhere. Pilgrims reportedly travelled to Knidos for the statue alone, and a shrine was built so it could be viewed from every angle, itself an unusual arrangement for a cult image.

Like almost every major Greek sculptor, none of his originals survive; his reputation rests on Roman marble copies, ancient descriptions, and one marble at Olympia sometimes, contentiously, claimed as an original.

name: Polykleitos

claims.text: Polykleitos of Argos wrote a treatise, the Canon, setting out the proportions of the ideal human body.
The Canon itself is lost; it is known through later authors such as Galen, who quotes and paraphrases it.
The Roman marble Doryphoros is generally accepted as a copy of the bronze he made to embody his Canon.
His figures rest their weight on one leg, with the opposite arm and shoulder answering the hip, a stance later called contrapposto.
He made the gold-and-ivory cult statue of Hera for the Argive Heraion, which Pausanias and Strabo saw.
No securely identified original by him survives; every work is known from copies and descriptions.

summary: Argive bronze sculptor who tried to reduce the perfect human body to a system of proportions, and wrote the book to prove it.
significance: The Canon made proportion a subject of theory, not only of craft, and shaped how Greek and Roman sculptors built the human figure for centuries.
body:
Polykleitos worked in Argos in the second half of the fifth century BC, a generation after Pheidias, and was best known for bronze athletes. Ancient writers ranked him beside Pheidias: Pheidias for gods, Polykleitos for men.

His reputation rested on an idea. He is said to have written a treatise, the Canon, arguing that beauty arises from the exact ratio of each part of the body to every other, and to have made a statue as its demonstration. The book is lost. Galen, writing some six centuries later, reports its claim that beauty lies in the proportion of the parts to one another: finger to finger, the fingers to the palm and wrist, the wrist to the forearm, and so on up the whole body. Scholars have argued for over a century about whether the Doryphoros, the spear-bearer, is the statue in question, and about whether the ratios can be recovered from the copies. The identification is the usual working assumption, not a proven fact.

What the copies do show is a new way of standing. The Doryphoros carries his weight on the right leg and relaxes the left; the shoulders and hips tilt in opposite directions, so the whole body is balanced without being symmetrical. This is the stance that Renaissance artists later revived as contrapposto. His seated Hera at the Argive Heraion, in gold and ivory, was judged by Strabo to be the finest in workmanship of all, though smaller and cheaper than the work of Pheidias.

Because bronze was routinely melted down, nothing Polykleitos himself cast is certainly extant. He is known through Roman marble copies, made mostly for collectors, which preserve the design but not the surface or the metal.

name: Lysippos

claims.text: Lysippos of Sikyon worked mainly in bronze and was one of the most prolific Greek sculptors of the fourth century BC.
Ancient writers say Alexander the Great allowed only Lysippos to make his official portrait in bronze.
Pliny reports that Lysippos gave his statues smaller heads and slimmer bodies than earlier sculptors, so that they looked taller.
Plutarch and Arrian say Alexander commissioned from him bronze statues of the Macedonian cavalry killed at the Granicus in 334 BC.
The Apoxyomenos, a Roman marble of an athlete scraping oil from his arm, is widely taken to copy a Lysippan original, though the attribution is not certain.
Pliny credits him with some 1,500 works; the figure is an ancient tradition and cannot be checked.

summary: Bronze sculptor from Sikyon who made the portraits of Alexander the Great and gave Greek statues their taller, lighter Hellenistic proportions.
significance: Lysippos moved sculpture from the compact ideal of the fifth century towards the open, spatial figures of the Hellenistic age, and gave Alexander his enduring face.
body:
Lysippos came from Sikyon, near Corinth, and worked in the middle and late fourth century BC. Anecdote made him a self-taught craftsman who began as a bronze-worker, and claimed that his only teacher was nature. That is a tidy story, and it should be read as one.

Pliny preserves the clearest statement of his style. Earlier sculptors, he says, had made men as they were; Lysippos made them as they appear. His figures have smaller heads and slimmer bodies than Polykleitos's, and they seem to reach into the space around them instead of standing inside a block. In the Apoxyomenos, an athlete scrapes oil from an outstretched arm, so that the viewer must move round the figure to read it. The Vatican marble is a Roman copy, and its Lysippan origin is likely but not proven.

He is best known as Alexander's sculptor. Ancient writers report that Alexander would be portrayed in bronze by no one else, and Plutarch and Arrian say that Lysippos made the bronze portrait group of the horsemen who died at the Granicus. The turned head, upward gaze and lion-like hair of Alexander's later images probably come from his lost portraits, though Andrew Stewart cautions that most surviving heads are Hellenistic reworkings, not close copies.

Nothing certainly by his hand survives. His influence is visible instead in the Hellenistic portrait, the athlete statue and the ruler cult image.

name: Pindar

claims.text: Pindar composed victory odes, epinikia, for winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian games.
Four books of these odes survive complete; the rest of his work, including hymns, paeans and dithyrambs, survives only in fragments.
His latest datable poem, Pythian 8, celebrates a victory of 446 BC.
He wrote for aristocratic families and for tyrants, including Hieron of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas.
Alexander is said to have spared Pindar's house when he destroyed Thebes in 335 BC.
An ode of Pindar's praised Athens as "shining" and "violet-crowned", and later tradition says Athens rewarded him; the details are anecdotal.

summary: Theban poet whose victory odes for athletes turned a day at the games into myth, praise and moral instruction.
significance: Pindar is the great voice of aristocratic values in early Greece, and the main evidence for how athletic victory was understood and paid for.
body:
Pindar was born near Thebes about 518 BC and composed for over fifty years. He was a professional: families and rulers paid him to celebrate a victory in a chariot race, a wrestling match or a foot race, and the ode was performed by a chorus, often at the victor's home city.

The odes follow a rough pattern. They praise the victor and his family, tell a myth that mirrors or complicates the achievement, and close with a moral: success is a gift from the gods, and mortals should not reach beyond their measure. The Greek is dense and hard, and its abrupt shifts of subject are deliberate. Olympian 1, for Hieron of Syracuse, retells the story of Pelops in a version that pointedly rejects the cannibal feast, saying it is wrong to speak ill of the gods.

His patrons show how far the poetry travelled. He wrote for Aiginetan families, for Thessalian nobles, for Theron of Akragas, and for Hieron in Sicily. Pythian 1 places Hieron's power beside the defeat of Persian and Carthaginian invaders. Because so many odes name their commissioners, they are also a rare source for the social and political world of the Greek aristocracy in the early fifth century.

Thebes had sided with Persia in 480 BC, and Pindar's civic loyalties were awkward. Later anecdote says Alexander spared his house in 335 BC; the story fits the poet's afterlife as the "Theban" poet, more than it proves the fact.

name: Parmenides

claims.text: Parmenides of Elea wrote a single hexameter poem in two parts: the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion.
About 150 lines survive, quoted by later authors such as Simplicius.
The Way of Truth argues that what is cannot come to be or cease to be, and is one, whole and unchanging.
Plato has Socrates, as a young man, meet an aged Parmenides and his pupil Zeno of Elea in the dialogue Parmenides.
Whether Plato's meeting between Socrates and Parmenides ever happened is doubtful.
Diogenes Laertius links him with the Pythagorean Ameinias; the connection is not otherwise attested.

summary: Philosopher of Elea whose poem argued that change and plurality are illusions and only unchanging being is real.
significance: Parmenides began the argument about what can be said to exist, and every later Greek cosmologist, Plato among them, had to answer him.
body:
Parmenides lived at Elea, a Phocaean colony on the coast of southern Italy, and probably flourished in the early fifth century BC. His dates are uncertain: Diogenes Laertius places his prime in 504–501 BC, while Plato's dialogue, which has him about sixty-five when Socrates was young, points to a birth around 515. The two do not agree.

His poem opens with a chariot ride to the house of a goddess who reveals two paths of inquiry. The Way of Truth argues, step by step, that what exists cannot have come into being, since it would have to arise from what is not, and that it cannot perish, divide or change. On this argument the world of the senses, with its motion and multiplicity, cannot be what is really there. The Way of Opinion then gives a cosmology of light and night, presented as the best account of appearances.

Readers still disagree on what Parmenides meant. Some take him to deny plurality and change outright; others read him as making a claim about how we must speak and reason about what is. What no one disputes is that the argument was new, that it was strict, and that it could not be ignored. His pupil Zeno defended it with paradoxes of motion, and the atomists, Empedocles and Plato all built their systems in response.

The poem is fragmentary, and all of it comes down through later quotation. Every summary of it, including this one, is an interpretation.

name: Empedocles

claims.text: Empedocles of Akragas held that all things are formed from four "roots": earth, air, fire and water.
He named two forces, Love and Strife, that combine and separate the roots in a repeating cosmic cycle.
He wrote two poems in hexameters: On Nature and Purifications.
A papyrus found at Strasbourg and published in 1999 added several dozen lines of On Nature.
He is said to have died by leaping into Mount Etna to prove his divinity; the story is late and probably invented.
Later writers credit him with political activity in Akragas against tyranny and oligarchy.

summary: Sicilian philosopher, poet and self-styled holy man who explained the world as four elements moved by Love and Strife.
significance: His four roots became the standard Greek model of matter for two thousand years, and his career shows how blurred the lines between philosopher, healer and prophet could be.
body:
Empedocles lived in Akragas, in Sicily, in the fifth century BC. Parmenides had argued that nothing can come to be or pass away; Empedocles answered by keeping being intact and locating change in mixture. There are four unchanging roots, and everything else is their combination and separation, driven by Love (which unites) and Strife (which divides). The cosmos passes endlessly between the dominance of each.

Two poems are attributed to him, and their relationship is a long-running puzzle. On Nature is a physics; Purifications is a religious work about the fall of divine spirits into mortal bodies and the path back, with a ban on animal sacrifice and meat. Some scholars see one system in two registers; others see two moods. The Strasbourg papyrus, published in 1999, suggested that the two themes were closer than was thought, since its cosmological passages seem to speak of divine spirits and their cycle of rebirth.

The biography is mostly legend. He is said to have stopped a plague, revived a woman, and declined a crown. The best-known tale, that he threw himself into the crater of Etna to prove he was a god, is likely a later invention, and Diogenes Laertius reports it alongside less flattering versions.

The fragments show a poet as well as a thinker: images of the elements as painters' pigments, and of the eye as a lantern, make abstract argument vivid.

name: Protagoras

claims.text: Protagoras of Abdera was among the first to teach for a fee and to call himself a sophist.
He said that "man is the measure of all things", as quoted in Plato's Theaetetus.
He was a friend of Pericles and is said to have been invited to write laws for the colony of Thurii.
He professed agnosticism about the gods: he could not know whether they exist.
A later tradition says Athens tried him for impiety and burned his books; the story is doubtful.

summary: Sophist from Abdera who taught the Athenians to argue both sides of any question and held that man is the measure of all things.
significance: Protagoras helped turn argument into a subject of education and made relativism a live philosophical position.
body:
Protagoras (c. 490–420 BC) came from Abdera, in Thrace, and spent much of his career in Athens. He offered instruction in what Plato has him call "good judgement" in private and public affairs, and he charged high fees, which scandalised those who believed virtue could not be sold.

Almost nothing survives in his own words. The most famous line, that man is the measure of all things, of things that are that they are, and of things that are not that they are not, is quoted by Plato and left unexplained. Plato reads it as relativism: what seems true to each person is true for that person. Whether Protagoras meant this, or something narrower about perception or about public disputes, is disputed. He also wrote on arguing both sides of a case, and taught his students to make the weaker case appear the stronger, a phrase that became a slur.

In the Protagoras Plato gives him a long speech on how justice and respect for others are shared among citizens, and portrays him as a serious adversary of Socrates. That portrait is a philosopher's, not a biographer's. The report that he was prosecuted at Athens for impiety and that his books were burned in the agora appears only in later sources and is regarded with caution.

He is best understood as a teacher of democratic citizens: the skills he taught, speaking and arguing persuasively, were what the assembly and the law courts demanded.

name: Theophrastus

claims.text: Theophrastus of Eresos, on Lesbos, succeeded Aristotle as head of the Lyceum around 322 BC and led it for over thirty years.
His Enquiry into Plants and Causes of Plants are the earliest surviving systematic works on botany.
The Characters, thirty short sketches of human types such as the Flatterer and the Miser, is attributed to him.
The prefaces and epilogues of the Characters were probably added later.
Strabo says Theophrastus left his books, and Aristotle's, to Neleus of Scepsis; the later story of their concealment in a cellar is disputed.

summary: Aristotle's successor at the Lyceum, founder of systematic botany and author of the Characters.
significance: Theophrastus kept Aristotle's school alive and carried its method of collecting and classifying observations into the study of plants and minerals.
body:
Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was born at Eresos on Lesbos and came to Athens to study, first, according to later tradition, with Plato and then with Aristotle. Aristotle is said to have renamed him, from Tyrtamos to a "divine speaker"; the story is anecdotal. When Aristotle left Athens in 322 BC, Theophrastus took over the Lyceum and led it for some thirty-five years. In 307 a law restricting the philosophical schools briefly drove him from the city, and it was repealed within a year.

His surviving work is a fraction of his output. The Enquiry into Plants describes several hundred species by their structure, habitat and cultivation, and arranges them in categories; the companion Causes of Plants asks why they grow as they do. Both draw on the observations of farmers, root-cutters and travellers as well as on his own. He also wrote on stones, winds and weather signs, and on the history of earlier philosophers, a book that later survey-writers used heavily.

The Characters is the work most often read today. Its thirty sketches, each starting from a definition of a fault such as flattery or stinginess, and continuing through a list of typical actions, seem to be observed from Athenian life, though their purpose is unclear. They are often linked with the New Comedy of Menander, who is said to have studied under him.

The fate of his library is uncertain. Strabo says that Theophrastus left his books to Neleus, whose heirs hid them in a cellar; modern scholars doubt the dramatic form of the story, but not that the texts travelled.

name: Diogenes of Sinope

claims.text: Diogenes of Sinope left his home city under a charge connected with defacing or altering its coinage.
Counterstruck coins of Sinope from this period exist, but linking them to Diogenes is conjectural.
He lived in Athens and Corinth with minimal possessions, and ancient anecdote says he lived in a large storage jar.
He is credited with calling himself "a citizen of the world", kosmopolites.
The story of his meeting with Alexander, when he asked the king to stand out of his sunlight, is an anecdote of uncertain historical value.
Diogenes Laertius records that he died in 323 BC, in the same year as Alexander.

summary: Exiled Sinopean who turned poverty, shamelessness and wit into a philosophy, and became the archetype of the Cynic.
significance: Diogenes made the rejection of convention a way of life, and through his followers passed that ideal to the Stoics.
body:
Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BC), the founder of Cynic philosophy, came from Sinope on the Black Sea and lived mostly in Athens and Corinth.

Almost everything about Diogenes comes from anecdote, collected centuries after his death by Diogenes Laertius. What can be said with some confidence is that he came from Sinope on the Black Sea, was exiled, and spent his adult life in Athens and Corinth teaching by example. The reason for his exile was said to be that he "defaced the currency". The phrase became his motto, in the sense that Cynics defaced the values of convention, and it may be a pun added to the story later.

The Cynic life, as told of him, consisted in reducing existence to what nature requires: a cloak, a staff, a wallet, food from the market, and a jar for shelter. He ate, argued and relieved himself in public, on the principle that nothing natural is shameful. His weapon was the joke. Asked where he came from, he called himself a citizen of the world; seen carrying a lamp in daylight, he said he was looking for a human being.

The best-known story is the meeting with Alexander in Corinth, when the young king offered him any favour and he replied that he wanted only for Alexander to step out of the sun. It is told in several versions and is almost certainly a moral fable, but it captures the Cynic claim: a man who needs nothing cannot be given anything.

He wrote, according to the ancient lists, but nothing survives. His significance lies in his followers. Crates of Thebes passed the tradition on to Zeno of Citium, who founded the Stoa, and the Cynic view that virtue alone is sufficient for happiness became a central Stoic thesis.

name: Menander

claims.text: Menander was the leading writer of Athenian New Comedy.
His Dyskolos ("The Grouch") won first prize at the Lenaia festival in 316 BC.
Dyskolos survives almost complete on a papyrus published in 1958; before then, Menander was known only from fragments and Roman adaptations.
Ancient sources say he won first prize eight times.
The Roman playwrights Plautus and Terence adapted his plots.
A tradition reports that he drowned while swimming in the harbour at Piraeus.

summary: Athenian comic dramatist whose plays of mistaken identity, family quarrels and reconciliation set the pattern for European comedy.
significance: Menander moved comedy from political satire to private life, and his plots reached Rome and then the modern stage.
body:
Menander was born at Athens in 342 or 341 BC and wrote for the theatre from his early twenties. By then the city had lost real independence, and his plays reflect a world in which the household, not the assembly, is the stage of drama. The old comedy of Aristophanes had attacked politicians by name; New Comedy stays inside the family, with fathers and sons, young lovers, slaves, soldiers and courtesans, and a story that turns on misunderstanding and ends in recognition or marriage.

For most of history his work was known only from quotations and from Roman versions by Plautus and Terence. Since 1905 papyri from Egypt have changed that. The Cairo codex added long stretches of Samia, Epitrepontes and Perikeiromene; in 1958 the Bodmer papyrus published Dyskolos in nearly complete form, along with the record that it took first prize in 316 BC. It is a light story of a misanthropic old farmer, and it is the only Menander play we can read from start to finish.

The plays are quiet and observational. Speech is natural, characters are seldom plain villains, and ethical questions, such as whether a man should acknowledge a child, are decided through feeling as much as rule. The ancients admired this: Aristophanes of Byzantium reportedly asked who imitated whom, life or Menander.

He died young, in his early fifties, about 290 BC. Tradition says he drowned while swimming at Piraeus.

name: Nicias

claims.text: Nicias negotiated the peace of 421 BC that ended the first phase of the Peloponnesian War.
He opposed the Sicilian Expedition but was appointed one of its three commanders.
After Alcibiades was recalled, Nicias delayed the retreat from Syracuse for twenty-seven days because of a lunar eclipse.
He was captured and put to death by the Syracusans in 413 BC, though one ancient tradition says he took his own life.
Xenophon says Nicias owned a thousand slaves whom he hired out to work in the silver mines at Laurion.
Thucydides judged that of all the Greeks of his time Nicias least deserved such a fate.

summary: Wealthy, cautious Athenian commander who made a peace, opposed the Sicilian Expedition, and then led it to disaster.
significance: Nicias's career shows how a hesitant, pious leader can be worse for a city than a reckless one when placed in a war he did not want.
body:
Nicias was one of the richest Athenians of the fifth century, with a fortune from silver mines and a reputation for careful piety, and he became the leading moderate after the deaths of Pericles and Cleon. He pursued a negotiated settlement with Sparta, and the peace that bears his name was concluded in 421 BC. It did not hold, but it gave Athens some years of respite.

He was also the man who tried to stop the expedition against Sicily. In the assembly debate of 415 he argued that the island was too far and too large, and that the city had enemies at home; when the assembly voted to go anyway, he was named one of the commanders, alongside Alcibiades, who had championed the plan, and Lamachus. Alcibiades was recalled to face charges of sacrilege and defected to Sparta. Nicias, now effectively in sole command, moved slowly, let the moment to isolate Syracuse pass, and was outmanoeuvred when Sparta sent the general Gylippus to help the city.

In 413, with the army trapped and losing, he could have withdrawn. When the moon was eclipsed on 27 August, his seers said to wait "thrice nine days", and he obeyed. The Athenians were then defeated in the harbour and ambushed on the road inland; the survivors were held in the stone quarries. Nicias and his fellow general Demosthenes were executed.

Thucydides, who did not spare Nicias's faults, wrote that he least deserved to come to this end, because his whole life had been regulated by virtue. The verdict is one of the most striking in the history.

name: Cleon

claims.text: Thucydides calls Cleon the most violent of the citizens and the most persuasive with the people.
In 427 BC Cleon urged the Athenian assembly to execute the men of rebellious Mytilene; the assembly voted for it, then reversed the decision the next day.
In 425 BC he took command at Sphacteria after promising to bring back the Spartans within twenty days, and succeeded.
Cleon was killed at Amphipolis in 422 BC, the same battle in which the Spartan Brasidas fell.
Aristophanes attacked him repeatedly, most extensively in the Knights of 424 BC.
The tribute assessment of 425/4 BC substantially raised Athens's demands on her allies; its association with Cleon comes from later tradition.

summary: Athenian popular leader of the 420s, blamed by Thucydides and mocked by Aristophanes, who won at Sphacteria and died at Amphipolis.
significance: Cleon became the type of the demagogue, and the debate over whether he deserves that name is a debate about how to judge Athenian democracy through hostile sources.
body:
Cleon rose after Pericles's death in 429 BC to become the most influential speaker in the Athenian assembly. Both of our main hostile witnesses, Thucydides and Aristophanes, wrote with personal grievance: Thucydides was exiled after failing to save Amphipolis from Brasidas, and Aristophanes had been prosecuted by him. So the portrait we have, of a loud, violent, self-promoting orator, is heavily coloured.

Two episodes define him. At Mytilene in 427, after the island's revolt was suppressed, Cleon proposed killing every adult man. The assembly agreed, sent out the order, and the next day reconsidered; a second ship arrived just in time. Thucydides gives his speech against mercy as a defence of harsh imperial rule. At Pylos and Sphacteria in 425, a Spartan force was cut off on an island. Cleon, provoked by Nicias's offer to yield him the command, accepted it, and with Demosthenes he captured 292 men, of whom about 120 were Spartiates. It was the most unexpected success of the war.

He was less lucky in 422. Leading an expedition to the northern coast, he camped near Amphipolis, was surprised by Brasidas, and was killed while retreating. Brasidas died in the same fighting. With the two most determined advocates of war gone, the Peace of Nicias followed within a year.

Modern historians have partly rehabilitated him as the first prominent politician not from the old aristocracy, and see much of the criticism as class snobbery. Whether he was a demagogue or a capable public servant depends heavily on how far Thucydides is trusted.

name: Brasidas

claims.text: Brasidas won early distinction in 431 BC by holding the coastal town of Methone against an Athenian landing.
In 424 BC he led a Spartan army to the northern Aegean and captured Amphipolis with unusual speed.
The expedition included 700 helots armed as hoplites and 1,000 Peloponnesian mercenaries.
The Athenian general at Amphipolis was Thucydides, who was exiled for failing to prevent its fall.
Brasidas was killed at Amphipolis in 422 BC and was given a hero-cult there as founder of the city.

summary: The most inventive Spartan commander of the Peloponnesian War, who broke Athenian control of the north and died winning Amphipolis.
significance: Brasidas showed Sparta could fight the war beyond the Peloponnese, and his death at Amphipolis removed the strongest opponent of peace.
body:
Thucydides called Brasidas an energetic man, unusual for a Spartan in being a capable speaker. His first prominent action was at Methone in 431 BC, where he ran through an Athenian cordon to relieve the town, and was formally praised at Sparta. He later helped to relieve Megara in 424.

The northern campaign was his greatest achievement. He marched through Thessaly and Macedon in 424 with a small force made up in part of helots freed for the purpose, which Thucydides says Sparta was happy to send out of the country. He appealed to cities under Athenian rule by promising liberation and respect for their laws, and many of them, including Amphipolis, changed sides. Thucydides, commanding a fleet at Thasos, arrived a few hours late to save it, and was exiled. This gave him the leisure to write his history.

Brasidas's freedom of action was limited. Sparta's leaders wanted the prisoners taken at Sphacteria back, and once a truce was agreed, Brasidas kept campaigning against its terms. In 422, when Cleon arrived to recover Amphipolis, Brasidas attacked, won, and was fatally wounded. The city buried him within its walls, honoured him as its founder in place of the Athenian Hagnon, and offered yearly games and sacrifices.

Thucydides, generally sparing with praise, treats him as the one Spartan who understood what the war demanded.

name: Agesilaus II

claims.text: Agesilaus became king of Sparta about 400 BC, with the support of Lysander, over the claim of Leotychidas.
He was lame from birth, and an oracle warning of a "lame kingship" was cited against him at the succession.
He led a campaign in Asia Minor against Persian satraps in 396–394 BC and was recalled by the outbreak of the Corinthian War.
At the peace conference of 371 BC Agesilaus insisted that Thebes swear only for itself and not for the Boeotian cities; Thebes refused, and Sparta lost at Leuctra.
At about eighty he led mercenaries in Egypt and died in Cyrenaica on the way home in about 360 BC.
Xenophon, who served with him, wrote a eulogy, the Agesilaus, which is both a source and an apology.

summary: Long-lived Spartan king who took the war to Persia, defeated Athens' allies, and presided over Sparta's fall from supremacy.
significance: His reign spans the peak of Spartan power and its collapse, and much of the blame for the collapse is laid at his door.
body:
Agesilaus was born lame and was not expected to rule. When his half-brother King Agis died about 400 BC, the succession was contested by Agis's reputed son Leotychidas, whose paternity was rumoured to be Alcibiades. Lysander backed Agesilaus, and an oracle that warned against a "lame kingdom" was read as a warning against a false heir instead. Thus he began his long reign in debt to a man he later resented.

His early years were successful. In Asia Minor in 396–394 he raided the satrapal territory around Sardis and presented himself as a panhellenic champion, a role that recalled the Trojan War, though his campaign ended when Persian money stirred up Athens, Thebes, Corinth and Argos against Sparta. He won at Coronea in 394 and, in the King's Peace of 387, secured a settlement that left Sparta arbiter of Greek affairs.

Then his policy hardened. Sparta seized the Theban acropolis in 382 and tried to break up the Boeotian league; the consequence was the Theban revival that led to defeat at Leuctra in 371 and the loss of Messenia. Agesilaus's personal hostility to Thebes is commonly seen as a cause. He nevertheless helped to defend Sparta itself when Epaminondas invaded Laconia in 370/69, and again in 362, when he was over eighty.

At the age of about eighty he took mercenary service in Egypt to raise money for Sparta. He died on the return voyage, and his body was embalmed in wax and carried home for burial.

name: Pelopidas

claims.text: In winter 379/8 BC Pelopidas led a group of Theban exiles who killed the pro-Spartan leaders and freed Thebes from its Spartan garrison.
He commanded the Sacred Band at Tegyra in 375 BC, where a small Theban force beat a larger Spartan one.
At Leuctra in 371 BC he led the Sacred Band alongside Epaminondas's deepened left wing.
He negotiated with the Persian king in 367 BC, and secured a rescript favourable to Thebes.
He was killed in Thessaly in 364 BC, at the moment of victory over Alexander of Pherae.
Philip of Macedon spent part of his youth as a hostage at Thebes in the period when Pelopidas was prominent.

summary: Theban leader who freed his city from Spartan occupation in 379 BC and helped to make it, briefly, the strongest state in Greece.
significance: Pelopidas was the political and military partner of Epaminondas, and their cooperation is the foundation of Theban hegemony.
body:
Pelopidas came from a wealthy Theban family, and after Sparta seized the Cadmea, Thebes's citadel, in 382 BC, he went into exile at Athens. In December 379, he and a few companions slipped back into the city in disguise, killed the leaders of the Spartan party at a banquet, and rallied the citizens. The Spartan garrison, though sizeable, surrendered within days. Thebes was free, and the Boeotian league could be rebuilt around it.

He then took command of the Sacred Band, a corps of trained infantry, which he led at Tegyra in 375 BC to a victory that shocked Sparta, since it was a defeat of a Spartan unit in a fair fight. At Leuctra in 371 he commanded the Band on the left of the line, where Epaminondas's deep column smashed the Spartan right. Pelopidas was more of a diplomat than Epaminondas. He was sent north to Thessaly and Macedon, where he arbitrated a succession dispute and brought back Philip as a hostage. In 367 he went to the Persian court and returned with the King's endorsement of Theban claims.

In 364 he took a small force against Alexander of Pherae, the tyrant who had imprisoned him earlier. His army won at Cynoscephalae in Thessaly, but Pelopidas, charging ahead to kill the tyrant, was killed himself. Thessalian cities honoured him with bronze statues.

Plutarch's life of Pelopidas is the main source, and it is a warm one.

name: Dionysius I of Syracuse

claims.text: Dionysius took power at Syracuse in 405 BC during a war with Carthage and ruled until his death in 367 BC.
He fortified Ortygia and built long walls across the Epipolae plateau, with a fortress at Euryalus.
Diodorus says catapults were first developed for his siege of Motya in 397 BC.
He fought four wars with Carthage with mixed results and extended Syracusan control over much of Sicily and into southern Italy.
His tragedy The Ransom of Hector won at the Athenian Lenaia in 367 BC, shortly before his death.
Plato visited his court, probably around 388 BC; the surviving letters describing the trip are of debated authenticity.

summary: Tyrant who made Syracuse the largest Greek city of the west and fought Carthage for control of Sicily.
significance: Dionysius created a Greek military monarchy on a new scale, and his career shaped later thinking about tyranny, including Plato's.
body:
Dionysius came to power at Syracuse in 405 BC, during a crisis. Carthage was besieging Greek cities in the south of Sicily and the Syracusan generals had failed. He took the general's office, quickly won unlimited authority, and made peace, leaving Carthage in control of much of the island.

The peace did not last. He spent years preparing for war: building a strong fleet, recruiting mercenaries, and fortifying the city. Ortygia, the island citadel, became his palace; walls across the Epipolae, with the great fortress at Euryalus, made Syracuse difficult to besiege. In 397 he attacked the Carthaginian city of Motya, using new kinds of artillery, including an early catapult, which Diodorus says was invented in his workshops. His campaigns were up and down: Syracuse itself was besieged in 396 and rescued by an outbreak of plague in the Carthaginian camp. Later he extended his power to the toe of Italy, capturing Rhegion in 387.

Tyranny made his name a synonym for suspicion. Anecdotes describe a ruler who slept behind a moat and never let barbers near him; in one of them, a courtier is given a seat under a sword hung by a single hair. Plato visited about 388 and later tried to educate Dionysius's son; the resulting quarrel is one of the sources of Plato's political thought.

Dionysius also wrote poetry, and his tragedy won at Athens in the year he died. His son inherited a state too big for him to control.

name: Aristides

claims.text: Aristides was an Athenian general at Marathon in 490 BC and one of the archons in the following years.
He was ostracised in about 482 BC, after a political conflict with Themistocles.
Ostraka bearing his name have been found in Athens.
He was recalled under the amnesty of 480 BC and fought at Salamis and Plataea.
After the founding of the Delian League, he set the first assessment of allied contributions.
The story that an illiterate voter asked Aristides himself to write "Aristides" on an ostrakon is an anecdote.

summary: Athenian statesman nicknamed "the Just", rival of Themistocles, who assessed the tribute of the Delian League.
significance: Aristides was remembered as the incorruptible politician, and his rivalry with Themistocles frames the early history of the Athenian empire.
body:
Aristides (c. 530–468 BC) was an Athenian of good family, active in politics from Marathon to the founding of the Delian League. His reputation was for justice, and the epithet "the Just" attached to him early, though Herodotus, who calls him the best and most just man in Athens, does not use it as a title.

The quarrel with Themistocles was about policy. Themistocles wanted to spend the silver from Laurion on a fleet; Aristides is said to have preferred to keep Athens an army city. In the ostracism of about 482, Aristides lost and was sent away for ten years, and the fleet was built. The Athenian Agora has yielded ostraka with his name. Plutarch's tale of the illiterate voter, who asked Aristides to write his own name, belongs to the moral tradition.

When Xerxes invaded, Aristides was recalled. He appears at Salamis, where he landed troops on the island of Psyttaleia and killed the Persian garrison, and at Plataea, where he commanded the Athenian contingent. In 478/7, after the Ionian Greeks turned to Athens, he assessed the contributions that each member of the new League would pay, a figure of 460 talents, which Thucydides and later writers recalled as fair.

Plutarch says he died so poor that the city paid for his funeral and dowered his daughters. The detail is a tribute to his image, not a proven fact.

name: Xenophanes

claims.text: Xenophanes of Colophon criticised Homer and Hesiod for attributing theft, adultery and deceit to the gods.
He argued that people make gods in their own image: Ethiopians make theirs snub-nosed and dark, Thracians red-haired and blue-eyed, and horses would make theirs horses.
He described one supreme god, unlike mortals in body or thought, who governs all things by the power of his mind.
Later writers report that he cited fossil shells found inland as evidence that the sea had once covered the land.
Antiquity called him the founder of the Eleatic school, a tradition modern scholars question.

summary: Ionian poet-philosopher who ridiculed the human-shaped gods of Homer and argued for a single, unlike-mortal divinity.
significance: Xenophanes is the earliest surviving critic of Greek religion from inside the tradition, and a pioneer of the argument that human beliefs about the gods reflect the people who hold them.
body:
Xenophanes came from Colophon, in Ionia, and by his own account spent sixty-seven years wandering the Greek world after leaving his home. Tradition connects the departure with the Persian conquest of Ionia in the 540s BC. He is later found in Sicily and southern Italy, and one ancient story places him at Elea, where he is said to have taught.

He wrote in verse, including elegies for symposia and satirical poems. The surviving lines are among the earliest sustained criticism of religion in the Greek world. He objected that Homer and Hesiod had ascribed to the gods everything that is shameful among men, and observed that people picture gods like themselves: Ethiopians with snub noses, Thracians with red hair, and, if horses or oxen could draw, gods in the shape of horses and oxen. He proposed instead a single greatest god, unlike mortals in body and in thought, who shakes all things without moving by the thinking of his mind.

The fragments also touch on knowledge. He wrote that no one has seen or will know the truth about the gods and about all he speaks of, and that even one who spoke the truth by chance would not know it. Scholars debate whether this is a sceptical claim or an admission of the limits of human inquiry into what cannot be observed.

Later writers say he noted fossils of shells and fish in quarries, and reasoned that the land had once been under water. The evidence is a report in a Christian author, so it should be treated with care. Aristotle already ranked him with the Eleatics, but modern scholars are divided on how far he influenced Parmenides. He is best understood as an independent critic whose questions later thinkers were able to use.

name: Zeno of Elea

claims.text: Zeno of Elea was a pupil and defender of Parmenides.
His paradoxes of motion, including the Achilles and the tortoise, the dichotomy and the arrow, are preserved in Aristotle's Physics.
He argued that if reality were a plurality, it would have to be both limited and unlimited, and both large and small.
Plato's Parmenides has a young Socrates meet the elderly Zeno and Parmenides at Athens; the meeting is probably fictional.
Several conflicting stories describe Zeno's death in a failed attempt to overthrow a tyrant, in which he bit off his tongue rather than betray his companions.

summary: Eleatic philosopher whose paradoxes of motion and plurality set a problem about infinity that took two thousand years to resolve.
significance: Zeno showed that everyday ideas about space, time and motion lead to contradictions, and forced later thinkers to say more precisely what they meant.
body:
Zeno (c. 490–430 BC) was a citizen of Elea in southern Italy and a follower of Parmenides. According to Plato, he wrote a book in his youth to defend Parmenides against those who mocked the claim that reality is one. If there are many things, Zeno argued, the consequences are even more absurd than those of monism.

Aristotle preserves the four best-known arguments against motion. In the dichotomy, to reach any goal one must first go half of the way, then half of what remains, and so an infinite number of tasks must be completed. In the Achilles, the fastest runner can never overtake a tortoise with a head start, since he must first reach where it was, by which time it has moved on. In the arrow, a flying arrow occupies at each instant a space equal to itself, and so is at rest at every instant. In the stadium, the same distance seems to take both a time and its double. Aristotle answered them, and later thinkers used Zeno's arguments to press questions about infinity and continuity.

The paradoxes were not intended to prove that motion is impossible for its own sake. They tested the assumption that space and time are infinitely divisible. Mathematicians in the nineteenth century, with the theory of limits, supplied a way to sum an infinite series to a finite value, and many scholars think this answers the first two paradoxes; the arrow and stadium raise more debated questions about the nature of instants.

The ancient biographical tradition reports that Zeno died opposing a tyrant, though the tyrant's name and the manner of his death vary in every account. It is best treated as a legend shaped by the image of the philosopher as a man of courage.

name: Leucippus

claims.text: Aristotle and Theophrastus name Leucippus as the originator of atomism, and Democritus as his associate or pupil.
The atomists held that reality consists of indivisible bodies moving in an infinite void.
Leucippus's place of origin is given variously as Miletus, Abdera or Elea.
Diogenes Laertius reports that Epicurus denied Leucippus had ever existed.
A work called The Great World-System is attributed to him in the ancient lists, with Democritus as its possible author.

summary: Shadowy founder of atomism, who answered Parmenides by allowing empty space and unchangeable bodies to move within it.
significance: If Leucippus existed, he originated the idea that the world is built of atoms and void, one of the most successful explanatory ideas in the history of science.
body:
Leucippus (5th century BC) was a Greek philosopher, probably from Miletus or Abdera, credited with founding atomism.

Almost nothing is securely known about Leucippus. Aristotle and his pupil Theophrastus attribute the founding of atomism to him, and treat Democritus as his continuator. Later biographers place him at Miletus, at Abdera or at Elea, which suggests they did not know. Epicurus is reported to have denied that any such philosopher existed, perhaps because he wished to claim Democritus as the founder of atomism, or because the real evidence was thin.

The system attributed to him is a response to Parmenides. Parmenides said that what is cannot fail to be, so there can be no void and no change. Leucippus is said to have accepted that what is cannot come to be from nothing, but insisted that there is also what is not, empty space. Then the world consists of countless tiny bodies, invisible, indivisible and without internal change, moving in that void. Things come to be when atoms join and cease when they separate. Differences between things arise from the shape, arrangement and position of the atoms.

Two features of the theory were important. It explained the birth of worlds without appeal to divine purpose, since atoms collide and cluster by necessity. And it made the qualities we perceive, such as colour and taste, depend on the observer, a move Democritus developed further.

We cannot separate Leucippus's own contribution from Democritus's with any confidence, since the ancient reports often name them together. Only one sentence is quoted as his: that nothing happens at random, but everything for a reason and by necessity. Anything more detailed comes from Democritus, the sources that describe the atomists, or later Epicurean writers.

name: Gorgias

claims.text: Gorgias of Leontini led an embassy from his city to Athens in 427 BC and impressed the Athenians with his speaking.
His Encomium of Helen and Defence of Palamedes survive complete.
On Not-Being argues that nothing exists, that if anything existed it could not be known, and that if it could be known it could not be communicated; it survives only in summaries.
Scholars disagree about whether On Not-Being is a serious position, a parody of Eleatic arguments or a demonstration of rhetorical skill.
Plato's dialogue Gorgias uses him to question whether rhetoric without knowledge of justice is a genuine skill.

summary: Sicilian sophist and teacher of rhetoric who brought ornate prose to Athens and argued that nothing exists or can be known.
significance: Gorgias made the power of speech itself a theme of philosophy, and his lost treatise on non-being remains one of the boldest arguments in Greek thought.
body:
Gorgias came from Leontini in Sicily. In 427 BC, when his city sought Athenian help against Syracuse, he headed the embassy, and Diodorus says his oratory astonished an audience unused to its ornate balance and rhythm. He stayed in Greece for the rest of a very long life, teaching for high fees and speaking at Olympia and Delphi.

Two speeches survive. In the Encomium of Helen he argues that Helen is blameless for going to Troy, whether she was carried off by force, persuaded by words, or overcome by love, and in doing so describes speech as a powerful ruler that can drive out fear and awaken pity. In the Defence of Palamedes he speaks for a mythical man falsely accused of treason. Both are exercises in argument as much as sincere claims.

His treatise On Not-Being is known through summaries by Sextus Empiricus and the author of On Melissus, Xenophanes and Gorgias. It has three theses: nothing exists; if anything exists, it cannot be known; and if it can be known, it cannot be communicated. It reads as a reply to Parmenides that uses Eleatic methods against Eleatic conclusions. Readers are still divided over whether it is a serious metaphysical claim, a spoof, or a showpiece.

Plato gave the name Gorgias to a dialogue in which Socrates questions the value of rhetoric without knowledge of justice, and in which Gorgias is a courteous but outmatched opponent. It is our most influential judgement of him, and a hostile one. Gorgias's own view was that rhetoric offers persuasion and pleasure, and that teachers of it are not responsible for the uses to which their pupils put it.

name: Antisthenes

claims.text: Antisthenes was a close follower of Socrates and is named among those present at his death in Plato's Phaedo.
He is said to have studied first under the sophist Gorgias.
He taught that virtue is sufficient for happiness and can be taught, and that virtue is shown in deeds, not in many words.
Diogenes Laertius makes him the founder of the Cynic way of life, teaching at the Cynosarges gymnasium; modern scholars doubt that he founded a school.
Ancient lists give him about ten volumes of works; only fragments survive.

summary: Athenian follower of Socrates who emphasised virtue and self-sufficiency, and was later counted as the first Cynic.
significance: Antisthenes represents the austere line in Socrates's legacy, and the link that ancient writers drew between Socrates and the Cynics and Stoics.
body:
Antisthenes (c. 445–365 BC) was an Athenian of mixed background who, according to Diogenes Laertius, walked daily from Piraeus to hear Socrates. Before that he had studied with Gorgias, and his writing shows the influence of both men. Plato, who mentions him only once, lists him among those with Socrates at his death.

He is said to have taken from Socrates the ideal of self-mastery and made it austere. Virtue, he held, can be taught, is sufficient for happiness, and requires only a Socratic strength of character. Wealth, reputation and pleasure are not goods. Diogenes Laertius records that he wore a doubled cloak, carried a staff and a wallet, and wrote on language, logic, ethics and Homer. In Xenophon's Symposium he is a lively participant, arguing that riches and poverty lie in the soul.

His reputation as the first Cynic comes from later writers, who needed a line of descent from Socrates through Antisthenes and Diogenes to Crates and Zeno of Citium. Modern scholars are more cautious. The evidence for a Cynic school before Diogenes is thin, and Antisthenes's other interests, in logic, language and Homeric allegory, are hardly Cynic.

His works are lost apart from fragments and a few titles. He counts as one of the "minor Socratics" who developed different sides of Socrates's teaching, alongside Plato, Xenophon, Aristippus and Euclides of Megara.

name: Aristippus of Cyrene

claims.text: Aristippus of Cyrene came to Athens to hear Socrates and, according to Plato's Phaedo, was not present at his death.
He held that pleasure, especially present bodily pleasure, is the goal of life.
He is reported to have accepted fees, to have lived at the court of Dionysius I of Syracuse, and to have taught that one should enjoy without being enslaved by enjoyment.
The Cyrenaic school was probably systematised by his grandson, Aristippus the Younger, and by later followers.
Xenophon has Socrates argue against Aristippus in the Memorabilia; the portrait is hostile.

summary: Socratic from Cyrene who taught that pleasure is the highest good, in contrast to the austere followers of Socrates.
significance: Aristippus began the hedonist tradition in Greek ethics that Epicurus later refined into a system centred on tranquillity.
body:
Aristippus (c. 435–356 BC) was born at Cyrene, the Greek city in Libya, and came to Athens attracted by the fame of Socrates. Unlike Plato and Antisthenes, he charged for teaching and lived comfortably, often at the courts of tyrants. Plato in the Phaedo says he was not with Socrates on the last day, a remark some ancient writers took as a criticism.

The teaching attributed to him, or to his school, places the good in pleasure, and pleasure in the bodily sensation of the present moment. The future is uncertain and the past is gone, so only the present counts. But he is also said to have insisted on self-command, summed up in the remark that he possessed pleasure without being possessed by it. Anecdotes present him as adaptable, at ease with the poor and the powerful alike. In Xenophon's Memorabilia, Socrates rebukes him with the story of Heracles choosing between virtue and vice, which portrays him as a warning.

Knowing Aristippus is difficult because he may have written little, and the surviving reports are anecdotes gathered by Diogenes Laertius. The philosophical doctrines of the Cyrenaic school, including the claim that we can know only our own experiences, are more securely attested for his successors, especially his grandson Aristippus the Younger and the later Cyrenaics Hegesias and Anniceris.

Epicurus rejected the Cyrenaic emphasis on passing bodily pleasure, and defined pleasure as freedom from pain and disturbance. Even so, the debate between the two shaped Hellenistic ethics.

name: Pyrrho of Elis

claims.text: Pyrrho of Elis accompanied Alexander the Great's army to India, in the entourage of the philosopher Anaxarchus.
He wrote nothing; his teaching is known through his follower Timon of Phlius, and through later summaries.
He taught that things are indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable, and that the wise person should suspend judgement to reach tranquillity.
Whether Pyrrho's ideas were influenced by what he met in India, and by early Buddhism in particular, is disputed.
Pyrrhonism was revived as a formal school by Aenesidemus in the first century BC and set out by Sextus Empiricus in the second century AD.

summary: Elean philosopher who travelled to India with Alexander and taught that suspending judgement leads to tranquillity.
significance: Pyrrho gave his name to the most radical form of ancient scepticism, and his encounter with the East is one of the classic questions in the history of philosophy.
body:
Pyrrho (c. 360–270 BC) was born at Elis and began as a painter, according to Diogenes Laertius. He then studied under Anaxarchus, a follower of Democritus, and joined Alexander's expedition to Asia. Ancient sources say he met Indian ascetics, the gymnosophists, and Persian magi, and that this changed his thinking.

He left no writings. What we know comes from his pupil Timon of Phlius, a satirical poet, through a passage that survives in the fourth-century Christian author Eusebius, who quotes the Peripatetic Aristocles. It says that for anyone who wishes to be happy, three questions arise: what things are like, how we should relate to them, and what will result. The answer is that things are equally indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable, that we should therefore neither trust nor distrust the senses or opinion but remain without judgement, and that the outcome will be first silence, then freedom from disturbance.

Scholars disagree about what Pyrrho believed. Some read him as an epistemological sceptic; others take the claim to be metaphysical, that things themselves lack a fixed nature. The suggestion that he was influenced by Indian thought, and by early Buddhist ideas of impermanence and non-attachment, has been defended by Christopher Beckwith and criticised by others for the thinness of the evidence.

Whatever he thought, he won great respect. Elis made him high priest and Athens gave him citizenship. Later Pyrrhonists, especially Sextus Empiricus, presented themselves as his heirs, and his name became a synonym for radical doubt.

name: Chrysippus

claims.text: Chrysippus of Soli became the third head of the Stoic school around 230 BC, after Zeno of Citium and Cleanthes.
Diogenes Laertius credits him with more than 700 books; none survives complete.
He is regarded as the systematiser of Stoic logic, including a logic of propositions.
An ancient saying ran that without Chrysippus there would be no Stoa.
The story that he died laughing at a donkey eating figs is legendary.

summary: Third head of the Stoa, whose voluminous writing turned Zeno's teaching into a complete philosophical system.
significance: Chrysippus's work on logic and on fate and freedom made Stoicism the dominant philosophy of the Hellenistic and Roman world.
body:
Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BC) was born at Soli in Cilicia and came to Athens as a young man. He studied with Cleanthes, Zeno's successor, and also with sceptical members of the Academy, which gave him an unusual skill in arguing against his own positions. When Cleanthes died about 230 BC, Chrysippus took charge of the Stoa.

Diogenes Laertius lists more than 700 books and adds that he wrote as many as 500 lines a day. All of them are lost, and the tradition depends on quotation. Yet the scale of the work explains the ancient saying that without Chrysippus there would be no Stoa: he elaborated Zeno's ideas into a coherent account of logic, physics and ethics, and defended them against Academic and Epicurean objections.

His most lasting contribution was in logic. Where Aristotle's syllogistic reasons about terms, Chrysippus worked out a logic of propositions, with rules for combining "if", "and" and "or", and modern logicians regard this as a real precursor of the propositional calculus. In physics he argued that the cosmos is a single rational whole, permeated by a breath he called pneuma, and that everything happens by fate. In ethics he faced the problem of freedom: he argued that we are responsible for our actions because they follow from our own character, even though that character is itself part of the causal chain.

The old anecdote that he died laughing at a donkey eating figs, after telling its owner to give it wine to wash them down, may be a joke made at the expense of a famously serious man.

name: Melissus of Samos

claims.text: Melissus commanded the Samian fleet that defeated an Athenian squadron in the Samian revolt of 440 BC.
He wrote a prose treatise defending Parmenides, of which about ten fragments survive in Simplicius.
Unlike Parmenides, he argued that what exists is unlimited in extent and in time.
He argued that what is one must be unchanging and without a body, since a body would have parts.

summary: Samian admiral and Eleatic philosopher who defended Parmenides in prose and argued that being is boundless.
significance: Melissus gave the Eleatic argument its clearest prose form, and is the rare early philosopher known to have won a naval battle.
body:
Melissus of Samos is one of the few ancient philosophers who also held military command. Plutarch reports that when Samos revolted from Athens in 440 BC, Melissus led the Samian fleet and defeated an Athenian squadron while Pericles was away, at least for a time. The revolt ended in Athenian victory the following year.

As a philosopher he belongs to the Eleatic tradition. Where Parmenides had written a hexameter poem, Melissus wrote plain prose, and the ten or so fragments that survive in Simplicius read as a chain of short arguments. He argues that what is has no beginning or end, since it would have to come from nothing; that it is therefore unlimited in time; and, unlike Parmenides, who described being as a finite sphere, that it is unlimited in extent. A single, unlimited thing cannot move, since there is nowhere for it to move into, and cannot have a body, since bodies have parts.

He took the conclusion seriously. The world of change that our senses report must therefore be an illusion, or the senses are unreliable. Aristotle thought his arguments were crude compared with Parmenides', but later thinkers, including the atomists, took them as a challenge, and a work critical of him appears among the writings in the Aristotelian corpus.

name: Philolaus of Croton

claims.text: Philolaus was a Pythagorean, reported to have been the first to set the school's doctrine down in writing.
He described a cosmos with a central fire, around which the earth, the sun, the moon, the planets and a counter-earth revolve.
He held that all things are composed of limiters and unlimiteds, joined in harmony.
Whether the fragments attributed to him are authentic is debated; some scholars treat them as later forgeries.
