Plato's Phaedo names Simmias and Cebes as having been taught by Philolaus at Thebes.

summary: Pythagorean from southern Italy whose cosmos, with a central fire and a moving earth, broke with the idea that the earth is the centre.
significance: Philolaus's system is the earliest Greek account that set the earth in motion, and our best witness to Pythagorean thought before Plato.
body:
Philolaus was a Pythagorean, born at Croton or Taras, who in the fifth century BC left Italy, perhaps after the political attacks on the Pythagorean communities, and taught at Thebes. According to Plato's Phaedo, two of the people present at Socrates's death, Simmias and Cebes, had been his pupils. Ancient tradition calls him the first Pythagorean to write his teaching down.

Aristotle describes his cosmology. At the centre of the universe is a fire, not the sun. The earth is one of ten bodies revolving around it: the sphere of the fixed stars, the five planets, the sun, the moon, the earth and a hidden "counter-earth", probably added to bring the number up to ten, the perfect number. It is not a heliocentric model, and it was not based on observation, but it removes the earth from the centre and puts it in motion, and later astronomers, including Aristarchus, sometimes cited it.

The surviving fragments say that everything consists of "limiters" and "unlimiteds" fitted together by harmony, and that number makes things knowable. Their authenticity is disputed. Walter Burkert regarded them as forgeries of the Hellenistic age, and other scholars, led by Carl Huffman, defend most of them as genuine. The question matters, because on Huffman's view Philolaus supplies the only reliable early evidence for Pythagorean philosophy in the writers' own words.

name: Archytas of Tarentum

claims.text: Archytas led the city of Taras (Tarentum) as a general, reportedly elected seven times, although the law normally barred re-election.
He found a solution to doubling the cube by a three-dimensional construction.
He applied mathematics to music, giving ratios for the tetrachords.
Plato's Seventh Letter says Archytas intervened to bring him safely from Syracuse, though the letter's authenticity is debated.
A story preserved by Aulus Gellius says he built a wooden dove that could fly.

summary: Pythagorean statesman and mathematician who ruled Taras, solved the doubling of the cube, and was a friend of Plato.
significance: Archytas shows the Pythagorean tradition in its most rigorous form, and is the model of the philosopher in politics that Plato admired.
body:
Archytas lived in Taras, the Spartan colony in southern Italy, and led it in the first half of the fourth century BC. Diogenes Laertius says he was chosen as general seven times, in defiance of a law that barred anyone from holding the office more than a year, and was never defeated.

As a mathematician he is the most important figure between the early Pythagoreans and Euclid. He found a solution to the problem of doubling the cube, which asks for the edge of a cube with twice the volume of a given one, by finding the intersection of three surfaces. It is an ingenious construction in three dimensions and was much admired. He also studied harmonic ratios and proved, according to Boethius, that no mean proportional can exist between numbers in a superparticular ratio, a result important for the theory of musical intervals.

Plato knew him and visited Taras on his trip to Italy. The Seventh Letter, whose authenticity is debated, says that Archytas sent a ship to bring Plato away from Syracuse when the tyrant Dionysius II held him. A late Roman author reports a wooden dove that could fly, powered by compressed air. It is best treated as a legend that grew around a well-known engineer.

Only fragments of his writings survive, some of which may be authentic. His importance lies in the combination of political leadership, mathematical originality and musical theory, which made him for later writers the ideal Pythagorean.

name: Archelaus of Athens

claims.text: Archelaus was a pupil of Anaxagoras and is reported to have taught natural philosophy at Athens.
Later sources call him the teacher of Socrates.
Ion of Chios is said to have reported that Socrates travelled to Samos with Archelaus.
He taught that air is infinite, and that hot and cold drive the formation of the world.
He held that animals first arose from warm slime.

summary: Pupil of Anaxagoras, traditionally the link between the natural philosophers and Socrates.
significance: Archelaus is the figure through whom ancient writers connected Ionian natural philosophy to Socrates, which shows how they wanted the story to run.
body:
Archelaus (5th century BC) was an Athenian philosopher, a pupil of Anaxagoras and, by tradition, a teacher of Socrates.

Archelaus is known almost entirely from short reports in Diogenes Laertius and later doxographers. He is said to have been the pupil of Anaxagoras, to have been born in Athens or Miletus, and to have taught natural philosophy at Athens. Ancient writers added that Socrates was his pupil, and that the Socratic turn to ethics came from Archelaus's own remark that just and shameful things exist not by nature but by convention.

The link with Socrates is weak. Diogenes Laertius cites Ion of Chios, a contemporary, for a journey that Socrates made to Samos in the company of Archelaus, which suggests a real acquaintance, but Plato never mentions Archelaus and Aristotle never calls him the teacher of Socrates. It is probably an invention that made Socrates the heir of natural philosophy, which is exactly the place Plato's Socrates denies he held.

His own doctrine, as reported, was a modified form of Anaxagoras's. The world began as a mixture in which air, which is infinite, is moved by the opposition of hot and cold; the cold condenses into earth and the hot rarefies into fire. Living things arose from warm slime and were later reproduced sexually. These are the ideas that place him among the natural philosophers, and for which he is remembered.

name: Prodicus of Ceos

claims.text: Prodicus was a sophist from Ceos who visited Athens as an envoy and taught for fees.
He was known for distinguishing the exact meanings of near-synonymous words.
Xenophon preserves his parable of Heracles at the crossroads, choosing between Virtue and Vice.
Later writers say he explained the gods as deifications of useful things, such as bread, wine and the sun.
Plato makes Socrates joke that he had attended only the cheap lecture of Prodicus, not the fifty-drachma one.

summary: Sophist from Ceos known for distinguishing the exact meanings of words and for the parable of Heracles' choice.
significance: Prodicus shows the Sophists' interest in language itself, and his parable of Heracles became one of the most retold moral fables in antiquity.
body:
Prodicus (c. 465–395 BC) came from the island of Ceos and visited Athens often, sometimes as his city's envoy, and lectured for fees throughout Greece. Plato's dialogues treat him with mild mockery. In the Protagoras he appears lying in bed surrounded by blankets, expounding on the exact sense of words; in the Cratylus Socrates says that he took only the one-drachma lecture.

His speciality was what he called the correctness of names: he insisted on separating words that people use as if they were the same, such as "angry" and "irritated", "wish" and "desire". It is one of the earliest attempts at a systematic study of meaning, and it affected the way Socrates and Plato approached definitions.

The best-known work attributed to him is the story of Heracles at the crossroads, told by Xenophon in the Memorabilia. The young hero is met by two women, Virtue and Vice, who offer him a hard road to glory or an easy road to pleasure, and he chooses Virtue. Xenophon gives the story a Socratic slant, so the exact wording is probably his, but the outline is Prodicus's.

Later writers credit him with a theory of religion in which people first worshipped the things that helped them, such as the sun, rivers, bread and wine, and then the discoverers of these things. The report comes from Sextus Empiricus, centuries later, and its details are uncertain.

name: Euclides of Megara

claims.text: Euclides of Megara was a close follower of Socrates and is named in Plato's Phaedo as present at his death.
After the trial of Socrates, Plato and others are said to have taken refuge at Megara with Euclides.
He held that the good is one, though called by many names, and that what is opposed to the good does not exist.
The Megarian school that followed him was known for logic and paradoxes such as the Liar.
He should not be confused with the mathematician Euclid, who lived a century later.

summary: Follower of Socrates who founded the Megarian school, known for logic and paradox, and who is not the mathematician Euclid.
significance: The Megarians developed the logical side of Socrates's questioning, and their puzzles helped make logic a separate discipline.
body:
Euclides (c. 435–365 BC) came from Megara, which lay on the road between Athens and the Peloponnese. Plato's Phaedo names him among those present at Socrates's death, and Plato's Theaetetus is framed as a conversation he had written down. Diogenes Laertius says that after the execution of Socrates, Plato and other followers withdrew to Megara and stayed with him.

His own teaching is poorly known. Diogenes Laertius attributes to him the view that the good is one, although it is called by several names, such as wisdom, god and intelligence, and that what is opposed to the good does not exist. It recalls Parmenides, and suggests that Euclides combined Socratic ethics with Eleatic arguments about unity. He also criticised arguments by analogy, which ancient writers took to show his interest in logic.

His followers carried that interest further. Eubulides of Miletus, a later Megarian, is credited with the Liar paradox ("a man says he is lying; is he telling the truth?") and with the Heap. Diodorus Cronus worked out an influential account of possibility, and Stilpo taught Zeno of Citium before he founded the Stoa, which is one way in which Megarian logic passed to the Stoics.

Modern readers sometimes confuse Euclides with Euclid, the author of the Elements. They lived a century apart, and the confusion goes back to the Middle Ages, when the geometer was often described as "Euclid of Megara".

name: Speusippus

claims.text: Speusippus was Plato's nephew and succeeded him as head of the Academy in 347 BC.
He held the school until his death in 339 BC, when Xenocrates succeeded him.
He rejected Plato's Forms, and treated mathematical objects and numbers as the basic realities.
Aristotle criticised his universe as "episodic", like a bad tragedy in which the parts are not connected.
He wrote widely, including on classification of plants and animals, but only fragments survive.

summary: Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy, who replaced the Forms with numbers as first principles.
significance: Speusippus shows how quickly the Academy moved away from Plato's own doctrine, and he anticipated the classification of living things that Aristotle carried out.
body:
Speusippus was the son of Plato's sister Potone, and lived in the philosopher's household. He went with Plato to Sicily and was the obvious choice as successor when Plato died in 347 BC. Diogenes Laertius records that he fell ill with paralysis in old age, and handed the school on to Xenocrates in 339.

He did not simply defend Plato's teaching. According to Aristotle, he rejected the Forms and made numbers and geometrical objects the basic realities, derived from a pair of principles, the One and multiplicity. He also denied that the One is the same as the Good, which he regarded as a later, emergent result. Aristotle complained that Speusippus's universe is "episodic", like a poor tragedy in which the episodes are not connected by any necessity.

Speusippus wrote on a huge range of subjects. His lists of similar and dissimilar things, reported by Athenaeus, mark an early attempt to classify plants and animals by their shared features, a programme that Aristotle and Theophrastus later developed.

He was also known as a defender of the claim that pleasure is not a good, and as a man of ill temper who quarrelled with Aristotle. The reports come largely from hostile anecdote, and only fragments of his work survive.

name: Xenocrates of Chalcedon

claims.text: Xenocrates succeeded Speusippus as head of the Academy in 339 BC and led it until 314 BC.
After Plato's death he left Athens with Aristotle for Assos, on the coast of Asia Minor.
He is credited with the division of philosophy into logic, physics and ethics, which the Stoics later adopted.
He taught that there are intermediate beings between gods and humans, daimons, some of them good and some evil.
Ancient biographies stress his moral seriousness and dignity.

summary: Head of the Academy for a quarter of a century, known for his moral gravity, his theory of daimons, and the threefold division of philosophy.
significance: Xenocrates turned the Academy's teaching into a tidy system, and is the probable source of the logic-physics-ethics scheme the Stoics took over.
body:
Xenocrates came from Chalcedon, on the Bosphorus, and joined Plato's Academy as a young man. After Plato's death in 347 BC he left Athens, with Aristotle, for Assos and the court of Hermias, and returned later. When Speusippus died in 339 he was chosen to lead the school, a position he held until 314.

He systematised Plato's later thought. Like Speusippus, he made numbers central, but he identified the Forms with mathematical objects instead of discarding them. He is credited with dividing philosophy into logic, physics and ethics, which later became the standard scheme in Stoic teaching. And he developed a theory of daimons, intermediate beings between gods and humans, which he used to explain why religious stories portray gods acting badly: such acts belong to the less perfect daimons.

Ancient writers admired his character. Anecdotes describe him as grave and incorruptible, said to have kept only a small part of a large gift from Alexander, and unmoved by the charms of the courtesan Phryne, and so respected that an Athenian jury is said to have refused to let him swear an oath. Plutarch reports that he led a delegation to the Macedonian regent Antipater in 322 BC to plead for Athenian prisoners.

Nothing of his many books survives except titles and fragments, preserved by Plutarch, Sextus Empiricus and others.

name: Arcesilaus of Pitane

claims.text: Arcesilaus became head of the Academy around 268 BC and led it until his death in 241 BC.
He turned the Academy towards scepticism, arguing that nothing can be known with certainty and that one should suspend judgement.
His main target was the Stoic claim that some impressions are so clear that they guarantee their own truth.
He wrote nothing, and taught by questioning and arguing against whatever thesis a student proposed.
Modern scholars call the sceptical Academy of Arcesilaus and his successors the Middle Academy.

summary: Head of the Academy who turned Plato's school towards scepticism, arguing against the Stoics that certainty is unattainable.
significance: Arcesilaus made doubt a method of teaching, and forced the Stoics to sharpen their theory of knowledge in reply.
body:
Arcesilaus was born at Pitane in Aeolis, studied in Athens and became head of the Academy about 268 BC. He reinterpreted Plato's Socrates as a questioner who claimed to know nothing, and taught in the same way, inviting a pupil to propose a thesis and then arguing against it, so that the student could see that reasons could be found on both sides.

His chief opponent was Zeno of Citium. Zeno claimed that the wise person could recognise certain impressions, which he called cognitive, as so clear and distinct that they must be true. Arcesilaus argued that for any such impression a false one indistinguishable from it could be found, so nothing is certain, and the wise person should suspend judgement on everything. The issue of how to act without certain knowledge led to the later Academic theory of the probable or reasonable.

He wrote nothing, so his positions are known through hostile or second-hand reports from Cicero, Plutarch and Sextus Empiricus. Scholars disagree about whether he was sincerely sceptical or simply a dialectician, using Stoic premises to embarrass them. Among those who heard him, according to Diogenes Laertius, was the young Chrysippus, who learned from him the skill of arguing both sides.

Ancient biographers describe a generous, witty, wealthy man with a love of Homer, who died after drinking too much undiluted wine.

name: Carneades

claims.text: Carneades of Cyrene became head of the Academy and carried its scepticism to its fullest form.
In 155 BC he went to Rome as part of an Athenian embassy, and spoke one day in favour of justice and the next against it.
Cato the Elder reportedly urged the Senate to send the embassy away quickly.
He argued that we can never have certain knowledge, but can act on impressions that are more or less convincing or probable.
He wrote nothing; his pupil Clitomachus recorded his teaching.

summary: Sceptical head of the Academy who argued both sides of justice before the Romans and developed a theory of probability.
significance: Carneades's arguments on justice introduced Greek philosophy to the Roman elite, and his theory of the probable is an early attempt to reason without certainty.
body:
Carneades (214–129 BC) was born at Cyrene and came to Athens, where he studied with the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon and the Academic Hegesinus, and later led the Academy. He wrote nothing, and what we know comes from Cicero and Sextus Empiricus, who used the records of his pupil Clitomachus.

In 155 BC the Athenians sent an embassy to Rome to appeal against a fine, and the three envoys included the heads of the three main schools: Carneades for the Academy, Diogenes of Babylon for the Stoa and Critolaus for the Peripatetics. Carneades gave two lectures. The first praised justice, in the manner of Plato and Aristotle. On the next day he refuted everything he had said and argued that justice is either foolish or merely conventional, since states that practise it cannot win empires. Plutarch says the young Romans were captivated, and that the elder Cato, alarmed, had the embassy sent home.

His philosophy attacked Stoic claims to certain knowledge. He argued that no impression is certain, but that some are more convincing than others, and that a person can act rationally by following the most plausible. This theory of the "persuasive" impression is an early example of reasoning under uncertainty.

He is reported to have said that without Chrysippus he would not exist, because his own arguments grew from answering the Stoic's. He died in 129 BC, at about eighty-five.

name: Strato of Lampsacus

claims.text: Strato succeeded Theophrastus as head of the Lyceum in about 287 BC and led it until his death.
He was nicknamed "the Physicist" for his concentration on the study of nature.
He served as tutor to the future Ptolemy II at Alexandria.
He argued that nature can account for the cosmos without a divine designer.
He held that small voids exist within matter, and supported the claim with experiments that showed air could be compressed.

summary: Third head of the Lyceum, nicknamed "the Physicist", who explained the cosmos by natural causes and tested ideas about air and void.
significance: Strato moved the Peripatetic school away from Aristotle's purposes in nature towards an experimental, more mechanical science.
body:
Strato came from Lampsacus on the Hellespont, studied under Theophrastus and took over the Lyceum after him, around 287 BC. Diogenes Laertius says he spent some years at Alexandria as tutor to the future Ptolemy II, and was well paid for it. He led the school until about 269.

His interest was in nature. He rejected the view that the world shows design, and argued that nature itself, with its heat and cold, weight and lightness, is enough to produce order. Cicero complained that he had "dismissed god from the task of making the world". He criticised Aristotle's claims that natural places pull bodies up and down, and argued that falling bodies accelerate.

The writer Hero of Alexandria reports, in his work on pneumatics, that Strato defended the existence of small voids between the particles of matter, and cited experiments with compressed air and with a vessel with a hole to show that air is a body that can be squeezed. The reports come from a much later writer, and scholars debate how far the experiments were Strato's own.

Strato's work is lost, although the titles list studies of motion, void, colour, animals and ethics. The Lyceum lost its vigour after his death, and later heads are hardly known.

name: Crates of Thebes

claims.text: Crates of Thebes became a Cynic and is reported to have given away his considerable property.
Diogenes Laertius makes him a pupil of Diogenes of Sinope, though other reports mention Stilpo.
He married the Cynic Hipparchia of Maroneia, who joined his way of life.
Zeno of Citium was his pupil before founding the Stoa.
He wrote philosophical verse, parodying Homer, and letters; only scraps survive.

summary: Theban Cynic who gave up his wealth, married Hipparchia, and taught Zeno, linking the Cynics to the Stoics.
significance: Crates carried the Cynic way of life into a gentler, more sociable form, and is the personal link between Cynicism and Stoicism.
body:
Crates (c. 365–285 BC) was born at Thebes into a wealthy family. Tradition says that he left his estate to the city, or gave it away, to become a Cynic, and lived with a wallet and staff, in the manner of Diogenes. The story is told in several versions, and Diogenes Laertius records that some sources say that he left a fortune in trust for his sons if they were ordinary people, and to the city if they became philosophers.

Where Diogenes was harsh, Crates was known for charm. Athenians nicknamed him the "door-opener" because he visited houses uninvited to offer advice and settle quarrels, and was welcomed. His poems, which parody Homer and Solon, describe an imaginary city called Pera, the Wallet, which is free of luxury and flatterers. Only fragments survive.

His marriage to Hipparchia of Maroneia is among the best known in antiquity. She took to the Cynic life with him, dressed as he did and debated in public. It is one of the earliest recorded philosophical partnerships between a man and a woman.

His most lasting effect was on Zeno of Citium, a Cypriot merchant shipwrecked at Athens, who heard him and then went on to study with other teachers. Stoic ideas of living according to nature and of virtue as the only good show the impress of Crates. Whether or not Crates truly studied with Diogenes of Sinope, later writers used him to tie the Cynic school to Stoicism.

name: Hipparchia of Maroneia

claims.text: Hipparchia of Maroneia, in Thrace, joined the Cynics and married Crates of Thebes.
According to Diogenes Laertius, she fell in love with Crates and threatened to kill herself if her parents did not let her marry him.
She lived as a Cynic, wearing the same simple cloak as Crates and taking part in men's discussions and dinners.
In a famous exchange she answered the logician Theodorus the Atheist with an argument of her own.
A Roman wall painting in the Villa Farnesina in Rome is thought to show her with Crates.

summary: Thracian woman who joined the Cynics, married Crates, and is one of the few ancient women philosophers with a recorded life.
significance: Hipparchia is the clearest case of a woman choosing the philosopher's life in the ancient world, and a rare corrective to a record made almost entirely by men.
body:
Hipparchia (c. 350–280 BC) was born at Maroneia on the Thracian coast, and came to Athens with her brother Metrocles, who studied under Theophrastus and later turned to Cynicism with Crates. According to Diogenes Laertius, she fell in love with Crates, despite his poverty and unattractive appearance, and was so determined to marry him that she threatened suicide. When her parents appealed to Crates to dissuade her, he is said to have stripped, pointed to his possessions and told her to decide.

She chose. She wore the Cynic cloak, travelled with Crates, and joined men's dinners and debates, something respectable Greek women did not do. The tradition adds that the couple made love in public, in the Cynic rejection of shame, although that story is typical of the stories told about Cynics and may be embellished.

One of the best-known anecdotes concerns the philosopher Theodorus the Atheist, who challenged her at a dinner with a sophism. She answered with a sophism of his own: what Theodorus may do to himself without wrong, Hipparchia may do to Theodorus. Asked why she had left the loom for study, she replied that she had not judged it a bad use of her time to educate herself. The point of the stories is her refusal to be silenced.

Some writings are credited to her, now lost, and our only real account is the brief biography in Diogenes Laertius. A fresco from the Villa Farnesina in Rome showing a man and woman in a Cynic pose is sometimes thought to depict the pair, but the identification is uncertain.

name: Cleanthes of Assos

claims.text: Cleanthes succeeded Zeno of Citium as head of the Stoa in 262 BC and led it until his death about 230 BC.
He is said to have been a boxer who arrived in Athens with little money, and supported his studies by drawing water at night.
His Hymn to Zeus, a prayer to the rational ordering power of the cosmos, survives complete.
He taught that the sun is the ruling centre of the cosmos.
Plutarch reports that Cleanthes thought the Greeks should prosecute Aristarchus of Samos for impiety for putting the earth in motion.

summary: Second head of the Stoa, the boxer who became a philosopher, and author of the Hymn to Zeus.
significance: Cleanthes kept the Stoa together after Zeno, and his Hymn is the most complete Stoic text to survive from the early school.
body:
Cleanthes (c. 330–230 BC) came from Assos in the Troad and, according to the biographical tradition, was a boxer before he turned to philosophy. Diogenes Laertius says that he arrived at Athens with four drachmas and worked at night, drawing water for a gardener, to pay for lessons from Zeno. The Athenians who saw this are supposed to have called him "the well-drawer". He became Zeno's pupil and, at his death in 262 BC, his successor.

Cleanthes was less inventive than Zeno and Chrysippus, but he was a reliable guardian of the school's doctrine, and stressed the physical side of Stoicism, in which a fiery breath pervades the cosmos. His Hymn to Zeus, preserved by Stobaeus, is a prayer in hexameters to Zeus as the ruler of nature, whose law governs all things, and asks to be led by fate willingly and not dragged unwillingly. It is the single best example of Stoic piety.

Plutarch records that Cleanthes believed Aristarchus of Samos ought to be charged with impiety for proposing that the earth moves around the sun, a remark that shows how disputed heliocentrism was. The passage is textually uncertain, and scholars debate how to read it.

Late in life he developed an illness of the gums and was told to fast. He recovered, but according to Diogenes Laertius, decided he had gone too far to turn back and starved himself to death. As so often in the Lives, the story may be shaped by its moral.

He was succeeded by Chrysippus, who had been his pupil.

name: Posidonius

claims.text: Posidonius, a Stoic from Apamea in Syria, taught at Rhodes and became its leading citizen.
He wrote widely on philosophy, history, geography, astronomy and the tides; his works are lost and survive only in quotations.
He travelled to Spain, where he observed the Atlantic tides at Gades and related them to the moon.
He made an estimate of the Earth's circumference, reported by Strabo and Cleomedes in differing versions.
Cicero describes an orrery, a mechanical model of the heavens, recently built by Posidonius.

summary: Stoic polymath of Rhodes who studied the tides, measured the earth and wrote a world history, and taught Cicero.
significance: Posidonius shows the Stoics at their most empirical, and his lost books were a main source for Roman writers on geography, astronomy and history.
body:
Posidonius was born at Apamea in Syria about 135 BC, studied in Athens under the Stoic Panaetius, and settled at Rhodes, where he led the city's government and ran a school. Cicero and Pompey both visited him there.

His interests were wide, and he treated them as parts of one Stoic system. In natural philosophy he held that the cosmos is bound together by a sympathy of its parts, which made it reasonable to link the tides to the moon. On a journey to Spain he watched the tides at Gades, present-day Cádiz, and recorded how they followed the lunar cycle. He also wrote a large history that continued Polybius, studies of peoples he encountered, including the Gauls, and works on ethics and the emotions, in which he returned to Plato's idea of a divided soul and criticised Chrysippus.

Two measurements are attributed to him. One was the circumference of the Earth, which Strabo and Cleomedes report in different values, so it is unclear which he chose. Cicero, in On the Nature of the Gods, describes a sphere "recently constructed by our friend Posidonius" that reproduced the motions of the sun, moon and planets. It has led some to think of the Antikythera Mechanism, which may have been made at Rhodes, although nothing ties Posidonius directly to it.

None of his books survives. Much of what we know comes from Strabo, Cicero, Seneca and Galen, who used him and often disagreed.

name: Panaetius of Rhodes

claims.text: Panaetius headed the Stoic school at Athens from about 129 BC until his death around 110 BC.
He was a friend of Scipio Aemilianus and spent time in Rome, where he taught the Roman elite.
His treatise On Duty was the model for Cicero's De Officiis.
He softened Stoic teaching, and doubted divination, astrology and the destruction of the world by fire.
He was a pupil of Diogenes of Babylon and of Antipater of Tarsus.

summary: Stoic from Rhodes who brought the school to the Roman elite and whose work On Duty shaped Cicero.
significance: Panaetius adapted Stoicism to Roman public life, and through Cicero his ideas about duty entered European moral thought.
body:
Panaetius was born on Rhodes about 185 BC, studied at Athens and Pergamon, and in the 140s BC travelled to Rome. There he joined the circle around Scipio Aemilianus, which also included the historian Polybius and the statesman Laelius, and accompanied Scipio on an embassy to the eastern Mediterranean. He became head of the Stoic school at Athens around 129 BC.

He reshaped Stoicism to suit men who held public office. He moved the emphasis from the ideal wise man, a figure few could be, to the ordinary person trying to do the right thing, and gave much attention to what is fitting in a given role. His treatise On Duty, now lost, set out four roles that each person plays: as a rational being, as an individual with particular talents, as a person of a given station, and as a person making choices. Cicero, in his own On Duties, says that he followed Panaetius closely, and through that book the Stoic ethics of duty reached medieval and modern Europe.

He also broke with earlier Stoics on several points. He doubted divination and astrology, which Chrysippus had defended, and denied that the world would be destroyed by fire, preferring Aristotle's view of an eternal cosmos. He admired Plato and Aristotle and quoted them often.

His writings are lost. The chief witnesses are Cicero and Seneca, and the later Stoic Posidonius, who was his pupil.

name: Metrodorus of Lampsacus

claims.text: Metrodorus was Epicurus's closest friend and pupil, who followed him from Lampsacus to Athens.
He died in 277 BC, seven years before Epicurus, who provided in his will for Metrodorus's children.
He wrote in defence of Epicurean doctrine against rival schools, including works against the physicians and the dialecticians.
He argued that the pleasures of the stomach are the origin of all good, a claim his critics took as crude.
Fragments of his writing were found among the papyri at Herculaneum.

summary: Epicurus's closest friend and first great disciple, who defended the Garden's teaching in writing.
significance: Metrodorus shows the Garden's ideal of friendship in practice, and was honoured as the second founder in the school's cult of its heroes.
body:
Metrodorus came from Lampsacus on the Hellespont, where Epicurus taught for a time before moving to Athens in 306 BC. He followed him, and stayed with him for the rest of his life. The Epicureans later ranked him next to Epicurus himself, along with Hermarchus and Polyaenus, as one of the four "leaders" of the school.

Epicurus's will, quoted by Diogenes Laertius, shows the depth of the tie. He asks that the children of Metrodorus be raised with the help of the school's funds, and orders that Metrodorus's memory, along with his own, be marked with a yearly feast. The images of the two men were preserved together, and several double herms survive.

Metrodorus wrote to defend the school against rivals. Titles include works against the physicians, the dialecticians and the sophists, against Timocrates, his own brother who left the school, and a treatise On Wealth. He has a reputation for taking Epicurus's position on pleasure at its crudest: a line preserved by Plutarch has him saying that "the belly" is the source of all good. Whether he meant it literally, or a more moderate point about bodily pleasure as the root of all others, is disputed.

Fragments of his work have been identified among the carbonised papyri from Herculaneum, together with quotations in Philodemus, Plutarch and Seneca. He died at fifty-three, and Epicurus's letters of consolation to his family are recorded.

name: Philodemus of Gadara

claims.text: Philodemus was an Epicurean philosopher and poet from Gadara in Syria, who settled in Italy.
His patron was Lucius Calpurnius Piso, the father-in-law of Julius Caesar.
Hundreds of his philosophical works were found as carbonised papyri in the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum.
About thirty of his witty, erotic epigrams are preserved in the Greek Anthology.
His treatises, on music, rhetoric, poetry, ethics and the gods, give first-hand evidence for Epicurean thought and for rival schools.

summary: Epicurean philosopher and poet whose library was buried at Herculaneum, and who brought Epicurean thought to Roman Italy.
significance: Philodemus's carbonised scrolls are the only philosophical library to survive from antiquity, and are still being read with new imaging techniques.
body:
Philodemus was born at Gadara in Syria and studied at Athens with the Epicurean Zeno of Sidon. He moved to Italy in the 70s BC and became the client of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul in 58 BC and father-in-law of Julius Caesar. Cicero attacked Piso in a speech, and in doing so gave a hostile sketch of his house-philosopher, who is agreeable but, he says, too refined for a rough patron.

He wrote on a range of subjects and gave a unique first-hand view of the Hellenistic schools' quarrels. Titles include On Music, On Poems, On Rhetoric, On Piety, On Signs, and a history of the philosophers. He also wrote light epigrams, about thirty of which survive in the Greek Anthology, and whose subjects are love and wine, in the Epicurean mode of enjoying the day.

In 1752 excavators at Herculaneum, the Roman town buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, found a villa with a library of more than 1,800 papyrus rolls, carbonised but partly legible. Most are works by Philodemus. The owner of this Villa of the Papyri was probably Piso himself. The scrolls were unrolled with great difficulty in the eighteenth century, and since then infrared imaging, multispectral imaging and other techniques have revealed more text.

As a result we can read a Hellenistic philosopher in his own words, including quotations from earlier Epicureans, such as Metrodorus, whose works are otherwise lost.

name: Nausiphanes of Teos

claims.text: Nausiphanes was a follower of Democritus from Teos, who is also said to have studied with Pyrrho.
Epicurus heard him lecture, according to Diogenes Laertius, and later denied that he had learned anything from him.
Epicurus insulted him as a "jellyfish" and an illiterate fraud.
He taught rhetoric as well as philosophy, and held that natural science is the best training for an orator.
Almost nothing of his writing survives.

summary: Democritean teacher from Teos, traditionally the link between the atomists and the young Epicurus.
significance: Nausiphanes is the route by which Democritus's atomism reached Epicurus, and Epicurus's hostility to him is a clue to how a founder disowned his debts.
body:
Nausiphanes (active late 4th century BC) came from Teos in Ionia and taught at Teos. Diogenes Laertius reports that he was a follower of Democritus and that he studied with Pyrrho, which connects him to two quite different traditions, atomism and scepticism. Epicurus spent time in Teos in his youth and, according to several ancient sources, attended Nausiphanes's lectures.

Epicurus later claimed to be self-taught, and went out of his way to denigrate his former teacher. Letters quoted by Diogenes Laertius call Nausiphanes a jellyfish, an illiterate and a fraud. The vehemence suggests a real debt, and modern scholars often see Nausiphanes as the man who introduced Epicurus to Democritean atomism.

Nausiphanes was known as a teacher of rhetoric. He is reported to have argued that the orator needs natural science more than any other training, and that nothing else prepares one so well for arguing either side. Epicurus rejected such claims.

A work called the Tripod is attributed to him. He seems to have admired an ideal of untroubled calm that Democritus and Pyrrho both valued, and its resemblance to Epicurus's own goal of freedom from disturbance is what makes the attribution of influence plausible, although it cannot be proved.

name: Timon of Phlius

claims.text: Timon of Phlius was a pupil of Pyrrho and the main source for his teaching.
He wrote the Silloi, a satirical poem in hexameters that mocked dogmatic philosophers.
The key statement of Pyrrho's teaching survives because Timon reported it, in a passage preserved by Eusebius from Aristocles.
He lived for periods at Chalcedon, Athens and possibly Alexandria, where he is said to have enjoyed royal favour.
Only fragments of his verse and prose survive.

summary: Pyrrho's pupil and satirical poet, who mocked rival philosophers in verse and preserved his teacher's thought.
significance: Since Pyrrho wrote nothing, Timon is the main reason we know what Pyrrho taught, and his Silloi are the earliest surviving philosophical satire.
body:
Timon (c. 320–230 BC) came from Phlius in the Peloponnese. According to Diogenes Laertius, he began as a dancer, then turned to philosophy, studied with the Megarian Stilpo and met Pyrrho at Elis, whom he followed. He lived in Chalcedon and Athens, and grew rich as a teacher of rhetoric and philosophy, before ending his life in Athens, where he died at about ninety.

His Silloi, in three books, was a hexameter poem of mockery in which the shades of the dead philosophers are summoned and laughed at. Parodying Homer, Timon ridiculed Plato for his inflated style, Zeno for his dogmatism, and the pretensions of the scholars at Alexandria, whom he called birds fed in a birdcage, the Museum. Only about 140 lines survive, and they are a mix of abuse and brilliant phrases. Pyrrho and Xenophanes are among the few spared.

More important is what he reported. A passage in Eusebius, taken from the Peripatetic Aristocles, gives Timon's summary of Pyrrho: that things are equally indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable, that we should therefore not trust the senses or opinions, and that the result will be silence and freedom from disturbance. Modern accounts of Pyrrho's own philosophy rest largely on this one text.

After Timon the school lapsed, and Pyrrhonism was revived only in the first century BC by Aenesidemus.

name: Anaxarchus of Abdera

claims.text: Anaxarchus of Abdera belonged to the atomist tradition of Democritus, and is called the "Eudaemonic" or happiness philosopher.
He accompanied Alexander the Great on his Asian campaign, and Pyrrho went with him.
He is reported to have flattered Alexander by calling him a god, and by arguing that a king could do no wrong.
Pyrrho is said to have learned from him.
According to a tale told by Diogenes Laertius, the tyrant Nicocreon of Salamis on Cyprus had him pounded to death in a mortar, and he defied him to the end.

summary: Democritean philosopher from Abdera who followed Alexander to Asia and taught Pyrrho.
significance: Anaxarchus is the link between Democritus and Pyrrho, and a case study in the philosopher as courtier.
body:
Anaxarchus (c. 380–320 BC) came from Abdera, the home of Democritus, and was trained in his tradition. He joined Alexander the Great's expedition and stayed with the king during the campaigns in Asia. His pupil Pyrrho of Elis went too, and this is how Pyrrho reached India. Both men are said to have observed the Indian ascetics, although the sources for that are later.

His reputation at court was mixed. Plutarch and Arrian portray him as a flatterer who urged Alexander to accept the honours due to a god, in contrast to the historian Callisthenes, who refused. In one story he consoled Alexander, who was tormented by remorse after killing his friend Cleitus, with the argument that the king's will is the law and whatever the king does is right. The philosopher's reputation as a flatterer stayed with him in the ancient biographies.

He was also known as the "Eudaemonic", a name that Diogenes Laertius connects to his attitude of cheerful contentment. A story told of him says that he was driven by a storm to Cyprus, where he fell into the hands of Nicocreon of Salamis, whom he had offended. Nicocreon had him pounded in a mortar with iron pestles. Anaxarchus is supposed to have replied, "Pound the pouch of Anaxarchus; you do not pound Anaxarchus." The story is a moral legend, meant to show a philosopher's indifference to pain.

Nothing survives of his writings.

name: Ephialtes

claims.text: In 462/1 BC Ephialtes carried reforms stripping the Areopagus council of most of its political powers.
The powers removed from the Areopagus passed to the Council of 500, the Assembly and the popular courts.
Ephialtes was assassinated soon after his reforms.

summary: The Athenian politician whose reforms of 462/1 BC took power from the aristocratic Areopagus and completed the democracy.
significance: The reformer who turned Cleisthenes' system into radical democracy — and was murdered for it.
body:
Ephialtes (died 461 BC) was a leading Athenian democratic politician of the 460s BC, known for his honesty and his prosecutions of corrupt officials. Little else is known of his life; he appears mainly in Aristotle's *Constitution of the Athenians* and in Plutarch.

The main remaining stronghold of aristocratic power in Athens was the Areopagus, a council of former archons who served for life and had broad powers to supervise officials and protect the laws. In 462/1 BC, while the conservative leader Cimon was away helping Sparta against a helot revolt, Ephialtes persuaded the Assembly to strip the Areopagus of these powers, leaving it chiefly a court for homicide. Its political functions passed to the Council of 500, the Assembly and the popular law courts — bodies drawn from the whole citizen body.

The reforms were bitterly contested. When Cimon returned, humiliated after Sparta sent his army home, he was ostracised. Soon afterwards Ephialtes was assassinated, one of the very few political murders in Classical Athens. His younger ally Pericles took over leadership of the democrats and extended the reforms, introducing pay for jurors.

Aeschylus' *Eumenides*, staged in 458 BC, which presents the Areopagus as a court founded by Athena to try homicide, has often been read as a response to these divisive events.

name: Hippias

claims.text: Hippias succeeded his father Peisistratus as tyrant of Athens in 527 BC.
His rule grew harsher after his brother Hipparchus was murdered in 514 BC.
A Spartan army under Cleomenes I expelled him in 510 BC.
He accompanied the Persian expedition to Marathon in 490 BC.

summary: The last tyrant of Athens, son of Peisistratus, expelled in 510 BC, who later guided the Persians to Marathon.
significance: His fall in 510 BC opened the way to Athenian democracy; his return with the Persians in 490 BC made Marathon a fight for the democracy's survival.
body:
Hippias (c. 570–490 BC) was the eldest son of Peisistratus, tyrant of Athens, and succeeded him in 527 BC, ruling with his brother Hipparchus. At first the brothers continued their father's moderate rule, keeping the laws, patronising poets and building temples.

In 514 BC Hipparchus was murdered at the Panathenaic festival by Harmodius and Aristogeiton, in a plot that Thucydides says grew from a personal quarrel. Hippias survived and became suspicious and harsh, executing and exiling opponents. The exiled Alcmaeonid family, with the backing of the Delphic oracle, persuaded Sparta to intervene. In 510 BC King Cleomenes I besieged Hippias on the Acropolis; when his children were captured trying to escape, he surrendered and left Athens. Within three years Cleisthenes had founded the democracy.

Hippias went to Sigeion in the Troad and then to the Persian court, hoping to return to power. In 490 BC, now old, he sailed with the Persian expedition against Athens and, Herodotus says, chose Marathon as the landing place. The Athenian victory there ended his hopes; he died soon after, perhaps on the way back to Asia.

His career shows how tyranny ended in Athens, and how closely the new democracy's survival was tied to the Persian Wars.

name: Harmodius and Aristogeiton

claims.text: Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus, brother of the tyrant Hippias, at the Panathenaia in 514 BC.
Thucydides says their motive was a personal quarrel, not opposition to tyranny.
A statue group of the pair by Kritios and Nesiotes was set up in the Agora in 477/6 BC.

summary: The two Athenians who killed Hipparchus, brother of the tyrant Hippias, in 514 BC, and were honoured as the heroes of Athenian freedom.
significance: The founding heroes of Athenian democracy's memory, whose statue group stood in the Agora as a symbol of resistance to tyranny.
body:
Harmodius and Aristogeiton were Athenian aristocrats and lovers. In 514 BC, at the Panathenaic festival, they attacked the ruling family of Athens. They meant to kill the tyrant Hippias, but killed his brother Hipparchus instead. Harmodius was cut down on the spot; Aristogeiton was caught and executed.

According to Thucydides, their motive was personal. Hipparchus had made advances to Harmodius, been rejected, and in revenge insulted his sister by excluding her from a festival procession. Thucydides tells the story precisely to correct the popular belief that the pair had freed Athens: tyranny in fact lasted four more years, until the Spartans expelled Hippias in 510 BC.

Nevertheless, democratic Athens remembered them as the Tyrannicides, the liberators of the city. Their descendants received special honours, and drinking songs celebrated them. A bronze statue group of the two by the sculptor Antenor was set up in the Agora; when the Persians carried it off in 480 BC, the Athenians commissioned a replacement from Kritios and Nesiotes in 477/6 BC. Alexander the Great later reportedly sent the original back from Persia.

The Kritios and Nesiotes group is known from Roman copies, the best in Naples, showing the two striding forward to strike. It became a symbol of resistance to tyranny.

name: Artemisia I of Caria

claims.text: Artemisia ruled Halicarnassus as a vassal of Persia and commanded five ships in Xerxes' fleet in 480 BC.
Herodotus says she advised Xerxes not to fight at Salamis.
At Salamis she escaped pursuit by ramming a ship on her own side.

summary: The queen of Halicarnassus who commanded ships for Xerxes at Salamis in 480 BC — the only woman commander in Herodotus' account of the war.
significance: A rare woman commander in a Greek war, praised by Herodotus, a fellow citizen of Halicarnassus, for her judgement and courage.
body:
Artemisia (active around 480 BC) ruled the Greek city of Halicarnassus in Caria, south-western Asia Minor, and nearby islands as a vassal of the Persian king. After her husband's death she governed on behalf of her young son. When Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BC she joined his fleet with five ships, which Herodotus calls among the best in the navy.

Herodotus, himself from Halicarnassus, gives her a prominent role. Before the battle of Salamis, she alone among Xerxes' commanders advised him not to fight at sea, warning that the Greeks were stronger on water and that he could win by waiting. Xerxes praised her advice but did not take it.

In the battle, chased by an Athenian ship, she escaped by ramming and sinking another ship of the Persian side. The Athenian captain, thinking she must be an ally, broke off the pursuit, while Xerxes, watching from the shore and thinking she had sunk an enemy, is said to have remarked: "My men have become women, and my women men." After the defeat she advised Xerxes to return to Asia, and he entrusted his children to her care.

The Athenians, Herodotus says, offered a large reward for her capture, angry that a woman had fought against them. Later legend added a romantic death, which has no basis.

name: Gorgo

claims.text: Gorgo was the daughter of King Cleomenes I and the wife of Leonidas.
Herodotus says that as a child she warned her father against being bribed by Aristagoras of Miletus.
Herodotus credits her with discovering a secret warning hidden under the wax of a writing tablet.

summary: A Spartan queen, daughter of Cleomenes I and wife of Leonidas, remembered by Herodotus for her shrewdness.
significance: One of the few Spartan women whose words and actions are recorded, and an emblem of the outspoken independence of Spartan women.
body:
Gorgo (born around 518 BC) was the only child of King Cleomenes I of Sparta, and married her uncle Leonidas, who became king and died at Thermopylae in 480 BC. Herodotus mentions her twice, both times for her good sense.

In 499 BC Aristagoras of Miletus came to Sparta seeking help for the Ionian revolt against Persia. When Cleomenes refused, Aristagoras began offering him ever larger bribes. Gorgo, then about eight or nine years old, said: "Father, the stranger will corrupt you if you don't go away." Cleomenes left the room, and Sparta stayed out of the revolt.

Later, before Xerxes' invasion, the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, living at the Persian court, sent a warning to Sparta. He scraped the wax from a writing tablet, wrote his message on the wood beneath, and covered it with fresh wax so it would pass the guards as blank. No one in Sparta could understand it until Gorgo suggested scraping off the wax.

Plutarch preserves a famous saying attributed to her. Asked by a woman from Attica why Spartan women were the only ones who ruled their men, she replied: "Because we are the only ones who give birth to men." Such sayings, whether genuine or not, reflect the reputation of Spartan women for frankness and independence.

name: Cynisca

claims.text: Cynisca, daughter of King Archidamus II of Sparta, won the four-horse chariot race at Olympia in 396 and 392 BC.
She was the first woman to be recorded as an Olympic victor.
The inscribed base of her victory monument was found at Olympia.

summary: The Spartan princess who became the first woman to win at the Olympic Games, as owner of the victorious chariot team in 396 and 392 BC.
significance: The first recorded woman Olympic champion, whose victory monument at Olympia declared her the only woman in Greece to have won the crown.
body:
Cynisca (born around 440 BC) was a Spartan princess, the daughter of King Archidamus II and sister of King Agesilaus II. Women could not compete at the Olympic Games, and married women were not even allowed to watch. But in the equestrian events the victor was the owner of the horses, not the driver, so a wealthy woman could win.

Cynisca entered a four-horse chariot team and won the race at Olympia in 396 BC and again in 392 BC. She set up a bronze monument of her chariot and horses in the sanctuary, and a statue of herself, made by the sculptor Apelleas. Its inscribed base was found at Olympia. The inscription reads in part: "Kings of Sparta were my fathers and brothers. Cynisca, victorious with her chariot of swift-footed horses, erected this statue. I declare that I am the only woman in all Greece to have won this crown."

Xenophon and Plutarch claimed that her brother Agesilaus encouraged her to compete to show that chariot victories depended only on wealth, not on manly virtue. Modern historians suspect this underplays Cynisca's own ambition, and the wealth and independence of Spartan women.

After her, other women, mostly from Sparta and Macedon, won equestrian victories at Olympia. Cynisca was honoured in Sparta with a hero shrine.

name: Plutarch

claims.text: Plutarch was born at Chaeronea in Boeotia around AD 46.
He served for many years as a priest of Apollo at Delphi.
His Parallel Lives pairs Greek and Roman statesmen and generals.
His works preserve material from many lost earlier sources.

summary: The Greek biographer and philosopher of the Roman age, author of the Parallel Lives, through whom later Europe came to know the ancient world.
significance: Perhaps the most influential ancient writer on later ideas of Greek and Roman history and character, from Shakespeare to the American founders.
body:
Plutarch (c. AD 46–after 119) was born into a wealthy family at Chaeronea in Boeotia, the town where Philip II had defeated the Greeks in 338 BC. He studied philosophy at Athens, travelled to Egypt and Rome, and gained Roman citizenship, but chose to spend most of his life in his small home town, serving it in local offices. For the last thirty years of his life he was also one of the two priests of Apollo at Delphi.

He wrote prolifically. His *Parallel Lives* are biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, mostly in pairs — Alexander and Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero, Pericles and Fabius — written to show character and moral example. Writing centuries after his subjects, he drew on many sources now lost, so his Lives are often the fullest surviving account of figures such as Lycurgus, Solon, Themistocles and Pericles. His *Moralia*, more than seventy essays and dialogues, range over ethics, religion, politics, education and much else, including the decline of the oracles.

Plutarch is not a critical historian: he collects anecdotes and moralises. But his vivid storytelling made him one of the most widely read ancient authors. In translation, his Lives shaped Renaissance and Enlightenment views of antiquity; Shakespeare took the plots of his Roman plays from them, and the leaders of the American and French revolutions read him as a guide to civic virtue.

name: Pausanias

claims.text: Pausanias wrote the Description of Greece in ten books in the 2nd century AD.
He was probably from Lydia in western Asia Minor.
Archaeological discoveries have repeatedly confirmed the accuracy of his descriptions.

summary: The Greek traveller of the 2nd century AD whose Description of Greece is an invaluable guide to its sanctuaries, monuments and works of art.
significance: The ancient world's great travel writer, whose detailed descriptions have guided archaeologists to sites and helped identify countless monuments.
body:
Pausanias (c. AD 110–180) was a Greek writer, probably from Lydia in western Asia Minor, who travelled widely in Greece during the reigns of the Roman emperors Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius. His *Description of Greece*, in ten books, covers Attica, the Peloponnese, Boeotia and Phocis region by region.

Pausanias was most interested in the past — the monuments, temples, statues, tombs and paintings of Archaic and Classical Greece, and the myths, local traditions and religious customs attached to them. He describes, for example, the Acropolis of Athens, the sanctuaries of Olympia and Delphi with their hundreds of statues, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia and the Lion Gate and tombs of Mycenae. He took little interest in the Roman monuments of his own day.

For a long time he was dismissed as a dull compiler. But archaeology has shown him to be an accurate observer. His descriptions guided excavators at Olympia, Delphi and Athens, and helped Schliemann at Mycenae, and they are still used to identify buildings and statues. Many works of art known only through his descriptions would otherwise be entirely lost.

The *Description of Greece* remains the most important guidebook of the ancient world and a key source for Greek art, religion and topography.

name: Myron

claims.text: Myron was a bronze sculptor from Eleutherae working in Athens in the mid-5th century BC.
His Discobolus is known through Roman marble copies.
His bronze cow on the Athenian Acropolis was celebrated in many ancient epigrams for its realism.

summary: A leading Athenian bronze sculptor of the mid-5th century BC, famous for the Discobolus and his lifelike animals.
significance: A master of figures in motion at the turn from the Severe Style to High Classical sculpture.
body:
Myron was born at Eleutherae, on the border of Attica and Boeotia, and worked in Athens around 470–440 BC, an older contemporary of Pheidias and Polykleitos. He worked mainly in bronze, and none of his original works survives; they are known from ancient descriptions and Roman copies.

His most famous work is the *Discobolus*, a discus thrower captured at the top of his backswing, his body twisted into two crossing arcs — a solution to the problem of showing violent motion in a still figure. Ancient critics praised his skill at movement and proportion, though they thought his faces lacked emotion.

He also made a group of Athena and the satyr Marsyas for the Acropolis, showing the goddess casting away the flutes she had invented, known from Roman copies, and statues of athletes and gods. His bronze cow on the Athenian Acropolis was so lifelike that dozens of ancient epigrams joked that calves tried to suckle it and herdsmen tried to drive it away.

Pliny the Elder says Myron was more varied and more careful with proportion than Polykleitos, but less concerned with expressing feeling. His work marks the moment when Greek sculptors mastered the human body in action.

name: Julius Caesar

claims.text: Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in Thessaly in 48 BC.
He supported Cleopatra VII in the Alexandrian War of 48–47 BC, and she bore him a son, Caesarion.
His calendar reform of 46 BC drew on the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes.
He was assassinated in Rome on 15 March 44 BC.

summary: The Roman general and dictator who won the civil war against Pompey, allied with Cleopatra VII, and was assassinated in 44 BC.
significance: His alliance with Cleopatra and his civil wars, fought partly in Greece and Egypt, shaped the final years of the last Hellenistic kingdom.
body:
Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC) was a Roman politician and general who conquered Gaul in 58–50 BC and then fought a civil war against Pompey and the Senate. Much of that war was fought in the Greek world: Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in Thessaly in 48 BC.

Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival. Caesar followed him to Alexandria and became involved in the struggle between Cleopatra VII and her brother Ptolemy XIII. Supporting Cleopatra, he was besieged in Alexandria in the Alexandrian War of 48–47 BC; during the fighting fire spread from the burning ships in the harbour and destroyed some of the city's books. After Ptolemy XIII's death, Caesar placed Cleopatra on the throne. She bore him a son, Ptolemy XV Caesar, called Caesarion, and later visited Rome.

Caesar admired Alexander the Great: Plutarch pairs their lives, and tells how Caesar wept at a statue of Alexander because at his age he had achieved so little. His reform of the Roman calendar in 46 BC, the basis of today's calendar, drew on the knowledge of the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes.

Caesar became dictator for life and was assassinated by a group of senators on 15 March 44 BC. The civil wars that followed set his adopted son Octavian against Mark Antony and Cleopatra.

name: Mark Antony

claims.text: Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar's assassins at Philippi in Macedonia in 42 BC.
Antony governed the Roman East and was hailed as the New Dionysus.
Antony and Cleopatra were defeated by Octavian at Actium in 31 BC.
Antony killed himself at Alexandria in 30 BC.

summary: The Roman general who ruled the eastern Mediterranean, allied with Cleopatra VII, and lost the struggle for Rome to Octavian at Actium.
significance: His alliance with Cleopatra was the last attempt to build a power centred on the Greek East, and its defeat ended the Hellenistic age.
body:
Marcus Antonius (83–30 BC) was a Roman general and a close ally of Julius Caesar. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC he joined Octavian and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, and in 42 BC he and Octavian defeated Caesar's assassins, Brutus and Cassius, at Philippi in Macedonia.

Antony took charge of Rome's eastern provinces. He lived for a time in Athens, where he was honoured as the "New Dionysus" and took part in Greek festivals. In 41 BC he summoned Cleopatra VII to Tarsus; she arrived on a gilded barge dressed as Aphrodite, and they became political and personal partners. They had three children. Antony's invasion of Parthia in 36 BC failed badly. In 34 BC, in the "Donations of Alexandria", he granted Roman eastern territories to Cleopatra and her children, which Octavian used to portray him in Rome as a traitor under the spell of a foreign queen.

Octavian declared war on Cleopatra in 32 BC. In 31 BC his admiral Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra's fleet at Actium off north-western Greece. They escaped to Egypt, but as Octavian took Alexandria in 30 BC, Antony fell on his sword on a false report that Cleopatra was dead.

Shakespeare's *Antony and Cleopatra*, based on Plutarch, made their story famous.

name: Octavian (Augustus)

claims.text: Octavian's forces under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC.
He captured Alexandria in 30 BC and made Egypt a Roman province.
He founded the city of Nicopolis near Actium to commemorate his victory.
He took the name Augustus in 27 BC and is regarded as the first Roman emperor.

summary: Caesar's adopted heir who defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, annexed Egypt in 30 BC and became Augustus, the first Roman emperor.
significance: The victor who ended the last Hellenistic kingdom and brought the entire Greek world under one Roman ruler.
body:
Gaius Octavius (63 BC–AD 14), known as Octavian, was the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC he fought to take Caesar's place, joining Mark Antony to defeat the assassins at Philippi in 42 BC, then dividing the Roman world with him, Octavian taking the West and Antony the East.

As their rivalry grew, Octavian turned Roman opinion against Antony and his partner Cleopatra VII of Egypt, presenting the coming war as Rome against a foreign queen. In 31 BC his fleet, commanded by Marcus Agrippa, defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium off north-western Greece. The next year he took Alexandria; Antony and Cleopatra died, Caesarion was killed, and Egypt became a Roman province under a governor answerable to Octavian himself, ending the last of the Hellenistic kingdoms.

At Alexandria he visited the tomb of Alexander the Great; asked if he wished to see the tombs of the Ptolemies too, he reportedly replied that he had come to see a king, not corpses. To celebrate Actium he founded the city of Nicopolis, "Victory City", nearby.

In 27 BC the Senate gave him the name Augustus, and he ruled as the first Roman emperor until AD 14. Under him and his successors the Greek East enjoyed two centuries of peace, while Greek culture shaped Rome itself.

name: Archilochus

claims.text: Archilochus of Paros is the earliest Greek poet whose personal poetry survives in substantial fragments.
One fragment describes a total solar eclipse, usually dated to 648 BC.
In a famous poem he admits throwing away his shield to save his life.

summary: The soldier-poet of Paros in the 7th century BC, the earliest Greek poet to speak in a sharply personal and often mocking voice.
significance: The first great personal voice in Greek poetry after Homer — candid, satirical and anti-heroic.
body:
Archilochus came from the island of Paros in the Cyclades and lived in the mid-7th century BC. He took part in the Parian colonisation of the island of Thasos, fighting the Thracians on the mainland, and seems to have lived as a soldier. A fragment describing the sun blotted out at midday is usually linked to the total eclipse of 6 April 648 BC.

His poems, surviving only in fragments, are in iambic and elegiac metres. They speak of war, wine, love, politics and enmity, in a frank personal voice very unlike epic. In the most famous, he admits leaving his shield behind in a bush to escape the Thracians: "Let it go — I'll get another just as good." For a hoplite, losing one's shield was a disgrace, and the poem cheerfully mocks heroic values.

Ancient writers knew him above all for his invective. They told how, when Lycambes broke off his daughter Neobule's engagement to the poet, Archilochus attacked the family so savagely in verse that they hanged themselves — almost certainly a legend built from his poems. A papyrus published in 1974, the "Cologne Epode", preserves a long, explicit seduction scene.

Ancient critics ranked him with Homer, and he was honoured with a hero shrine on Paros.

name: Alcaeus

claims.text: Alcaeus was a lyric poet of Mytilene on Lesbos and a contemporary of Sappho.
Many of his poems attack the tyrants Myrsilus and Pittacus.
The Alcaic stanza, used by Horace, is named after him.

summary: The aristocratic poet of Mytilene on Lesbos, contemporary of Sappho, whose songs of politics, war and wine were sung at the symposium.
significance: A leading lyric poet of the Archaic age, whose songs give an inside view of aristocratic feuds and tyranny on Lesbos.
body:
Alcaeus was born around 625 BC into an aristocratic family of Mytilene, the chief city of Lesbos, and was a contemporary of Sappho. His life was taken up with the violent politics of his city. He and his brothers fought against the tyrant Myrsilus, and when Pittacus, once their ally, took power with popular support, Alcaeus turned his bitter verse against him, calling him "base-born" and mocking his looks. He spent years in exile, and later tradition says Pittacus finally pardoned him.

His poems, in the Aeolic dialect of Lesbos, were written for singing at the symposium among his companions. They celebrate wine ("let us drink — why wait for the lamps?"), describe a hall gleaming with weapons, praise the gods and lament exile. He used the image of the storm-tossed ship for a city in civil strife, the first known "ship of state". Like Archilochus, he confessed to losing his shield in battle.

Ancient scholars collected his work in ten books; it now survives only in quotations and papyrus fragments.

The stanza named after him, the Alcaic, was adopted by the Roman poet Horace, who saw Alcaeus and Sappho as his models.

name: Simonides

claims.text: Simonides of Ceos wrote epigrams and elegies commemorating the dead of the Persian Wars.
The famous Thermopylae epitaph "Go tell the Spartans" is traditionally attributed to him.
A papyrus published in 1992 preserves part of his elegy on the battle of Plataea.

summary: The poet of Ceos who wrote the memorials of the Persian Wars, and was said to have been the first to compose for pay.
significance: The voice of Greek remembrance for the dead of Marathon, Thermopylae and Plataea, and the legendary inventor of the art of memory.
body:
Simonides (c. 556–468 BC) came from the island of Ceos in the Cyclades and worked across the Greek world, for the tyrant Hipparchus in Athens, for noble families in Thessaly, and finally for Hieron of Syracuse, where he died. He wrote choral songs, victory odes, laments, elegies and epigrams, and was said to be the first poet to write for a fee.

He is above all the poet of the Persian Wars. Epigrams for the dead of Marathon and Thermopylae were attributed to him, including the famous epitaph for the Spartans: "Stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their words." Whether he wrote all of these is uncertain. In 1992 papyri from Oxyrhynchus revealed parts of a long elegy he wrote on the battle of Plataea, comparing the Greek dead to the heroes of Troy.

Ancient anecdotes made him clever and greedy. Cicero tells that when a banqueting hall collapsed, killing everyone inside, Simonides, called outside moments before, could identify the crushed bodies by remembering where each guest had sat — and so invented the "art of memory", the technique of placing things to be remembered in imagined locations.

His nephew Bacchylides was also a famous poet, and a rival of Pindar.

name: Anacreon

claims.text: Anacreon of Teos worked at the courts of Polycrates of Samos and Hipparchus of Athens.
His poems are chiefly about love and wine.
The Anacreontea, imitations of his style, were written centuries after his death.

summary: The lyric poet of Teos who sang of wine and love at the courts of tyrants in Samos and Athens in the 6th century BC.
significance: The poet of the symposium par excellence, whose light, graceful songs of wine and love were imitated for two thousand years.
body:
Anacreon (c. 570–485 BC) was born at Teos in Ionia. When the Persians conquered Ionia around 545 BC, its people moved to found Abdera in Thrace. Anacreon later became a poet at the court of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. After Polycrates was killed around 522 BC, Hipparchus, son of Peisistratus, brought him to Athens in a fifty-oared ship. He may have spent his last years in Thessaly, and was said to have died aged 85, choking on a grape seed — a legend fitting a poet of wine.

His poems, written in Ionic Greek for singing at the symposium, are short, witty and elegant, about love for boys and girls, wine, music and the approach of old age. He compares a girl to a Thracian filly who has not yet been broken, and jokingly complains that a girl from Lesbos prefers someone else. The tone is playful rather than intense.

He was hugely popular in Athens, where he appears on vases and a statue of him stood on the Acropolis.

In later antiquity a collection of light poems in his style, the *Anacreontea*, was composed. Rediscovered in the Renaissance, they inspired generations of "Anacreontic" verse about wine and love, and the drinking song "To Anacreon in Heaven" lent its tune to "The Star-Spangled Banner".

name: Tyrtaeus

claims.text: Tyrtaeus wrote elegies urging Spartans to fight bravely during the Second Messenian War.
His poems are among the earliest descriptions of hoplites fighting in close formation.
Later tradition claimed he was an Athenian schoolmaster sent to Sparta, a story generally rejected.

summary: The Spartan poet of the 7th century BC whose war songs urged citizens to stand and die in the front ranks.
significance: The voice of the Spartan ideal of courage, and key early evidence for hoplite warfare and the Spartan constitution.
body:
Tyrtaeus lived at Sparta in the mid-7th century BC, during the Second Messenian War, when the Messenians rose against Spartan rule. His poems, in elegiac couplets, survive in substantial fragments, mostly quoted by later writers who admired their message.

They urge young Spartans to fight bravely: "It is a fine thing for a brave man to die, falling in the front ranks, fighting for his country." He describes men standing foot to foot, shield pressed against shield, crest against crest — one of the earliest accounts of fighting in a close formation of hoplites. He contrasts the glory of the fallen warrior, honoured by the whole city, with the shame of the coward, and insists that courage, not wealth or athletic skill, is the true measure of a man.

Another poem, the *Eunomia* ("Good Order"), refers to the Spartan constitution granted by Apollo's oracle, with roles for the kings, the elders and the people — an early source for the system later credited to Lycurgus.

Later Athenians claimed Tyrtaeus was a lame Athenian schoolmaster sent to Sparta on the oracle's instructions, a story usually dismissed. Spartan soldiers sang his songs on campaign for centuries.

name: Callimachus

claims.text: Callimachus compiled the Pinakes, a catalogue of Greek literature in 120 books, at the Library of Alexandria.
He championed short, polished poems, declaring that a big book is a big evil.
Catullus translated his poem The Lock of Berenice into Latin.

summary: The scholar-poet of Hellenistic Alexandria who catalogued the Library and championed short, learned, polished poetry.
significance: The most influential Hellenistic poet, whose ideal of refined, learned verse shaped Roman poets from Catullus to Ovid.
body:
Callimachus (c. 310–240 BC) was born in Cyrene in Libya and moved to Alexandria, where he worked under Ptolemy II and Ptolemy III at the court and the Library. He never became head librarian, but he compiled the *Pinakes* ("Tables"), a catalogue of Greek literature in 120 books, listing authors by genre with their works — the first great library catalogue and a foundation of literary scholarship.

He was also a prolific poet. His surviving works include six hymns to the gods and over sixty epigrams; much else, such as the *Aetia* ("Causes"), a long poem explaining the origins of customs and rites, survives in papyrus fragments. In *The Lock of Berenice* he tells how a lock of hair dedicated by Queen Berenice II became a constellation.

Callimachus stood for a new poetic ideal: short, highly polished, learned poems full of rare myths and allusions, rather than long epic. "A big book is a big evil," he is said to have declared, and in the *Aetia* he says Apollo told him to keep his Muse slender and to drive his chariot along untrodden paths. Ancient tradition imagined a feud with Apollonius of Rhodes over epic, though this may be invented.

Roman poets — Catullus, Propertius, Virgil and Ovid — took him as their model, and Catullus translated *The Lock of Berenice*.

name: Arrian

claims.text: Arrian was a Greek from Nicomedia who held high Roman office, including governor of Cappadocia under Hadrian.
His Anabasis of Alexander is the most reliable surviving account of Alexander's campaigns.
He recorded the teachings of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus.

summary: The Greek historian and Roman governor of the 2nd century AD whose Anabasis is the best surviving account of Alexander's campaigns.
significance: The historian through whom the eyewitness accounts of Alexander's officers reach us.
body:
Arrian (c. AD 86–160) was born at Nicomedia in Bithynia, north-western Asia Minor. He studied with the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, whose teachings he wrote down in the *Discourses* and *Handbook*. He entered Roman service, became consul and, under the emperor Hadrian, governed the frontier province of Cappadocia, where he commanded legions against the Alans. Later he settled in Athens and held office there.

He saw himself as a new Xenophon, and named his history of Alexander the *Anabasis* after Xenophon's work. Writing more than four centuries after Alexander, he chose as his main sources the lost memoirs of Ptolemy, Alexander's general, and Aristobulus, an engineer on the campaign, explaining that both had been there. His knowledge of war makes his account of battles and sieges the most credible of all ancient Alexander histories, though he admired Alexander and treated his crimes as lapses.

He also wrote the *Indica*, on India and the voyage of Alexander's admiral Nearchus, and works on tactics, hunting and the Black Sea.

name: Diodorus Siculus

claims.text: Diodorus wrote a 40-book universal history, the Bibliotheca historica, in the 1st century BC.
He compiled his history from earlier writers, many of whose works are lost.
He visited Egypt around 60–56 BC.

summary: The Sicilian Greek historian of the 1st century BC whose universal history preserves material from many lost sources.
significance: For long stretches of Greek history, including the wars after Alexander, his compilation is the only continuous narrative that survives.
body:
Diodorus came from Agyrium in Sicily and lived in the 1st century BC, in the last decades of the Roman Republic. He visited Egypt around 60–56 BC and later lived in Rome. Over some thirty years he compiled the *Bibliotheca historica* ("Library of History"), a universal history in 40 books from the mythical past to Julius Caesar's conquests in Gaul. Books 1–5 and 11–20 survive complete.

Diodorus was a compiler rather than an original historian. He worked through earlier writers one at a time — Ephorus and Theopompus for the 4th century BC, Hieronymus of Cardia for the wars of Alexander's successors, Timaeus for Sicily — arranging events year by year. His chronology is often confused and he contradicts himself, but because almost all his sources are lost, his work is invaluable. For the Successors after 323 BC, it is the main narrative we have.

He believed history should teach moral lessons and saw the past of all peoples — Egyptians, Mesopotamians, Greeks and Romans — as one connected story.

name: Hecataeus of Miletus

claims.text: Hecataeus wrote a Journey Round the World describing the lands of the Mediterranean and Near East.
He improved Anaximander's map of the world.
Herodotus says Hecataeus advised the Ionians against revolting from Persia.

summary: The Milesian writer of the late 6th century BC who pioneered Greek geography and the critical study of legend.
significance: A forerunner of Herodotus, whose world map and sceptical approach to myth helped found geography and history.
body:
Hecataeus (c. 550–476 BC) was a citizen of Miletus in Ionia, the city of the first philosophers. He travelled widely, including to Egypt, and wrote two works now known only from fragments.

His *Periodos Gēs* ("Journey Round the World") described the coasts and peoples of Europe and Asia, including Libya, place by place, and was accompanied by a map improving that of his fellow Milesian Anaximander. His *Genealogies* treated the myths of heroic families critically. It opened: "Hecataeus of Miletus speaks thus: I write what seems to me to be true; for the stories of the Greeks are many and, in my opinion, ridiculous." He tried to rationalise legends — the many-headed dog Cerberus, he suggested, was really a dangerous snake.
