Herodotus, who used his work and sometimes mocked it, says Hecataeus advised the Ionians not to revolt against Persia in 499 BC, pointing to the size of the empire, and then suggested they seize the temple treasures to build a fleet. Both pieces of advice were ignored.

His combination of geography, ethnography and criticism of myth laid the ground for Herodotus' *Histories*.

name: Strabo

claims.text: Strabo wrote the Geography in 17 books, describing the known world under Augustus and Tiberius.
He was born at Amaseia in Pontus around 64 BC.
His Geography preserves the work of earlier geographers such as Eratosthenes.

summary: The Greek geographer of the Augustan age whose 17-book Geography describes the whole known world.
significance: The most complete geographical work to survive from antiquity, and a mine of information on the cities and peoples of the Greek world.
body:
Strabo (c. 64 BC–after AD 21) was born into a wealthy Greek family at Amaseia in Pontus, northern Asia Minor. He studied in Asia Minor, Rome and Alexandria, travelled from Armenia to Italy and up the Nile, and lived through the transition from the Roman Republic to the empire of Augustus.

His *Geography*, in 17 books, survives almost complete. After two books on the theory of geography — in which he discusses and criticises Eratosthenes, Polybius and others — he describes the inhabited world region by region: Spain, Gaul and Britain, Italy, the Balkans and Greece (three books), Asia Minor, the Near East, India, Egypt and Libya. He combines physical geography with history, myth, economy and customs, and often quotes Homer, whom he regarded as the first geographer.

His books on Greece describe many cities and sanctuaries, often in decline under Rome, and are a key source for ancient topography. He also wrote a history, now lost, continuing Polybius. Written for statesmen and administrators of the new Roman empire, the *Geography* shows how the Greek East looked at the dawn of Roman imperial rule.

name: Aeschines

claims.text: Aeschines was an Athenian orator and the chief political opponent of Demosthenes.
He served on the embassies to Philip II that produced the Peace of Philocrates in 346 BC.
After losing the case On the Crown to Demosthenes in 330 BC, he left Athens for Rhodes.

summary: The Athenian orator who favoured peace with Philip II, and the lifelong rival of Demosthenes.
significance: The other side of the great debate over Macedon, whose surviving speeches show Athenian democracy at work.
body:
Aeschines (c. 389–314 BC) came from a modest Athenian family and worked as an actor and a clerk before entering politics. He served on the embassies to Philip II of Macedon that negotiated the Peace of Philocrates in 346 BC, and from then on he argued that Athens should make peace and come to terms with Macedon.

This made him the great opponent of Demosthenes, who accused him of taking bribes from Philip and of betraying Athens. Their rivalry produced three pairs of speeches, the only such pairs to survive from Athens. In 343 BC Demosthenes prosecuted him for his conduct on the embassy; Aeschines was narrowly acquitted. In 330 BC Aeschines attacked a proposal to award Demosthenes a gold crown for his services, in the speech *Against Ctesiphon*. Demosthenes replied with *On the Crown*, his masterpiece. Aeschines won less than a fifth of the jury's votes, was fined, and left Athens.

He settled on Rhodes, where, by tradition, he taught rhetoric. His three surviving speeches are vivid sources for Athenian politics and law in the age of Philip.

name: Lysias

claims.text: Lysias was a metic speechwriter in Athens, famous for plain, natural style.
The Thirty Tyrants executed his brother Polemarchus and seized the family's property.
About 35 speeches survive under his name.

summary: The Athenian speechwriter, a resident foreigner whose family was ruined by the Thirty Tyrants, famous for his clear and natural style.
significance: The master of plain Attic prose, whose courtroom speeches give vivid glimpses of everyday life and law in Athens.
body:
Lysias (c. 445–380 BC) was the son of Cephalus, a wealthy shield-maker from Syracuse who settled in Athens as a metic, or resident foreigner, at the invitation of Pericles. Plato's *Republic* is set in the family's house in Piraeus. As a young man Lysias went to Thurii in southern Italy, returning to Athens after the Sicilian disaster.

In 404 BC the Thirty Tyrants, seeking money, arrested the rich metics. Lysias' brother Polemarchus was executed and the family's property seized; Lysias escaped and helped fund the democratic exiles. When democracy returned he was briefly granted citizenship, but it was annulled. In his speech *Against Eratosthenes* he prosecuted one of the Thirty for his brother's death.

As a metic Lysias could not speak in the Assembly, so he made his living as a *logographos*, writing speeches for citizens to deliver themselves in court. About 35 survive. Famous for their simple, clear language and their skill in suiting each speech to its speaker, they cover murder, wounding, inheritance and the scrutiny of officials. *On the Murder of Eratosthenes* tells of a husband who killed his wife's lover, and gives a vivid picture of an Athenian household.

name: Hyperides

claims.text: Hyperides was an Athenian orator and opponent of Macedon, ally of Demosthenes.
He led Athens into the Lamian War and gave the funeral speech for its dead.
Most of his speeches were known only from papyri discovered in the 19th and 20th centuries.

milestones.text: Papyri bought in Egypt begin to restore his speeches, unknown since antiquity.
Lost speeches are found in the Archimedes Palimpsest.

summary: The Athenian orator who led opposition to Macedon after Demosthenes, inspired the Lamian War and was executed by Antipater.
significance: A brilliant, witty orator of the last years of Athenian independence, whose speeches have been recovered from papyri.
body:
Hyperides (c. 390–322 BC) was a wealthy Athenian, a pupil of Isocrates, who became one of the leading orators of the 4th century BC. He worked as a speechwriter and prosecutor, and was famous for his wit and elegance; ancient critics ranked him second only to Demosthenes.

Politically he was a firm opponent of Macedon and an ally of Demosthenes, though he later prosecuted Demosthenes in the Harpalus affair of 324 BC. He is remembered for a celebrated defence of the courtesan Phryne, charged with impiety, in which, by later legend, he won acquittal by revealing her beauty to the jury.

After Alexander's death in 323 BC, Hyperides was a leader of the revolt that became the Lamian War, and delivered the funeral oration for the Athenian dead in its first year, part of which survives. When the war was lost in 322 BC, Antipater demanded the surrender of the anti-Macedonian leaders. Hyperides fled, was captured and executed.

His speeches were lost after antiquity. From 1847 onwards, papyri bought in Egypt restored several of them, and in 2002 parts of two more were identified in the Archimedes Palimpsest.

name: Scopas

claims.text: Scopas of Paros was a leading sculptor of the 4th century BC, famous for expressing intense emotion.
Pliny says he carved one side of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus.
He designed the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea.

summary: The sculptor of Paros in the 4th century BC who brought passion and emotion into Greek sculpture.
significance: With Praxiteles and Lysippos, one of the three great sculptors of the late Classical age, and a forerunner of Hellenistic drama in art.
body:
Scopas came from the island of Paros, famous for its marble, and worked across the Greek world in the first half of the 4th century BC. None of his works is securely identified, but ancient writers describe many, and some sculptures from buildings he worked on survive.

He was an architect as well as a sculptor: Pausanias says he designed the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea in Arcadia, and fragments of its pediment sculptures, with deep-set eyes and heads thrown back in strain, are the best guide to his style. Pliny the Elder says he was one of four great sculptors who each carved one side of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus.

Where Praxiteles was known for grace and calm, Scopas was known for passion. Ancient writers praised his raging Maenad, a follower of Dionysus in ecstatic frenzy, her head flung back and body twisting; a small Roman copy survives in Dresden. His figures expressed intense feeling through the face, with deep-set eyes and parted lips. His style influenced the dramatic sculpture of the Hellenistic age.

name: Apelles

claims.text: Apelles was considered the greatest painter of antiquity.
He was court painter to Philip II and Alexander the Great.
None of his paintings survives; they are known only from descriptions.

summary: The court painter of Alexander the Great, regarded in antiquity as the greatest of all painters — none of whose works survives.
significance: The most famous painter of the ancient world, whose lost works set the standard by which painting was judged for centuries.
body:
Apelles, probably from Colophon in Ionia, trained at Ephesus and Sicyon and worked in the second half of the 4th century BC. He became court painter to Philip II and then Alexander the Great, who, according to Pliny, would allow no one else to paint his portrait, just as only Lysippos might sculpt him and only Pyrgoteles engrave his image on gems.

Ancient writers praised his grace and his skill at lifelike images, made with a palette of only four colours. His most famous works included a portrait of Alexander holding a thunderbolt, painted for the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, whose hand seemed to stand out from the picture; and an *Aphrodite Anadyomene*, "rising from the sea", later taken to Rome by Augustus. A famous anecdote tells how he and the painter Protogenes competed by drawing ever finer lines on a panel.

He is credited with the saying "no day without a line" and with telling a shoemaker who criticised a painted sandal and then the leg: "Let the cobbler stick to his last."

None of his paintings survives. His reputation, preserved by Pliny and others, inspired Renaissance painters such as Botticelli, whose *Calumny of Apelles* recreates one of his described works.

name: Zeuxis

claims.text: Zeuxis was a leading painter of the late 5th century BC, famed for realism and shading.
Pliny tells that birds flew down to peck at grapes he had painted.
He painted the palace of King Archelaus of Macedon.

summary: The painter of the late 5th century BC whose illusionistic realism was so famous that birds were said to peck at his painted grapes.
significance: A pioneer of shading and illusion in painting, who made realism the goal of Greek painters.
body:
Zeuxis came from Heraclea, probably the Greek city in southern Italy, and worked from about 435 to 390 BC in Athens, Macedon and elsewhere. None of his paintings survives; we know them from writers such as Pliny the Elder and Lucian.

He was celebrated for developing light and shade (*skiagraphia*) to make figures look solid and real. Pliny tells a famous story of a contest between Zeuxis and his rival Parrhasius. Zeuxis painted grapes so lifelike that birds flew down to peck at them. Then he asked Parrhasius to draw back the curtain over his own painting — only to find that the curtain was the painting. Zeuxis conceded: he had deceived birds, but Parrhasius had deceived a painter.

Another story says that to paint Helen of Troy for the city of Croton, he chose the five most beautiful girls of the city as models and combined their best features — an idea of ideal beauty much quoted by Renaissance artists. He painted unusual subjects, such as a family of centaurs, and decorated the palace of King Archelaus at Pella.

He became rich and famous, and was said to have died laughing at a painting he had made of an old woman.

name: Polygnotus

claims.text: Polygnotus of Thasos was the leading Greek wall painter of the early Classical period.
He painted in the Stoa Poikile at Athens and the Lesche of the Knidians at Delphi.
Pausanias describes his paintings of the sack of Troy and the underworld at Delphi in detail.

summary: The great wall painter of the early 5th century BC, whose huge scenes of myth decorated public buildings at Athens and Delphi.
significance: The founder of large-scale Greek painting, known to us only through Pausanias' descriptions and the vase painters he influenced.
body:
Polygnotus came from the island of Thasos in the northern Aegean and worked mainly in Athens around 475–447 BC, under the patronage of the statesman Cimon, who reportedly granted him Athenian citizenship. Ancient writers ranked him as the first great Greek painter.

His works were huge wall paintings on wooden panels or plaster in public buildings. In Athens he painted the sack of Troy in the Stoa Poikile (Painted Stoa) and scenes in the Theseion and elsewhere. At Delphi he painted the Lesche (clubhouse) of the Knidians with two enormous compositions, the fall of Troy and Odysseus' visit to the underworld, which Pausanias describes figure by figure.

Aristotle praised him for showing people better than they are, with nobility of character, and others for the expressive faces of his figures. Instead of placing figures in a single row, he arranged them at different levels across a landscape, suggesting depth. He used only a few colours.

All his works are lost. Their influence can be seen in Athenian vase paintings of the mid-5th century BC, such as the Niobid Krater, which arrange figures across rocky landscapes in the manner described for Polygnotus.

name: Iktinos

claims.text: Iktinos was an architect of the Parthenon, with Kallikrates.
Pausanias names him as the architect of the temple of Apollo at Bassae.
He is said to have written a book about the Parthenon, now lost.

summary: The architect of the Parthenon and of the temple of Apollo at Bassae, the most celebrated Greek architect of the Classical age.
significance: The designer of the most famous building of antiquity.
body:
Iktinos was an architect working in the mid-5th century BC. With Kallikrates he designed the Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens, built from 447 to 432 BC under Pericles, with the sculptor Pheidias in charge of its decoration. The Roman architect Vitruvius says Iktinos wrote a book about the temple with a man named Karpion; it is lost.

Iktinos is credited with the Parthenon's bold design: an unusually wide temple, eight columns across instead of the usual six, so that it could house Pheidias' enormous statue of Athena, combining the Doric order outside with Ionic features such as a continuous frieze, and refined throughout by subtle curves and inclinations.

Pausanias names Iktinos as the architect of the temple of Apollo Epikourios at Bassae in Arcadia, built in the later 5th century BC, which has the earliest known Corinthian column. Plutarch also says he worked on the Telesterion, the great hall of initiation at Eleusis.

Almost nothing else is known about his life.

name: Herophilus

claims.text: Herophilus performed systematic dissections of human bodies at Alexandria.
Later Roman writers claimed he also vivisected condemned criminals.
He identified the brain as the centre of the nervous system and distinguished nerves from tendons.

summary: The Alexandrian physician of the early 3rd century BC who founded scientific anatomy through human dissection.
significance: The first person known to have dissected human bodies systematically, discovering much of the anatomy of the brain and nerves.
body:
Herophilus (c. 335–280 BC) was born at Chalcedon on the Bosporus and worked at Alexandria under the first Ptolemies. There, for a brief period unique in antiquity, the dissection of human corpses was permitted, and Herophilus used it to found the systematic study of anatomy. The Roman writers Celsus and Tertullian later claimed that he and his younger contemporary Erasistratus also cut open living criminals provided by the king; whether this is true is debated.

His writings are lost, but later authors, especially Galen, preserve many of his findings. He showed that the brain, not the heart as Aristotle thought, is the centre of the nervous system, and distinguished nerves from tendons and blood vessels, and sensory from motor nerves. He described the ventricles of the brain, the eye and the optic nerve, the liver, the reproductive organs, and the first part of the small intestine, which he named the *duodenum* ("twelve finger-breadths") for its length. He also studied the pulse, timing it with a water clock.

He founded a school of physicians at Alexandria. After his time human dissection was abandoned, and was not practised again systematically until the Renaissance.

name: Erasistratus

claims.text: Erasistratus described the valves of the heart and treated it as a pump.
He distinguished sensory from motor nerves.
A famous story credits him with diagnosing the lovesickness of the Seleucid prince Antiochus.

summary: The Alexandrian physician of the 3rd century BC who studied the heart, the brain and the nerves through dissection.
significance: With Herophilus, the founder of anatomy and physiology, who came close to understanding the circulation of the blood.
body:
Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BC) came from the island of Ceos and worked at the Seleucid court and then at Alexandria, a younger contemporary of Herophilus. His writings are lost, and his ideas are known mainly from Galen, who argued with them at length.

Through dissection he made important discoveries. He described the valves of the heart and understood that the heart works as a pump, and traced the veins and arteries, though he believed that arteries carried air (*pneuma*) rather than blood. He distinguished the brain from the cerebellum, and sensory nerves from motor nerves, and noted that the folds of the human brain are more complex than those of animals, linking this to intelligence.

He rejected the Hippocratic theory of the four humours, explaining disease instead by blockages and excess of blood, and preferred diet and exercise to the bleeding favoured by others.

A famous story told how, as a court physician, he discovered that the young Seleucid prince Antiochus was wasting away for love of his stepmother Stratonice, by noticing that his pulse quickened when she came near. King Seleucus I gave her to his son in marriage.

name: Ctesibius

claims.text: Ctesibius of Alexandria invented the force pump and the water organ (hydraulis).
He improved the water clock with a regulated, constant flow.
His works are lost and known through Vitruvius, Philo of Byzantium and Hero of Alexandria.

summary: The Alexandrian engineer of the 3rd century BC, inventor of the force pump and the water organ, and the father of pneumatics.
significance: The founder of the study of air and water pressure, whose inventions were used for over two thousand years.
body:
Ctesibius (active c. 270 BC) was an engineer at Alexandria under Ptolemy II. Later writers say he was the son of a barber, and began by designing a mirror on a counterweight for his father's shop. His own writings are lost, but the Roman architect Vitruvius and the Greek engineers Philo of Byzantium and Hero of Alexandria describe his inventions.

He is regarded as the founder of pneumatics, the science of air and water pressure. He invented the force pump, with two cylinders, pistons and valves, used later as a fire engine and for raising water. He built the *hydraulis*, a water organ in which air was forced through pipes by water pressure — the ancestor of the pipe organ, played at Roman games and festivals. He improved the water clock (*klepsydra*) by keeping the water at a constant level so that it flowed evenly, and added gears to drive pointers and moving figures, making it the most accurate clock until the invention of the pendulum clock. He is also credited with a catapult powered by compressed air.

His work began a tradition of Alexandrian engineering continued by Philo and Hero.

name: Apollonius of Perga

claims.text: Apollonius wrote the Conics in eight books, of which seven survive.
He gave the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola their names.
Books 5–7 of the Conics survive only in Arabic translation.

summary: The Hellenistic mathematician whose Conics, the study of curves cut from a cone, was the summit of Greek geometry.
significance: Called "the Great Geometer" in antiquity, his work on conic sections later made possible Kepler's laws of planetary motion.
body:
Apollonius (c. 262–190 BC) was born at Perga in Pamphylia, in southern Asia Minor, studied at Alexandria with the successors of Euclid, and later worked at Pergamon. Ancient writers called him the "Great Geometer".

His masterpiece, the *Conics*, in eight books, studies the curves produced by cutting a cone with a plane. Apollonius showed that all of them could be produced from a single cone by changing the angle of the cut, and gave them the names still used: the ellipse, the parabola and the hyperbola. He worked out their properties with great rigour and originality. Books 1–4 survive in Greek and Books 5–7 only in an Arabic translation; Book 8 is lost.

He also wrote on other problems of geometry, such as constructing a circle touching three given circles, and on astronomy, where he developed models using epicycles and eccentric circles to explain the irregular movements of the planets — models later used by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.

His work on conics seemed purely theoretical for nearly two thousand years, until Johannes Kepler discovered in 1609 that the planets move in ellipses, and Newton used conic sections to explain gravity.

name: Exekias

claims.text: Exekias was an Athenian potter and black-figure painter active around 545–525 BC.
He signed vases as potter and, on a few, as painter.
His cup showing Dionysus sailing among dolphins is in Munich.

summary: The greatest Athenian black-figure vase painter, active around 545–525 BC, famous for his Achilles and Ajax amphora.
significance: The master of black-figure painting, who brought drama and psychological depth to Greek vase painting just before the invention of red-figure.
body:
Exekias worked in Athens around 545–525 BC as both potter and painter. His name is known because he signed his vases — some as potter (*Exekias epoiēsen*, "Exekias made me"), a few as both potter and painter. Scholars attribute a few dozen vases to his hand.

He worked in the black-figure technique, painting figures in black slip and incising fine details through it. He brought to it a new seriousness and refinement. His most famous work, an amphora in the Vatican, shows Achilles and Ajax absorbed in a board game during a pause in the Trojan War. Another amphora, in Boulogne, shows Ajax alone, carefully fixing his sword in the ground before he kills himself — the moment before the act, not the act itself. A cup in Munich shows Dionysus reclining in a ship whose mast has sprouted vines, sailing among dolphins over a coral-red sea, one of the first cups painted across its whole interior.

Exekias' figures are often still and thoughtful, with intricately detailed armour and cloaks. His work marks the height of black-figure painting; within a few years, painters in his workshop tradition took up the new red-figure technique.

name: Thrasybulus

claims.text: In the winter of 404/3 BC Thrasybulus seized the fort of Phyle with a small band of exiles.
His victory at Munychia in 403 BC, where Critias was killed, led to the restoration of the Athenian democracy.
He was killed at Aspendus in 388 BC during a naval campaign.

summary: The Athenian general who overthrew the Thirty Tyrants in 403 BC and restored the democracy.
significance: The hero of the democratic restoration, whose amnesty of 403 BC became a model of reconciliation after civil war.
body:
Thrasybulus (c. 440–388 BC) first appears in 411 BC, when an oligarchy seized power at Athens. With the fleet at Samos he led the sailors in remaining loyal to democracy, and persuaded them to recall the exiled Alcibiades. He then commanded in the naval victories of the last years of the Peloponnesian War, including Cyzicus in 410.

After Athens surrendered in 404, the Spartan-backed Thirty Tyrants under Critias took power and Thrasybulus fled to Thebes. That winter he crossed the border with about seventy exiles and seized the mountain fort of Phyle. His force grew, and in spring 403 it took the Piraeus and defeated the Thirty at Munychia, where Critias was killed. With the agreement of the Spartan king Pausanias the democracy was restored, and an amnesty forbade prosecution for most acts committed during the civil war.

In the 390s Thrasybulus led Athenian recovery in the Corinthian War, and in 389 sailed to the Aegean and Asia Minor to win back allies and revenue. In 388 his soldiers' plundering provoked the people of Aspendus in Pamphylia, who killed him in his tent.

name: Critias

claims.text: Critias was the leading figure among the Thirty Tyrants who ruled Athens in 404–403 BC.
He was a relative of Plato and an associate of Socrates.
The 'Sisyphus fragment', which says the gods were invented to keep people obedient, is attributed to him, though some scholars assign it to Euripides.

summary: The Athenian aristocrat, poet and associate of Socrates who led the brutal regime of the Thirty Tyrants in 404–403 BC.
significance: His rule, and his link to Socrates, helps explain why Athens put Socrates on trial four years later.
body:
Critias (c. 460–403 BC) came from one of the oldest families in Athens; he was a cousin of Plato's mother, and appears in Plato's dialogues *Charmides*, *Protagoras*, *Timaeus* and the unfinished *Critias*, where the story of Atlantis is told. He spent time with Socrates, wrote elegies, tragedies and prose works on the constitutions of Sparta and other states, and was associated with the Sophists. A surviving fragment of a satyr play, *Sisyphus*, claims that the gods were invented by a clever man to frighten people into behaving; its author is disputed.

Critias admired Sparta and despised the democracy. Exiled in the last years of the Peloponnesian War, he returned after Athens' defeat in 404 and became the most powerful of the Thirty, the oligarchic board installed with Spartan support. Under the Thirty about 1,500 people were put to death and many more fled. When his colleague Theramenes urged moderation, Critias had him condemned and executed.

In spring 403 the democratic exiles under Thrasybulus defeated the Thirty at Munychia in the Piraeus, and Critias was killed in the fighting. Socrates' association with him and with Alcibiades was remembered at his trial in 399.

name: Cleomenes I

claims.text: Cleomenes I helped expel the Athenian tyrant Hippias in 510 BC.
He refused to support the Ionian Revolt when Aristagoras asked for help in 499 BC.
He defeated Argos at Sepeia around 494 BC.

summary: The forceful Spartan king of c. 520–490 BC who intervened in Athens, crushed Argos and made Sparta leader of the Peloponnese.
significance: The king who made Sparta the strongest power in Greece on the eve of the Persian Wars.
body:
Cleomenes I was king of Sparta from the Agiad royal house from about 520 to about 490 BC. Our knowledge of him comes almost entirely from Herodotus, who portrays him as able but unstable.

In 510 BC he led the Spartan army that drove the tyrant Hippias out of Athens. Two years later he returned to support the aristocrat Isagoras against Cleisthenes, expelling hundreds of families, but the Athenian people rose up and besieged him on the Acropolis, forcing him to leave — the moment that made Cleisthenes' democratic reforms possible. An attempt to restore Hippias failed when Sparta's allies refused to follow him.

In 499 BC Aristagoras of Miletus asked him to help the Ionian Revolt against Persia; Herodotus says that Cleomenes' young daughter Gorgo warned him against the bribes offered. Around 494 he crushed Argos at Sepeia, then burned a sacred grove in which Argive survivors had taken refuge. He later had his fellow king Demaratus deposed by bribing the Delphic oracle. When this was discovered he fled, was brought back, and died around 490 BC; Herodotus says he went mad and mutilated himself. His half-brother Leonidas succeeded him and married Gorgo.

name: Agis IV

claims.text: Agis IV proposed cancelling debts and redistributing Spartan land around 243 BC.
Debts were cancelled, but the land redistribution was blocked.
He was executed by the ephors in 241 BC.

summary: The young Spartan king of c. 244–241 BC who tried to restore Sparta through debt cancellation and land reform, and was executed.
significance: The first of Sparta's revolutionary kings, whose failed reforms inspired Cleomenes III.
body:
By the 3rd century BC Sparta had fallen far from its classical power. Land had become concentrated in a few hands, many Spartans were in debt, and the number of full citizens had fallen to about 700, of whom perhaps 100 owned land.

Agis IV, of the Eurypontid royal house, became king around 244 BC at about the age of twenty. Inspired by the idealised picture of Lycurgus' Sparta, he proposed to cancel all debts and to divide the land into 4,500 equal lots for Spartans, including new citizens drawn from the perioikoi and foreigners, and 15,000 for perioikoi. He gave up his own wealth, and his mother and grandmother, among the richest people in Sparta, supported him.

He was opposed by the other king, Leonidas II, whom his supporters had deposed. The debts were cancelled and the records of loans burned in the marketplace, but the redistribution was delayed. While Agis was away campaigning with the Achaean League, his opponents recovered. On his return Leonidas was restored, and in 241 BC the ephors had Agis strangled in prison, with his mother and grandmother — the first Spartan king put to death by his own people. Our main source is Plutarch's *Life of Agis*.

name: Cleomenes III

claims.text: In 227 BC Cleomenes III abolished the ephorate, cancelled debts and redistributed land at Sparta.
He was defeated by Antigonus III Doson and the Achaean League at Sellasia in 222 BC.
He died in Alexandria in 219 BC after a failed uprising.

summary: The revolutionary Spartan king of 235–222 BC who carried out land reform and briefly made Sparta a great power again.
significance: The last attempt to revive classical Sparta, ended by the Macedonian victory at Sellasia in 222 BC.
body:
Cleomenes III became king of Sparta, from the Agiad house, around 235 BC. He was the son of Leonidas II, the enemy of Agis IV, but he married Agis' widow Agiatis and adopted Agis' programme.

In 227 BC, after early successes against the Achaean League, he seized power in a coup. He killed four of the five ephors, abolished their office, cancelled debts and redivided the land, and raised the citizen body to about 4,000 by enfranchising perioikoi. He revived the old Spartan training (*agōgē*) and common messes, and reorganised the army in the Macedonian style. With this new army he defeated the Achaean League repeatedly and won over much of the Peloponnese.

In alarm, Aratus, leader of the Achaean League, turned to Sparta's old enemy Macedon. King Antigonus III Doson invaded, and in 222 BC crushed Cleomenes at Sellasia, north of Sparta. Cleomenes fled to Ptolemaic Egypt. In 219, held under guard in Alexandria by Ptolemy IV, he tried to raise the city in revolt; when it failed, he and his companions killed themselves. Polybius, from the Achaean side, is hostile; Plutarch's *Life* is admiring.

name: Timoleon

claims.text: Timoleon was sent from Corinth to Syracuse in 344 BC and removed the tyrant Dionysius II.
He defeated a Carthaginian army at the river Crimisus around 341 BC.
He resettled Syracuse and other Sicilian cities with new colonists.

summary: The Corinthian general who freed Syracuse from tyranny in 344 BC, defeated Carthage and refounded Greek Sicily.
significance: Remembered in antiquity as the ideal liberator, who gave up power once his work was done.
body:
Timoleon (c. 411–337 BC) was a Corinthian aristocrat. In the 360s his brother Timophanes tried to make himself tyrant of Corinth, and Timoleon consented to his killing — an act that left him under a cloud for twenty years.

In 344 BC the Syracusans, torn by civil war and threatened by Carthage, appealed to Corinth, their mother city, for help. Timoleon was sent with a small force. He won control of Syracuse, and the tyrant Dionysius II surrendered and was allowed to retire to Corinth. Timoleon pulled down the tyrants' fortress on the island of Ortygia and introduced a more moderate government.

Around 341 BC he defeated a much larger Carthaginian army at the river Crimisus in western Sicily, in a battle fought in a thunderstorm, and then removed the tyrants of other Sicilian cities. Many cities had been ruined or depopulated by decades of war, and he invited tens of thousands of settlers from Greece and Italy to resettle them; archaeology shows a revival of building and farming in Sicily in the following decades.

Timoleon then laid down his power and lived as a private citizen in Syracuse, where he went blind. When he died around 337 BC the city honoured him with a public tomb.

name: Gelon

claims.text: Gelon became tyrant of Gela around 491 BC and of Syracuse in 485 BC.
With Theron of Akragas he defeated the Carthaginians at Himera in 480 BC.
Herodotus says he offered to help the Greeks against Xerxes in return for command.

summary: The tyrant of Gela and Syracuse who made Syracuse the greatest Greek city in the west and defeated Carthage at Himera in 480 BC.
significance: Founder of Syracusan power, whose victory at Himera was seen as the western counterpart of Salamis.
body:
Gelon was a cavalry commander under Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela in southern Sicily, and seized power there after his death around 491 BC. In 485 the aristocrats of Syracuse, expelled by the common people, called on him for help; he took the city and made it his capital, leaving Gela to his brother Hiero.

He greatly enlarged Syracuse, moving there the populations of several other cities, including half of Gela and the wealthy citizens of Camarina and Megara Hyblaea. He built up a large army and navy.

When Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BC, Herodotus says, the Greeks asked Gelon for help; he offered a large force but demanded overall command, and was refused. In the same year a great Carthaginian army landed in Sicily and besieged Himera. Gelon and his ally Theron, tyrant of Akragas, destroyed it; the Carthaginian general Hamilcar was killed. Later Greeks claimed the battle was fought on the same day as Salamis. With the spoils Gelon dedicated a golden tripod at Delphi and built temples in Syracuse.

Gelon was popular, and when he died in 478 BC his brother Hiero I succeeded him.

name: Hiero I

claims.text: Hiero I ruled Syracuse from 478 to about 467 BC, succeeding his brother Gelon.
He defeated the Etruscan fleet off Cumae in 474 BC; an inscribed Etruscan helmet he dedicated at Olympia survives.
Pindar, Bacchylides, Simonides and Aeschylus all worked for him.

summary: The tyrant of Syracuse from 478 to 467 BC, victor over the Etruscans at Cumae and the most celebrated patron of poets of his age.
significance: His court made Syracuse a centre of Greek poetry; Pindar's grandest odes were written for his victories.
body:
Hiero I succeeded his brother Gelon as tyrant of Syracuse in 478 BC. In 474 the Greek city of Cumae near Naples asked for help against the Etruscans, and Hiero's fleet won a decisive victory off its coast, ending Etruscan sea power in southern Italy. He dedicated captured Etruscan helmets at Olympia; one, now in the British Museum, is inscribed "Hiero son of Deinomenes and the Syracusans, to Zeus: Etruscan spoils from Cumae".

Like Gelon, he moved populations by force. In 476 he expelled the people of Catana and refounded it as Aetna, with new settlers; Aeschylus wrote a play, *The Women of Aetna*, for the foundation, and later staged the *Persians* at Syracuse.

Hiero spent lavishly on the panhellenic games. His horse won the single-horse race at Olympia in 476, celebrated in Pindar's First Olympian Ode, and his chariot won at Delphi in 470 and at Olympia in 468; Pindar and his rival Bacchylides both wrote victory odes for him. The poet Simonides also lived at his court. Ancient tradition, however, remembered him as a harsher ruler than Gelon, with a network of informers. He died at Aetna around 467 BC, and the tyranny fell soon after.

name: Hiero II

claims.text: Hiero II ruled Syracuse for about fifty-five years, until his death in 215 BC.
He changed sides from Carthage to Rome in 263 BC and remained a loyal Roman ally.
Archimedes worked at his court; the story of the golden crown is told of him.

summary: The king of Syracuse from about 270 to 215 BC, ally of Rome and patron of Archimedes, under whom Syracuse enjoyed its last golden age.
significance: His long, stable reign kept Syracuse independent and prosperous between Rome and Carthage.
body:
Hiero II (c. 308–215 BC) was an officer under Pyrrhus during his Sicilian campaign, and was chosen general by the Syracusan army around 275 BC. After defeating the Mamertines — Italian mercenaries who had seized Messana — around 269, he was hailed as king.

When the First Punic War broke out in 264 BC over Messana, Hiero first sided with Carthage, but in 263 he made peace with Rome and became its ally. He kept that alliance for the rest of his life, supplying grain and money to Roman armies, and Syracuse kept its independence in eastern Sicily while the rest of the island became Rome's first province.

His reign was peaceful and prosperous. His grain-tax law, the *lex Hieronica*, was later kept by the Romans. He enlarged the great theatre of Syracuse, built a huge altar for public sacrifices, and had a giant ship, the *Syracusia*, built and sent as a gift to Ptolemy III in Egypt.

The mathematician Archimedes, said to be his relative, worked for him: on the story told by Vitruvius, Hiero asked him to find out whether a goldsmith had cheated him over a crown. Hiero died in 215 BC aged about ninety; his grandson joined Carthage, and Rome sacked Syracuse in 212.

name: Agathocles

claims.text: Agathocles seized power in Syracuse in 317 BC and took the title of king around 304 BC.
In 310 BC, while besieged by Carthage, he landed an army in Africa and campaigned there for three years.
Ancient sources say he was the son of a potter.

summary: The ruthless tyrant and then king of Syracuse (317–289 BC) who carried the war against Carthage to Africa itself.
significance: The first Greek to invade Carthaginian Africa, and the model of the self-made Hellenistic strongman.
body:
Agathocles (361–289 BC) was said to have been the son of a potter. He rose as a soldier, and in 317 BC seized power in Syracuse in a bloody coup against the oligarchs, in which thousands were killed or exiled, overturning the settlement of Timoleon.

He extended his power over much of Greek Sicily, provoking war with Carthage. In 311 he was defeated and besieged in Syracuse. In 310 he made a bold decision: slipping out with about 14,000 men, he sailed to Africa, burned his ships, and ravaged Carthaginian territory for three years, coming close to Carthage itself. The campaign failed — he abandoned his army and fled back to Sicily in 307 — but he made peace with Carthage on equal terms in 306.

Around 304, following the example of Alexander's successors, he took the title of king. He later fought in southern Italy and Corcyra, and married his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus of Epirus.

He died in 289 BC, possibly poisoned. Diodorus says that on his deathbed he restored freedom to the Syracusans. Ancient writers, especially the hostile historian Timaeus, whom he had exiled, portrayed him as a monster of cruelty.

name: Jason of Pherae

claims.text: Jason, tyrant of Pherae, united Thessaly under his rule as tagos in the 370s BC.
After Leuctra in 371 BC he arranged a truce that let the defeated Spartans withdraw.
He was assassinated in 370 BC while preparing to preside over the Pythian Games.

summary: The tyrant of Pherae who united Thessaly in the 370s BC and seemed poised to dominate Greece before his murder in 370 BC.
significance: His brief career anticipated Philip II: a northern ruler using a professional army to unite a region and dominate the Greek cities.
body:
Jason ruled the Thessalian city of Pherae in the 370s BC. Xenophon, our main source, gives a vivid picture of him through the speech of a Thessalian, Polydamas of Pharsalus, who warned Sparta that Jason was the most powerful man of his time. He kept a professional army of about 6,000 mercenaries, whom he trained hard and shared hardships with, and by about 374 had brought the cities of Thessaly together under him as *tagos*, the federal war-leader, controlling large forces of cavalry and infantry.

He was an ally of Thebes and of Athens. After the Theban victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC he marched south, and rather than help Thebes finish off the Spartans he arranged a truce that let them withdraw — keeping the balance of power in his own favour. He was said to be planning a campaign against Persia.

In 370 BC he announced that he would preside over the Pythian Games at Delphi and ordered a vast sacrifice of cattle, alarming the Greeks. Before the festival he was stabbed to death by seven young men while reviewing his cavalry. Thessaly fell into disorder, and twenty years later Philip II of Macedon took his place.

name: Aratus of Sicyon

claims.text: In 251 BC Aratus freed Sicyon from its tyrant and brought it into the Achaean League.
In 243 BC he captured the Acrocorinth from its Macedonian garrison.
He later invited Antigonus III Doson of Macedon into the Peloponnese against Cleomenes III.

summary: The statesman who built the Achaean League into the leading power in the Peloponnese in the 3rd century BC.
significance: The architect of the Achaean League, whose memoirs shaped Polybius' history of the age.
body:
Aratus (271–213 BC) was born at Sicyon in the northern Peloponnese. As a child he escaped when a tyrant killed his father. In 251 BC, aged twenty, he and a band of exiles scaled the walls of Sicyon at night and overthrew the tyrant Nicocles. He then brought the city into the Achaean League, a federation of small cities of the region.

From 245 he was elected the League's general (*stratēgos*) almost every other year, the maximum the law allowed. His greatest exploit came in 243, when he took by surprise the Acrocorinth, the citadel of Corinth, which Macedon had used to dominate the Peloponnese. Corinth and many other cities joined the League, which became the strongest power in the region.

Aratus was a better diplomat than general. When Cleomenes III of Sparta defeated the League repeatedly in the 220s, Aratus reversed his life's policy and called in Antigonus III Doson of Macedon, handing back the Acrocorinth. After the victory at Sellasia in 222 the League became a Macedonian ally. Aratus advised the young Philip V but fell out with him, and died in 213, believed to have been poisoned on Philip's orders. His memoirs were a main source for Polybius.

name: Philopoemen

claims.text: Philopoemen was elected general of the Achaean League eight times.
He killed the Spartan tyrant Machanidas in battle at Mantinea in 207 BC.
He was captured by the Messenians in 183 BC and forced to take poison; Polybius carried his funeral urn.

summary: The Achaean general from Megalopolis who led the League against Sparta and Macedon, called "the last of the Greeks".
significance: The last great general of independent Greece, who kept the Achaean League strong in the shadow of Rome.
body:
Philopoemen (253–183 BC) came from Megalopolis in Arcadia. As a young man he helped defend his city against Cleomenes III of Sparta, and at the battle of Sellasia in 222 BC he won fame by leading a cavalry charge on his own initiative. He then served for ten years as a mercenary commander in Crete.

Returning, he became the leading figure of the Achaean League after the death of Aratus, and was elected its general eight times. He reformed the League's army, re-equipping its infantry as a Macedonian-style phalanx and training its cavalry hard. In 207 BC he defeated the Spartans at Mantinea and killed their tyrant Machanidas with his own hand.

As Roman power grew after 200 BC, he tried to keep the League independent while staying on good terms with Rome. In 192 he brought Sparta into the League, and in 188, after a revolt, he tore down its walls and abolished its ancient Lycurgan way of life.

In 183, aged seventy, he was captured while campaigning against rebel Messene and forced to drink poison. The young Polybius carried his ashes at his funeral. Plutarch reports that a Roman called him "the last of the Greeks", meaning that Greece produced no great man after him.

name: Perdiccas

claims.text: Ancient sources say the dying Alexander gave his signet ring to Perdiccas.
At the settlement of Babylon in 323 BC Perdiccas became regent of the empire for Philip III and the infant Alexander IV.
After failing to cross the Nile against Ptolemy, he was murdered by his own officers in 320 BC.

summary: The Macedonian general who became regent of Alexander's empire on his death in 323 BC and was murdered three years later.
significance: The last man to try to hold Alexander's empire together; his failure began the wars of the Successors.
body:
Perdiccas (c. 355–320 BC) was a Macedonian noble who commanded a battalion of the phalanx in Alexander's campaigns and became one of his seven bodyguards. After Hephaestion died in 324 BC he was the king's leading officer, and ancient sources say the dying Alexander handed him his signet ring.

At the settlement of Babylon in 323, the generals agreed that Alexander's half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus and his unborn son by Roxana, Alexander IV, would rule jointly. Perdiccas became regent and commander of the royal army in Asia, and assigned provinces to the other generals: Egypt to Ptolemy, Thrace to Lysimachus, while Antipater and Craterus held Macedon and Greece.

Perdiccas soon aroused suspicion. He broke off a marriage to Antipater's daughter to seek the hand of Alexander's sister Cleopatra, which would have brought him close to the throne. When Ptolemy seized Alexander's body on its way to Macedon and took it to Egypt, Perdiccas invaded. In 320 his attempt to cross the Nile near Memphis ended in disaster, with many soldiers drowned or eaten by crocodiles. His officers, including Seleucus, murdered him in his tent.

name: Craterus

claims.text: In 324 BC Alexander sent Craterus to lead about 10,000 veterans home and to replace Antipater in Macedon.
He helped Antipater win the Lamian War at Crannon in 322 BC.
He was killed fighting Eumenes of Cardia in Asia Minor in 321 or 320 BC.

summary: Alexander's most trusted field commander, popular with the army, killed in battle against Eumenes in 321 or 320 BC.
significance: The general the Macedonian soldiers loved best, whose early death removed a likely ruler of Macedon.
body:
Craterus (c. 370–321 BC) was one of Alexander's most capable generals and often commanded the left wing or independent forces. At the Hydaspes in 326 BC he held the main camp opposite the Indian king Porus while Alexander crossed upstream. On the return from India he led part of the army back by an inland route.

He was known as a traditional Macedonian who disliked Alexander's adoption of Persian dress and customs; Plutarch says Alexander called Hephaestion "friend of Alexander" and Craterus "friend of the king". At the mass weddings at Susa in 324 he married a Persian princess, Amastris. That year Alexander sent him to lead about 10,000 discharged veterans home and to take over Macedon from Antipater.

He was still in Cilicia when Alexander died. He crossed to Europe and helped Antipater crush the Greek revolt in the Lamian War at Crannon in 322, and married Antipater's daughter Phila. In the first war of the Successors he crossed into Asia against Perdiccas' ally Eumenes, hoping the Macedonian troops would desert to him. In the battle, in 321 or 320, his horse fell and he was trampled; Eumenes found him dying and mourned him.

name: Roxana

claims.text: Roxana, daughter of the Bactrian noble Oxyartes, married Alexander in 327 BC.
Their son Alexander IV was born after Alexander's death in 323 BC.
Roxana and her son were killed on Cassander's orders around 310 BC.

summary: The Bactrian noblewoman who married Alexander the Great in 327 BC and bore his only legitimate heir.
significance: Mother of Alexander IV, the last of the Argead royal house, whose murder ended Alexander's dynasty.
body:
Roxana was the daughter of Oxyartes, a nobleman of Bactria or Sogdia in modern Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, who resisted Alexander during the hard campaign in Central Asia. When Alexander captured the mountain stronghold known as the Sogdian Rock around 327 BC, Roxana was among the captives, and he married her the same year. Ancient writers said it was a love match, but it also helped win over the local aristocracy.

She travelled with Alexander to India and back. When he died at Babylon in 323 BC she was pregnant, and a few months later bore a son, Alexander IV, who was proclaimed joint king with Alexander's half-brother Philip III. Plutarch says Roxana had Alexander's Persian wife Stateira murdered soon after his death.

Mother and son became pawns in the wars of the Successors. They were taken to Macedon and placed under the protection of Alexander's mother Olympias, but in 316 Cassander captured them at Pydna and kept them under guard at Amphipolis. Around 310 BC, as Alexander IV approached manhood, Cassander had them both secretly killed. The young king may be the boy buried in Tomb III at Vergina.

name: Nearchus

claims.text: Nearchus commanded Alexander's fleet on its voyage from the Indus delta to the Persian Gulf in 325–324 BC.
His account of the voyage survives through Arrian's Indica.
He was a boyhood friend of Alexander, exiled by Philip II after the Pixodarus affair.

summary: Alexander's Cretan-born admiral, who led the fleet from the Indus to the Persian Gulf in 325–324 BC and wrote an account of the voyage.
significance: His voyage opened the sea route between India and Mesopotamia to Greek knowledge.
body:
Nearchus (c. 360–300 BC) was born in Crete and grew up at Amphipolis in Macedon, where he became one of Alexander's boyhood friends. In 337 BC Philip II exiled him with other companions for supporting Alexander in a quarrel over a marriage alliance with the Carian ruler Pixodarus. After Alexander became king he recalled them, and Nearchus served as governor of Lycia and Pamphylia.

In India, Alexander built a fleet on the Hydaspes and sailed down the Indus. In 325 he chose Nearchus to command the fleet on a voyage of exploration along the unknown coast from the mouth of the Indus to the Persian Gulf, while he himself led the army through the Gedrosian desert. The voyage, of about 2,000 kilometres, was hard: the sailors met monsoon winds, whales, and the "Fish-Eaters" of the coast, and ran short of food. Nearchus rejoined Alexander in Carmania, and at Susa in 324 was honoured with a golden crown.

He later wrote an account of the voyage, which Arrian used for his *Indica*. After Alexander's death he served Antigonus I and disappears from history around 312 BC.

name: Callisthenes

claims.text: Callisthenes, a relative of Aristotle, accompanied Alexander as official historian of the campaign.
He opposed the introduction of prostration (proskynesis) at Alexander's court in 327 BC.
He died after being implicated in the Pages' Conspiracy; accounts differ on whether he was executed or died in captivity.

summary: The Greek historian and relative of Aristotle who recorded Alexander's campaigns and died after opposing his adoption of Persian court ritual.
significance: His fall marked the growing tension between Alexander and his Greek and Macedonian followers over the king's divine and Persian claims.
body:
Callisthenes (c. 360–327 BC) came from Olynthus in northern Greece and was a great-nephew of Aristotle, with whom he compiled a list of victors in the Pythian Games; an inscription at Delphi records the honours they received for it. He wrote a history of Greece and joined Alexander's expedition in 334 BC as its official historian.

His *Deeds of Alexander*, sent back to Greece in instalments, glorified the king: he described the sea off Pamphylia bowing before him, and supported the claim that the oracle of Ammon at Siwa had called Alexander son of Zeus. The work is lost but was used by later historians.

In 327 BC, in Bactria, Alexander tried to introduce *proskynesis*, the Persian custom of bowing down before the king, at his court. Callisthenes refused, arguing that such honour belonged to the gods, and the attempt was dropped. Soon after, some royal pages plotted to kill the king. Callisthenes had been their tutor and was accused of encouraging them. Accounts of his end differ: Ptolemy said he was tortured and hanged; others said he died of illness in captivity. His death embittered Aristotle's school against Alexander.

name: Eumenes of Cardia

claims.text: Eumenes, a Greek from Cardia, served as royal secretary to Philip II and Alexander.
He defeated and killed Craterus in Asia Minor in 321 or 320 BC.
In 316 BC he was handed over to Antigonus by the Silver Shields, who wanted their captured baggage back, and was executed.

summary: The Greek secretary of Philip and Alexander who became one of the ablest generals of the wars of the Successors, loyal to Alexander's family to the end.
significance: The one Successor who fought for the royal house rather than for himself; as a Greek, he could never command Macedonians as an equal.
body:
Eumenes (c. 362–316 BC) came from Cardia, a Greek city on the Thracian Chersonese. He served as chief secretary to Philip II and then to Alexander, keeping the royal journals, and late in the campaign was given a cavalry command.

At the settlement after Alexander's death in 323 he received Cappadocia and Paphlagonia, still unconquered. He supported Perdiccas, and in 321 or 320 BC defeated and killed the popular Macedonian general Craterus in Asia Minor. After Perdiccas' murder, the other generals condemned Eumenes to death.

For the next four years he fought Antigonus, the strongest of the Successors, in the name of the kings Philip III and Alexander IV and of Olympias. He held out under siege at Nora, then took command of the Silver Shields, Alexander's veteran infantry, in the east. To keep their loyalty he claimed that Alexander's spirit presided over his councils, held before an empty throne. In 317 and 316 he fought two great battles against Antigonus in Iran, at Paraetacene and Gabiene. After Gabiene, the Silver Shields, whose families and baggage had been captured, handed Eumenes over to Antigonus in exchange for them, and he was put to death.

name: Ptolemy II Philadelphus

claims.text: Ptolemy II ruled Egypt from 283/282 BC, after a period as co-regent with his father from 285, until his death in 246 BC.
He married his full sister Arsinoe II, following Egyptian royal practice.
Tradition credits him with commissioning the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Jewish Law.

summary: The second Ptolemaic king of Egypt (283–246 BC), under whom Alexandria became the cultural capital of the Greek world.
significance: The great patron of the Library and Museum of Alexandria, and the ruler who made the Ptolemaic monarchy a fusion of Greek and Egyptian kingship.
body:
Ptolemy II (309–246 BC) was born on the island of Kos, the son of Ptolemy I and Berenice I. His father made him co-regent in 285 BC, and he ruled alone from 283/282 until 246.

His reign was the height of Ptolemaic power and splendour. He expanded the Museum and Library founded by his father, bringing scholars and poets such as Callimachus and Theocritus to Alexandria; Theocritus' seventeenth *Idyll* is a poem in his praise. The great lighthouse on Pharos was completed early in his reign. According to the *Letter of Aristeas*, a later and partly legendary text, he commissioned the translation of the Jewish Law into Greek, the Septuagint. The Egyptian priest Manetho wrote a history of Egypt in Greek in this period.

Around 279–273 BC he married his full sister Arsinoe II, earning the title *Philadelphos*, "sibling-loving". He made his dead parents into gods, and later Arsinoe and himself, founding a royal cult. He staged a vast procession at Alexandria, described by a contemporary, with gold, exotic animals and huge floats.

He fought two wars with the Seleucids over Syria and backed Athens and Sparta against Macedon in the Chremonidean War, extending Ptolemaic control across the eastern Mediterranean.

name: Arsinoe II

claims.text: Arsinoe II was married in turn to Lysimachus, to her half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos, and to her full brother Ptolemy II.
She was deified and worshipped as Philadelphos in Egypt after her death.
Her death is usually dated to 270 BC, though 268 BC has also been argued.

summary: The Ptolemaic princess who was queen of Thrace and Macedon and then of Egypt, and was worshipped as a goddess after her death around 270 BC.
significance: The first Ptolemaic queen to be deified in her own name, and the model for later powerful queens down to Cleopatra VII.
body:
Arsinoe II (c. 316–270 BC) was the daughter of Ptolemy I and Berenice I. Around 300 BC, aged about sixteen, she was married to the elderly Lysimachus, king of Thrace, as part of an alliance. She had three sons by him and was accused of plotting the death of his heir Agathocles. She built a large round hall, the Arsinoeion, at the sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace.

After Lysimachus died at Corupedium in 281, she married her half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos, who had seized Macedon; he then murdered two of her sons. She fled to Egypt, and around 279–273 married her full brother Ptolemy II. The marriage shocked Greeks but followed the practice of the pharaohs. Ancient and modern writers have debated how much power she had at court; she appears beside her brother on coins and inscriptions.

After her death, usually dated to July 270 BC, Ptolemy II made her a goddess. Her cult spread across Egypt, a statue of her was placed in every Egyptian temple, and a district of the Fayum and many towns around the Mediterranean were named Arsinoe after her. Callimachus wrote a poem on her death and deification.

name: Antigonus II Gonatas

claims.text: Antigonus Gonatas defeated an army of Gauls near Lysimachia in 277 BC and became king of Macedon.
He won the Chremonidean War against Athens and Sparta, taking Athens in 262/261 BC.
He was a pupil and friend of Zeno, founder of Stoicism.

summary: The king of Macedon from 277 to 239 BC who established the Antigonid dynasty firmly on the Macedonian throne.
significance: Restored Macedon after the Gallic invasion and made it, for a century, one of the three great Hellenistic kingdoms.
body:
Antigonus II (c. 319–239 BC) was the son of Demetrius Poliorcetes and grandson of Antigonus the One-Eyed. His nickname Gonatas is of uncertain meaning. When his father was captured by Seleucus in 285, he held on to a few Greek cities, including Corinth and Demetrias, but not Macedon.

In 279 BC Gauls invaded Macedon and Greece, killing the king Ptolemy Keraunos and plundering the country. In 277 Antigonus defeated a Gallic army near Lysimachia in Thrace, and on the strength of this victory became king of Macedon. He was briefly driven out by Pyrrhus in 274–272 but recovered his throne.

From his capital at Pella he controlled Greece through garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis and the Piraeus. In the Chremonidean War (c. 267–261) he defeated an alliance of Athens and Sparta backed by Ptolemy II and took Athens. In 243 Aratus of Sicyon seized the Acrocorinth from his garrison.

Antigonus had studied philosophy in Athens and admired Zeno the Stoic, whom he invited to his court; he invited poets such as Aratus of Soli, author of the *Phaenomena*. He is said to have called kingship "noble servitude". He died in 239 BC aged about eighty.

name: Attalus I Soter

claims.text: Attalus I took the title of king after defeating the Galatians around 238 BC.
The Dying Gaul is generally thought to be a Roman copy of a bronze from his victory monuments at Pergamon.
He allied with Rome against Philip V of Macedon.

summary: The ruler of Pergamon from 241 to 197 BC who defeated the Galatians, took the title of king and made Pergamon Rome's ally in the east.
significance: Founder of the Attalid kingdom, whose victory monuments created one of the most famous styles of Hellenistic sculpture.
body:
Attalus I (269–197 BC) inherited the small principality of Pergamon in north-western Asia Minor in 241 BC. The Galatians — Celtic tribes who had crossed into Asia Minor in 278 — were extorting tribute from the Greek cities. Attalus refused to pay, and around 238 defeated them near the sources of the river Caicus. After the victory he took the title of king and the name Soter, "saviour".

He celebrated his victories over the Galatians and the Seleucids with bronze monuments on the acropolis of Pergamon. Marble copies made for the Romans, including the Dying Gaul in the Capitoline Museums and the Gaul killing himself and his wife in Palazzo Altemps, are generally thought to reproduce figures from them, showing the defeated enemy with dignity and pathos.

Attalus saw Philip V of Macedon as the main threat and became one of Rome's first allies in the Greek east, fighting beside Rome in the First and Second Macedonian Wars. In 205/204 BC he helped Rome bring the sacred black stone of the Great Mother, Cybele, from Asia Minor to Rome. He collapsed while addressing a meeting at Thebes in 197 and died soon after. His son Eumenes II succeeded him.

name: Eumenes II Soter

claims.text: Eumenes II fought with Rome against Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC and received much of Asia Minor at the Peace of Apamea in 188 BC.
The Great Altar of Pergamon is usually dated to his reign.
Pliny, citing Varro, says parchment was developed at Pergamon when Egypt cut off papyrus exports.

summary: The king of Pergamon from 197 to 159 BC who, as Rome's ally, made Pergamon a great power and a rival of Alexandria in culture.
significance: The king under whom Pergamon reached its height, with the Great Altar and a library second only to Alexandria's.
body:
Eumenes II succeeded his father Attalus I in 197 BC and continued his alliance with Rome. When the Seleucid king Antiochus III invaded Greece, Eumenes fought with the Romans, and his cavalry played a key part in their victory at Magnesia in 190 BC. At the Peace of Apamea in 188, Rome rewarded him with most of Seleucid Asia Minor, making Pergamon one of the largest kingdoms of the Greek world.

He spent his wealth on his capital. The upper city was rebuilt with terraces, a theatre built into the steep hillside, and a library said to have held 200,000 scrolls; Pliny, citing Varro, tells a doubtful story that Egypt banned the export of papyrus to stop it rivalling Alexandria, and that Pergamon then developed parchment (Latin *pergamena*). The Great Altar, with its frieze of gods fighting giants, is usually dated to his reign, perhaps in celebration of victories over the Galatians.

In 172 BC he travelled to Rome to denounce Perseus of Macedon, leading to the Third Macedonian War; on his way back he was injured at Delphi by rocks rolled down on him, an attack blamed on Perseus. Rome later grew suspicious of him and he lost favour. He died in 159 or 158 BC.

name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes

claims.text: Antiochus IV ruled the Seleucid empire from 175 to 164 BC.
In 168 BC a Roman envoy forced him to withdraw from Egypt by drawing a circle around him in the sand.
His ban on Jewish religious practice and rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem provoked the Maccabean revolt.

summary: The Seleucid king (175–164 BC) who invaded Egypt, was turned back by Rome, and provoked the Maccabean revolt in Judaea.
significance: Remembered in Jewish tradition as the archetypal persecutor; the revolt he provoked is commemorated in the festival of Hanukkah.
body:
Antiochus IV (c. 215–164 BC) was a son of Antiochus III. After his father's defeat by Rome he spent about fourteen years as a hostage in Rome, then lived in Athens, and in 175 BC seized the Seleucid throne. He took the title *Epiphanes*, "god made manifest"; critics punned it into *Epimanes*, "madman".

In 170–168 BC he invaded Ptolemaic Egypt and was about to take Alexandria when a Roman envoy, Gaius Popillius Laenas, met him outside the city and handed him a decree of the Senate ordering him to leave. When Antiochus asked for time to consider, Popillius drew a circle around him in the sand and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus withdrew.

In Judaea, a conflict between rival high priests and between Hellenising and traditional Jews led him to intervene. In 167 BC he banned Jewish religious practices and rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem to Zeus Olympios. This provoked the revolt of the Maccabees, who recaptured and purified the Temple in 164.

Antiochus was a lavish patron of Greek culture. He staged a great festival at Daphne near Antioch and paid for the resumption of work on the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens. He died on campaign in Iran in 164 BC.

name: Bacchylides

milestones.text: Papyrus rolls with his poems bought in Egypt for the British Museum
First edition of the recovered poems by Frederic Kenyon

claims.text: Bacchylides was the nephew of Simonides and came from the island of Ceos.
He wrote victory odes for Hiero I of Syracuse, including one for his Olympic chariot victory of 468 BC.
His poems were almost entirely lost until a papyrus acquired by the British Museum was published in 1897.

summary: The lyric poet from Ceos, rival of Pindar, whose victory odes and dithyrambs were rediscovered on papyrus in 1896.
significance: One of the nine canonical Greek lyric poets, recovered almost entire from the sands of Egypt.
body:
Bacchylides (c. 518–451 BC) was born at Ioulis on the island of Ceos, the nephew of the poet Simonides. Like his uncle and his rival Pindar, he wrote choral songs for paying patrons: victory odes (*epinikia*) for winners at the great games, and dithyrambs and other songs for festivals.

His most important patron was Hiero I of Syracuse. Bacchylides wrote odes for Hiero's horse-race win at Olympia in 476 BC (the same victory celebrated in Pindar's First Olympian), his chariot win at Delphi in 470, and his Olympic chariot victory of 468, which Pindar did not celebrate. His Fifth Ode tells how Heracles met the ghost of Meleager in the underworld. Ancient critics judged him smooth and elegant but less sublime than Pindar.

For centuries his work was known only from scattered quotations. In 1896 the British Museum bought papyrus fragments found in Egypt, and in 1897 Frederic Kenyon published about twenty poems — fourteen victory odes and six dithyrambs. They include Ode 17, in which the young Theseus dives into the sea to prove he is the son of Poseidon, and Ode 18, a dialogue between the king of Athens and a chorus about the approach of Theseus.

name: Theocritus

claims.text: Theocritus is regarded as the inventor of pastoral (bucolic) poetry.
His Idyll 17 praises Ptolemy II and Idyll 16 appeals to Hiero II of Syracuse for patronage.
Virgil's Eclogues are modelled on his pastoral poems.

summary: The Hellenistic poet from Syracuse, active around 270 BC, who invented pastoral poetry.
significance: The founder of the pastoral tradition, from Virgil's Eclogues to Renaissance and modern poetry of the countryside.
body:
Theocritus came from Syracuse and was active in the first half of the 3rd century BC. He seems to have spent time on the island of Kos and at Alexandria. Two of his poems are bids for royal patronage: *Idyll* 16 appeals, apparently without success, to Hiero II of Syracuse, while *Idyll* 17 is a poem of praise for Ptolemy II.

About thirty poems are attributed to him, called *Idylls* ("little pieces"), though some are not his. The most famous are the bucolic poems, set among the herdsmen of Sicily and southern Italy. Shepherds and goatherds compete in songs, mourn the dead herdsman Daphnis, or suffer unrequited love; the Cyclops Polyphemus woos the sea-nymph Galatea. Written in a literary Doric dialect and in the hexameter verse of epic, they combine scholarly refinement with rustic detail, and invented a new kind of poetry: the pastoral.

Other poems are scenes of city life, such as *Idyll* 15, in which two Syracusan housewives in Alexandria push through the crowds to see the festival of Adonis in the royal palace, or the story of a woman who uses magic to win back her lover (*Idyll* 2). The Roman poet Virgil modelled his *Eclogues* on Theocritus.

name: Apollonius of Rhodes

claims.text: Apollonius wrote the Argonautica, an epic in four books on the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts.
A papyrus list of librarians from Oxyrhynchus names him as head of the Library of Alexandria.
The story of a bitter quarrel with Callimachus is probably a later invention.

summary: The Alexandrian scholar-poet of the 3rd century BC, head of the Library, who wrote the Argonautica, the epic of Jason and Medea.
significance: Author of the only full Greek epic to survive between Homer and the Roman period, and a major influence on Virgil.
body:
Apollonius (c. 295–215 BC) was probably born in Alexandria; he was called "of Rhodes" because he later lived on that island. Ancient biographies say he was a pupil of Callimachus, and a list of librarians on a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus confirms that he was head of the Library of Alexandria, succeeding Zenodotus, probably in the reign of Ptolemy II, and tutor to the future Ptolemy III. Later stories of a fierce quarrel with Callimachus, and of his retreat to Rhodes after his poem was poorly received, are probably invented.

His *Argonautica*, in four books, tells the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts to Colchis at the eastern end of the Black Sea to win the Golden Fleece, and their long journey home. Apollonius wrote in Homer's language and metre but in a new spirit: his Jason is an uncertain, unheroic leader, and the centre of the poem is the young Colchian princess Medea, whose love for Jason is described with deep psychological insight. The poem is also full of learned detail on geography, the origins of cults and place-names.

The Roman poet Virgil drew on it closely for the *Aeneid*, modelling Dido's passion for Aeneas on Medea's for Jason.
